Used for: natural intake with no weir in old times, temporary seasonal weirs, half-river closures; weir materials (timber frames packed with stone, gabions, brushwood); the oblique weir; the Tatai weir of 1183 rebuilt each irrigation season; the Ishi-ibi of 1615 returning its surplus to the main river; the intake on the concave bank of a bend; the 1902 rule to place the head works where the river leaves the mountains

maff-toshuko-sand-basin

MAFF (Japan, Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries), land-improvement design standard, technical appendix on head works (土地改良事業計画設計基準 設計 頭首工 付録技術書), chapter 20, the general design of settling basins (https://www.maff.go.jp/j/nousin/attach/pdf/tousyukou-79.pdf)

What it is: The chapter on the general design of settling basins from the same technical appendix to the Ministry of Agriculture's head-works design standard: where the basin that drops a canal's sand stands relative to the intake mouth, and how its transitions are shaped.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the settling basin - immediately after the intake mouth, at the start of the canal - which tells us what the first stretch of a head race is for. Its limits are that it is modern design guidance with no historical content, that its shapes and angles belong to concrete works, and that it gives no distance from the intake to anything, so the length of a head race rests on nothing here.

Used for: the settling basin at the canal's start, immediately following the intake mouth

jsidre-miwa-2023

三輪弌 (Hajime Miwa), "Taking water from rivers on the principles of how rivers flow" (川の流れの原理に基づく河川取水), JSIDRE special lecture slides, 2023 (https://www.jsidre.or.jp/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/ouyouR5_tokubetsukoen.pdf)

What it is: The slides of a special lecture by Hajime Miwa to the Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering on taking water from rivers according to how rivers flow: the intake forms (natural intake on the bank the current follows, a fixed weir, a combined weir, a fully movable weir), why a weir is needed when the river falls, and the old oblique weir that ran diagonally upstream from the intake mouth to dam a shallow riffle.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the rule for where a canal leaves a stream - on the bank along which the current's deep line runs - and describes the historical oblique weir starting at the intake mouth, which is the form our weir glyph takes. Its limits are that it is a lecture rather than a paper, that its subject is rivers rather than brooks (the Tama, the Kizu, the Tone, the Chikugo) and its interest modern intake failure, and that its one worked old case is a river weir, the Yamada weir on the Chikugo.

Used for: natural intake on the bank the current follows; the weir as what keeps the intake level when the river falls; the old oblique weir extended diagonally upstream from the intake mouth to dam the riffle

shimane-toshuko-lecture

Shimane University, rural-engineering lecture notes on irrigation facilities, chapter 3, head works (頭首工) (https://zoukou.life.shimane-u.ac.jp/ruraleng/shisetsuken/12kougisiryou/15.pdf)

What it is: A printed textbook chapter on the head works, hosted as course material by Shimane University's rural engineering program: their parts, a line on their history (small timber-and-stone works up to the end of the Sengoku period), the rule of one-bank against two-bank intake, where the intake mouth is set, and the intake court between the mouth and the canal.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states two rules a map needs plainly - the intake is on one bank, the side of the land it serves, on every kind of river from torrent to gentle, and it stands where the current's deep line touches that bank - and it dates the small timber-crib form to the period before the early modern age. Its limits are that it is teaching material for modern design, its velocities and depths belong to concrete works, and it gives no distance from the intake to the first division.

Used for: intake works up to the end of the Sengoku period as small timber frames packed with stone; one-bank intake on the benefited side, the rule on torrent, steep and gentle rivers; the intake where the current touches the bank; the intake court between mouth and canal

maff-nogyoyosui-suiden

MAFF (Japan, Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries), land-improvement planning standard, technical volume on agricultural water for paddy (土地改良事業計画設計基準 計画 農業用水 水田 技術書, the new-old comparison table), section 1.1 on Edo-period paddy and water development and section 7.3 on separating irrigation from drainage (https://www.maff.go.jp/j/nousin/noukan/tyotei/kizyun/attach/pdf/nougyouyousui_suiden-1.pdf)

What it is: The technical volume of the Japanese Ministry of Agriculture's planning standard for paddy irrigation water, in its published old-against-new comparison form. Its opening history describes Edo-period development - in a drought every drop of a mountain catchment's runoff and every district's return flow was taken up downstream - and its figure of irrigation types names the three layouts: field to field, one combined channel for supply and drainage, and separate supply and drainage channels, the last the standard of postwar field consolidation.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the ministry's own account of how paddy water was used before modern works, and it is the source for two things on our maps: that a village's drainage went on to be used again downstream rather than being wasted, and that a separate drainage channel is the modern layout while the older ones ran drainage field to field or back into a shared channel. Its limits are that it is a planning standard whose history is a preface; that the page linked is an amendment's comparison table, in which every unamended passage is elided, so a reader following the link finds fragments of the standard rather than the whole; that its Edo passage is about the whole basin in drought rather than one brook; and that it gives the separated layout a modern date without dating the older ones.

Used for: in an Edo drought all mountain runoff and all return flow taken up basin-wide; the three irrigation layouts (field to field, combined, separated); separation as the field-consolidation standard; separation raising the water requirement because return flow is no longer reused

jawiki-yosuiro

ja.wikipedia 用水路 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/用水路)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the yosuiro, the supply channel: a channel built to draw water for irrigation, drinking or industry, taking its water by a weir, dam, wheel or pump or by natural inflow, and distinguished from a channel whose purpose is drainage alone.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the plain distinction between a channel that brings water and one that takes it away, which is the distinction the map's two ditch classes draw. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary with no history of when the two were separated and nothing on where drainage went, so those rest on other sources; and that the page itself says a supply channel today often carries rainwater and household waste water too, so the clean two-way split is the older form rather than the present one.

Used for: the supply channel defined, and set apart from a channel for drainage alone

asaza-yatsuda

NPO Asaza Fund, "The water cycle of the yatsuda" (谷津田の水の循環), a public education page (https://www.asaza.jp/activity/yatsuda2/)

What it is: A page from a Japanese conservation group working on the Lake Kasumigaura catchment, explaining for a general reader how a valley-head paddy is watered: rain stored in the upland woods seeps out as springs, a pond is made where the water issues, the paddies lie below it, and the used water runs on to the river and the lake.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the small valley paddy's water from source to river in one page, and it is the one source read that says in so many words that the water, once used, goes on to the river. Its limits are that it is a present-day outreach page, not scholarship, describing one region's valley paddies, and that it says nothing about a stream running beside the paddies, so it neither confirms nor denies a brook surviving its intake.

Used for: the spring impounded where it issues, the paddies below, the used water flowing on to the river

fao-irrigation-manual-m7

FAO, Irrigation Manual (planning, development, monitoring and evaluation of irrigated agriculture with farmer participation), Module 7, chapter 6 "Hydraulic structures" (https://www.fao.org/4/ai596e/ai596e03.pdf)

What it is: A chapter of the FAO's irrigation manual for small schemes in southern and eastern Africa, on hydraulic structures: what a head work is and its parts (a side offtake, a regulating structure across the river or part of it, a sediment flushing arrangement), when a river can be tapped without a weir and when a temporary or permanent weir is needed, where to place the offtake and at what angle, and how an intake takes the cleaner upper flow and returns the sediment-laden lower flow to the river.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the physics of the intake in plain English at the scale of a small gravity scheme built with local labor - gabion and masonry weirs - which is the scale of a hamlet's field, and it is the clearest statement read that the river continues below the works. Its limits are that it is modern engineering guidance for a different continent, so we take from it the mechanics that do not depend on period or place - the weir raising the level, the surplus passing over, the offtake on the outside of a bend - and never a number for what a premodern village built.

Used for: the parts of a head work; run-of-river offtake without a weir when the level suffices, a temporary or permanent weir when it does not; the intake taking the upper part of the flow and disposing of the lower part down the river; the offtake in a straight reach or on the outside of a bend, at an angle when silt-free and at a right angle when silt-laden

fao-water-sources-u5835e

FAO irrigation training manual "Scheme Irrigation Water Need and Supply", chapter 2 "Water sources and water availability", section 2.2.2 on tapping water from rivers (https://www.fao.org/4/u5835e/u5835e03.htm)

What it is: The chapter on water sources of an FAO training manual for irrigation scheme planning: how a river's level rises and falls over the year, why a weir across the river steadies the level upstream of it so a canal can take water in the dry season, that the excess flows over the weir when the river is high, and how a control gate at the intake keeps the canal's discharge even.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states in the plainest words read what a diversion weir does and what becomes of the water it does not take - it goes over the crest and on down the river - which is the fact our maps rest on when the brook runs on past the intake. Its limits are that it is modern training material for scheme planners anywhere in the world, so it is used for the mechanics of a weir and not for what any premodern village built.

Used for: a weir steadies the upstream level; water flows over the weir in high discharge; a control gate at the intake

icid-diversion-weirs

International Commission on Irrigation and Drainage, technical term list, "Diversion Weirs" (https://icid-ciid.org/Knowledge/basic_term/0/Diversion%20Weirs/2247)

What it is: The entry for "diversion weir" in the ICID's list of basic irrigation and drainage terms: a low dam or wall across a stream for diverting part or all of its water into a canal.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the profession's own definition, and it settles one point the record was otherwise silent on: that taking all of a stream's water is within the ordinary meaning of a diversion weir. Its limits are that it is a one-line definition with no case, no condition and no period, so it establishes that whole diversion is a possibility and nothing about whether a village ever did it.

Used for: a diversion weir diverts "part or all" of a stream's water

zhwiki-dujiangyan

zh.wikipedia 都江堰 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/都江堰)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on Dujiangyan, the irrigation works built across the Min River in 256 BC: the fish-mouth divide that splits the river into an outer channel for floods and an inner channel for irrigation in proportions that shift with the season, the spillway that returns the surplus and the sand to the outer river, and the bottle-neck opening that limits what the inner river takes.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the best-known premodern Chinese case of a river divided rather than taken, with the split stated in numbers, and it grounds the rule that the parent stream keeps flowing below an intake. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary, that Dujiangyan is a river-scale state work and not a village brook, and that its weirless form is exceptional rather than typical.

Used for: the Min divided into outer (flood) and inner (irrigation) rivers, four to six in spring and six to four in flood; the spillway returning surplus and sand to the outer river; a weirless diversion

zhwiki-lingqu

zh.wikipedia 灵渠 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-cn/灵渠)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Lingqu canal of 214 BC in Guangxi: the plowshare-snout that divides the Xiang River so that seven parts return to the Xiang over the Great Balance and three pass by the Little Balance into the canal, the two balances being overflow crests that let floods spill back into the old river bed.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a second premodern division of a river in stated proportions, with the barrier an overflow crest rather than a closure, corroborating the rule that the stream continues below a diversion. Its limits are the same as Dujiangyan's: a tertiary summary of a river-scale state work, not a village brook.

Used for: the Xiang divided seven to the river and three to the canal; the balances as overflow crests spilling floods into the old bed

zhwiki-zhengguoqu

zh.wikipedia 郑国渠 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/郑国渠)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Zhengguo canal of 246 BC in Shaanxi: its head set where the Jing River leaves the northern hills, and the three scholarly views of what its head works were - a large earth-and-stone dam, stone-filled crib baskets or a low weir raising the level, or no dam at all and a weirless diversion using the river bend.

Why it applies, and its limits: It shows that the two intake forms our maps roll between - a low weir of stone-filled cribs, or a bare intake off a river bend - are both readings of the same ancient work, and it places the head where the river leaves the hills, as the Japanese rule does. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary, that the form is expressly disputed, and that the work is a great state canal rather than a village ditch.

Used for: the canal head where the river issues from the hills; the disputed head-works form - dam, stone-filled cribs or low weir, or weirless diversion off the bend

wangzhen-nongshu-18

王禎 (Wang Zhen), 《農書》 卷十八 農器圖譜十三 灌溉門 (Yuan dynasty, 1313), Wikisource text (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/王禎農書/卷十八)

What it is: The irrigation chapter of Wang Zhen's Treatise on Agriculture of 1313, an illustrated catalog of farm implements and works: entries on the water palisade (a row of timbers set across a brook upstream of high-lying fields so that the water issues sideways and runs down to them), the water gate, and the pond-and-weir pair, each with its rationale.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a primary premodern Chinese source, and its water palisade is the one description read of the village-scale case our maps draw - a small brook, a timber barrier placed upstream of the fields, the water turned out of the channel to reach them. Its limits are that it is a prescriptive illustrated manual - what a farmer ought to build, with idealized pictures - and not a survey of what villages had; that it gives no dimensions and does not say what share of the brook is left in its channel; that it is a Yuan compendium of practice across China rather than a record of one place; and that what we read is a Wikisource transcription of a later imperial edition, rendered into English by this project.

Used for: the water palisade - timbers set across a brook upstream of high fields, turning the water out sideways to run down to them; the water gate of coursed stone and stacked timber; the pond-and-weir pair

yamen-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Yamen (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamen)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the yamen, the office and residence compound of a Chinese official: its typical parts - gate, courtyard, hall of judgment, offices, cells and stores - and the residence of the official and his family within it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states plainly that the official lived inside the compound he worked in, which is why the Chinese seat on our maps has no separate magistrate's house. It is a tertiary summary, and the sentence we rest on sits in a section the article itself marks as citing no sources, so it carries the discount of any uncited encyclopedia line; the Columbia teaching page beside it corroborates the rotation and avoidance rules that made the official an outsider, not the residence itself.

Used for: the official's residence inside the yamen

columbia-qing-state

Asia for Educators, Columbia University, "The Grandeur of the Qing" - the Qing state (https://afe.easia.columbia.edu/qing/state.html)

What it is: A university teaching page from Columbia's Asia for Educators program, written with the Qing historian Madeleine Zelin as consultant, describing the Qing state: the examination-recruited bureaucracy, the rule that an official never served in or beside his home province, and the short three-year postings after which he rotated on.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the rotation and avoidance rules that made the Chinese local official a short-term outsider living in the yamen, the institutional fact behind the Chinese seat's form on our maps. Its limit is that it is a teaching summary for schools, not the administrative statutes.

Used for: three-year postings and the rule of avoidance for Qing officials

baidu-yangzhou-city-site

Baidu Baike (English edition), Yangzhou City Site (https://baike.baidu.com/en/item/Yangzhou%20City%20Site/934310)

What it is: The English edition of Baidu Baike's entry on the Yangzhou city site, the archaeological remains of the Tang city: a zicheng of offices on the old Sui palace ground and a luocheng below Shu hill holding the commercial, craft and residential quarters, enlarged in the mid Tang.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the two-ring form of a Tang prefectural city and which ring held what, the case our capital's citadel-and-town pairing is drawn from. Its limits are serious and stated: Baidu Baike is an open-edit encyclopedia and its English edition a machine rendering of the Chinese, so it is cited only for a statement the scholarly literature makes too, and the monograph that makes it, Heng Chye Kiang's Cities of Aristocrats and Bureaucrats, is in print only.

Used for: Tang Yangzhou's zicheng of offices and luocheng of commerce and housing

lifang-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 里坊制 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%87%8C%E5%9D%8A%E5%88%B6)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the lifang system, the walled and gated residential wards of the Chinese city from the Han to the Tang: how the wards were closed at night, how the Song did away with the wards, the markets and the curfew together, and that the system did not return after the Song and Yuan.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the end of the walled ward, which is why the Chinese half of our block-gate argument turns on palings across streets rather than ward walls. It is a tertiary summary used for the dating, with the essayist Wu Gou's account of the same change beside it.

Used for: the Song's abolition of the walled ward and the night curfew, and the system's disappearance after the Song and Yuan

wugou-lifang-rujia

吴钩, 1000年前的小区围墙是怎样被推倒的, 儒家网 (https://www.rujiazg.com/article/7581)

What it is: An essay of 2016-02-24 by Wu Gou, a published writer on Song history, on the Confucian-studies portal 儒家网, tracing how the walled wards of the Tang city broke down and the ward walls came down in the Song, with the officials who argued over it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the Song end of the ward wall in a historian's narrative beside the encyclopedia summary. Its limits are that it is a popular essay whose author writes to a thesis about the openness of Song cities, and that it names the period texts it reads in its prose without footnotes, so it cannot be checked passage by passage.

Used for: the ward walls torn down by the Song

kurayashiki-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 蔵屋敷 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%94%B5%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kurayashiki, the warehouse compounds the domains kept in Osaka and other cities to store and sell the tax rice and produce shipped in from their territories, with the counts of such compounds at Osaka in the 1670s and the 1840s.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the concentration of the domains' rice trade at Osaka with two counts, which is the attested fact behind our capital's wharf-side granary district. It is a tertiary summary used for those counts only; the article carries a notice that it lacks sufficient sources and states the counts as what is said to have been, uncited - the discount that matters most where two numbers are taken - and it says nothing about how much of any domain's rice went there.

Used for: eighty domain kurayashiki at Osaka in the 1670s and 125 in the 1840s

mizu-no-bunka-mokuhi

ミツカン 水の文化センター (Mizkan Water Culture Center), 木で作られた水道管 ～江戸時代のインフラを支えた上水道のかたち～, seminar report, 2022-12-26 (https://www.mizu.gr.jp/news/221226_report.html)

What it is: A report of a public seminar held in 2022 by the Mizkan Water Culture Center, a corporate foundation for the study of water in Japanese life, with speakers from the Tokyo Waterworks Historical Museum and the Tokyo Metropolitan Archaeological Center, on the wooden water mains of Edo: how the pipes were made and laid, and the lengths of open channel and buried conduit of the Kanda and Tamagawa systems, which it takes from the Meiji-era survey 東京通志.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the two systems' conduit lengths separately, which is what shows that a figure often quoted for Edo belongs to the Kanda system alone; our drawn capital's buried mains are sized from the pair. Its limits are that it is a seminar report rather than the survey it cites, that the Meiji survey it rests on measured the systems at the end of their life, and that Edo was the largest city in the country, so its conduit lengths are an upper bound no provincial capital approaches.

Used for: the Kanda system's 67 km and the Tamagawa's 84.7 km of stone and wooden conduit

ktjplus-josui-ido

上下水道情報plus, 連載水道の話いろいろ(7) 江戸明治の上水 (https://ktjplus.jp/org/masukosuidou01/masukosuidou07/)

What it is: An installment, dated 2024-10-25, of a serialized column on the history of Japanese water supply by Masuko Atsushi, a former head of the Tokyo Waterworks Bureau, published on a water-industry information site, covering the Edo and Meiji water systems and giving a count of the draw-wells that the Edo aqueducts fed across the city.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one readable page that gives a city-wide count of aqueduct wells, which shows that a smaller figure often quoted belongs to one system alone. Its author ran the successor utility, which is more authority than a trade column usually carries; its limits are that it is a column without its own citations, and that its count spans Edo and early Tokyo together.

Used for: the 8,000 aqueduct wells across Edo-Tokyo

nippon-com-suidobashi

Nippon.com, "Carp Over the Kanda River: 'Suidō Bridge and Surugadai'" (guide to Japan) (https://www.nippon.com/en/guide-to-japan/gu004006/)

What it is: A feature of 2018-05-01 on Nippon.com, the Nippon Communications Foundation's public-interest site, pairing Hiroshige's print of Suidō Bridge and Surugadai from his One Hundred Famous Views of Edo with the place today, and explaining the bridge's name from the wooden water pipe it once carried.

Why it applies, and its limits: It ties the name of a real Edo bridge to the aqueduct that crossed at it and confirms which waterway the print shows, which is what our flume-bridge glyph and its caption rest on. Its limit is that it is a popular feature that says the name is said to derive from the pipe, not a documentary history of the bridge.

Used for: the name Suidōbashi from the conduit the bridge carried, and the Kanda Jōsui in Hiroshige's print of it

tamagawa-aqueduct-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Tamagawa Aqueduct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamagawa_Aqueduct)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Tamagawa Jōsui, the aqueduct dug in 1653 to 1654 to bring the Tama river's water 43 km into Edo: its route from Hamura to the Yotsuya gate, its open earth cut across the Musashino plateau, and the buried wooden and stone conduits that carried the water on under the city.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the length, the route and the two forms of the channel - open cut outside the city, buried pipe within - which is exactly the division our capital's water supply draws. It is a tertiary summary and is used only for facts its own references and the Edo-Tokyo Museum's exhibition page state as well.

Used for: the Tamagawa Jōsui's 43 km, its open earth cut from Hamura to the Yotsuya gate, and its buried conduits inside Edo

edo-tokyo-museum-tamagawa

Edo-Tokyo Museum, special exhibition page "Tamagawa Josui" (English) (https://www.edo-tokyo-museum.or.jp/en/s-exhibition/tamagawajosui/)

What it is: The Edo-Tokyo Museum's English page for its exhibition on the Tamagawa Jōsui: the aqueduct's branching from the Tama river at Hamura, its 43 km run, and the underground network of conduits that carried its water on from the Yotsuya gate to the city's households.

Why it applies, and its limits: A museum's own exhibition text for the aqueduct's length and the change from open channel to buried conduit at the city gate, corroborating the encyclopedia article cited beside it. Its limit is brevity: it is an exhibition summary, not a technical history.

Used for: the 43 km from Hamura and the underground conduits from the Yotsuya gate

worksinprogress-samurai-city

Samuel Hughes, "Samurai city", Works in Progress, 2026-06-02 (https://worksinprogress.co/issue/samurai-city/)

What it is: A long-form essay in the magazine Works in Progress on how Edo was governed and laid out: the walled daimyo estates of the High City, the gated commoner blocks and alleys of the Low City, and the night closing of the whole mesh of internal gates.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states in plain English two things the Japanese reference pages state separately - that each samurai estate was its own walled enclosure with one or two gates, and that the commoner city was cut up by thousands of gates that closed at night - and it gives the scale of the block system. Its limits are that it is a magazine essay rather than scholarship, written for a general reader, and that its estates are Edo's greatest, not a provincial castle town's.

Used for: the per-estate wall and gate of a samurai compound, and the night closing of Edo's internal gates

daqing-luli-yejin

《大清律例》兵律, article 夜禁 (the Great Qing Code, the night prohibition), Chinese Wikisource transcription (https://zh.wikisource.org/zh-hans/%E5%A4%A7%E6%B8%85%E5%BE%8B%E4%BE%8B/%E5%85%B5%E5%BE%8B)

What it is: The military-law chapter of the Great Qing Code, the penal code in force across Qing China, in a Wikisource transcription of the primary text; its night-prohibition article sets the hours of the curfew by the watch bells and the punishment for breaking it, in the capital and in the provinces.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the law itself, the best kind of source for what a curfew was and what it cost to break, and it applies directly to the Chinese half of the two-traditions argument our block gates rest on. Its limits are that a statute records the rule and not how often it was enforced, and that the hours are given in watches, which this page converts to clock time only roughly.

Used for: the curfew's hours by the watch bells and its penalties, graded between the capital and the provinces

visitbeijing-zhalan

Visit Beijing (Beijing Municipal Culture and Tourism Bureau), 《乾隆京城全图》展现清代治安管理思路 大栅栏是'封闭小区'的雏形 (https://www.visitbeijing.com.cn/article/47QkXx9caZ2)

What it is: A popular urban-history article by Zhang Tian, reprinted on 2020-07-21 from the Beijing Evening News on the Beijing municipal tourism bureau's portal, reading the Qianlong-era map of the capital for how the Qing kept order: the palings set across street and lane mouths from a Ming edict of 1488, their number in the inner city, the three soldiers at each, and the curfew behind them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the count and the manning of the palings, which is the Chinese half of the two-traditions argument our night gates rest on, and it dates the institution to the Ming. Its limits are that it is a newspaper feature on a tourism portal rather than the Qing statutes it summarizes, and that Beijing was the imperial capital and the most policed city in the empire, so its counts and manning are an upper bound a provincial town's night gates do not approach.

Used for: palings at the lane mouths from 1488, more than a thousand in the inner city, three soldiers at each, and the curfew

kotobank-kido

Kotobank, 木戸 - 改訂新版 世界大百科事典 (Heibonsha) and 山川 日本史小辞典 entries (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%9C%A8%E6%88%B8-51154)

What it is: The kotobank reference page for the kido, the wooden gate that closed an Edo street block at night, carrying side by side the entries of five Japanese reference works, of which two are quoted here: the Heibonsha World Encyclopedia, revised edition, and the Yamakawa Concise Dictionary of Japanese History.

Why it applies, and its limits: It says what the block gates were for and who paid for them, from standard reference works rather than a hobby page, and it gives the machi-kido's hours. Its limits are those of an encyclopedia: it summarizes without citing the ordinances it summarizes, and its hours for the town gate differ from another page this record cites, which the note at that sentence discloses.

Used for: the block gate's role in public order, its upkeep from the block's own levy, and its hours

mnwhstq-quanzhou-walls

闽南文化生态保护区 (Minnan Culture Ecological Protection Zone, Fujian), 府志里的泉州古城垣成长记 《泉州府志》城垣研究成果新近推出, 2026-04-17 (https://www.mnwhstq.com/whdt_347/202604/t20260417_220969.htm)

What it is: A news account on a Fujian provincial cultural-heritage portal of newly published research on the walls of Quanzhou, the prefectural seat of southern Fujian, drawn from the successive editions of the prefecture's own gazetteer, the 泉州府志: when each ring was built, how many gates each carried, and how the circuit grew to thirty li by 1352.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one readable page that states the nested rings of a Chinese prefectural seat in the gazetteer's own terms - the yacheng of the offices inside the zicheng inside the luocheng - which is the pattern our capital's walled citadel follows. Its limits are that it is a portal's summary of scholarship rather than the scholarship, and that it describes one city; Quanzhou was a great port and grew a fourth ring, so it is an upper case rather than a typical one.

Used for: the yacheng, zicheng, luocheng nesting of a prefectural seat, with the gate counts and the 1352 circuit

ming-neige-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 明朝内阁 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E6%98%8E%E6%9C%9D%E5%86%85%E9%98%81)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Ming Grand Secretariat, the body of grand secretaries who drafted the emperor's decisions: its origin, its standing, and where its offices stood inside the Forbidden City.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the emperor's secretariat inside the palace, which is the Chinese half of the rule this page draws - the ruler's council beside the ruler, the executive bureaus outside. A tertiary summary used for that placement, and it also warns that the body was never a first-rank organ of state.

Used for: the Grand Secretariat's offices east of the Meridian Gate, inside the palace

keep-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Keep (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the keep, the great tower of the European castle: its square and round forms, the vulnerability of a square tower's corners to mining and to the dead ground they create, and how little that weakness mattered before the siege engines and crossbows of the twelfth century.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the European comparison this page draws - the corner as the weak point of a curtain - and, read fully, it corrects the comparison by calling the weakness theoretical for most of the period. A tertiary summary, and about Europe rather than East Asia.

Used for: the theoretical weakness of a square tower's corners and the date after which it mattered

odawara-castle-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 小田原城 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B0%8F%E7%94%B0%E5%8E%9F%E5%9F%8E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Odawara Castle, the Hojo seat whose outer enclosure, the sogamae, took in the whole town within nine kilometers of rampart and dry moat running from Mount Hachiman to the sea.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the length and extent of the largest town enclosure of its age, the exemplar behind our capital's single rampart around the whole population. It is a tertiary summary used for those two facts, and the article carries a notice asking for its sources; the nine-kilometer sentence itself is uncited, which matters because a map is scaled against it.

Used for: the nine-kilometer sogamae from Mount Hachiman to the sea

kuruwa-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 曲輪 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9B%B2%E8%BC%AA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kuruwa, the baileys of a Japanese castle: what a bailey is, the names of the principal ones, and the classification of layouts by how the baileys are arranged - concentric, in a row along a ridge, backed against a natural obstacle, circular, spiral.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the standard layout taxonomy our castle's bailey arrangement is drawn from, and it says which forms follow the terrain. It is a tertiary summary used for the definitions, and it is also the page that shows one of those forms is circular, which keeps this record from calling them all angular.

Used for: the rinkaku, renkaku and teikaku layouts and the terrain the renkaku form follows

shirobito-615-ore

城びと (Shirobito), 第46回【構造】お城の塀や石垣はどうして折れ曲がっているの？ (https://shirobito.jp/article/615)

What it is: An explainer of 2018-12-10 by the Kamiyu History Editorial Department in the castle web magazine Shirobito's structure series on why Japanese castle walls and stone revetments are built with folds and projections: to bring flanking fire onto an attacker and to leave no blind angle.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the flanking logic behind the angular Japanese wall, which is why our castle's stone revetments are drawn in straight runs with hard corners rather than curves. Its limit is that it is a popular explainer rather than a survey of surviving plans.

Used for: folds and projections in a castle wall for flanking fire

chen-2016-song-yamen

陈凌 (Chen Ling), 建筑空间与礼制文化：宋代地方衙署建筑象征性功能诠释, 西南大学学报（社会科学版） 42(5): 182-187, September 2016 (https://xbgjxt.swu.edu.cn/data/article/preview-pdf?doi=10.13718/j.cnki.xdsk.2016.05.023)

What it is: A peer-reviewed article in the journal of Southwest University on the Song local yamen as a symbolic building: how its central axis and its front-hall, rear-residence layout expressed the ritual order of rank, from an author at Nanyang Normal University's college of humanities.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the axial and hierarchical plan of the Chinese local government compound from the architectural-history literature, which is why the yamen on our city maps is drawn axial and symmetrical. Its limits are period - the Song, some centuries before the Qing yamen that survive - and that it argues from ritual meaning rather than from surveyed plans.

Used for: the central axis and front-hall, rear-residence layout of a local yamen

bjd-qing-yamen

北京日报 (Beijing Daily), 清代各级地方官署旧址巡礼 (https://xinwen.bjd.com.cn/content/s68f22db6d5dee3918d4d209e.html)

What it is: A local-history feature by Wang Milin in the Beijing Daily of 2025-10-17, touring the surviving Qing local government compounds: the halls ranged along a central axis, the symmetry of the plan, and the courtyards and room counts of a surviving example.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the surviving Qing yamen's plan in plain terms, the courtyard-and-axis form our maps give the seat of government. Its limit is that it is a newspaper feature, not an architectural survey.

Used for: the axial, symmetrical courtyard plan of a Qing local yamen

kaogongji-wikisource

《周禮·冬官考工記》 (the Zhouli, Kaogongji chapter), Chinese Wikisource transcription (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%91%A8%E7%A6%AE/%E5%86%AC%E5%AE%98%E8%80%83%E5%B7%A5%E8%A8%98)

What it is: The artificers' chapter of the Rites of Zhou, the classical Chinese text that prescribes the ideal capital - nine li square, three gates a side, nine avenues each way, the court before the market - in a Wikisource transcription of the primary text.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the primary source for the square ideal every discussion of Chinese city plans starts from, quoted rather than paraphrased. Its limit is that it is an ideal, compiled long before the cities our maps are modeled on, and says nothing about how far real cities followed it - which is why the essay beside it is cited for the shape's actual cause.

Used for: the Kaogongji's square capital, its gates, its avenues and the court before the market

jining-museum-qiandao

济宁博物馆 (Jining Museum), 浙东运河古纤道 - - 秋水长堤 通古鉴今 (https://www.jiningmuseum.com/list/article_details.do?articleId=1932)

What it is: A feature article of 2018-11-09 from the Jining Museum, a municipal museum on the Grand Canal in Shandong, on the ancient towpath of the Eastern Zhejiang Canal at Shaoxing: its Tang origin under the commissioner Meng Jian in 815, and its two forms, along the bank and out in the water.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the towpath and describes its two forms from a canal museum's own account, which is what our river capital's hauling path is drawn from. Its limits are that it is a museum feature rather than the gazetteer it draws on, and that it gives no dimensions.

Used for: the 815 date and the towpath's two forms

zhedong-qiandao-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 浙东运河纤道 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E6%B5%99%E4%B8%9C%E8%BF%90%E6%B2%B3%E7%BA%A4%E9%81%93)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the towpath of the Eastern Zhejiang Canal at Shaoxing: its Tang reconstruction under Meng Jian in 815, its total length of nearly a hundred li, the 7.5 km protected stretch, and its two forms along the bank and out in the water.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the towpath's overall length and its forms, which set the scale and shape of the hauling path our river capital draws. A tertiary summary; it carries no dimensions of the deck, and its length and forms describe the towpath as it survives, whose fabric is later than the Tang institution.

Used for: the towpath's length and its two forms

shiue-2002

Carol H. Shiue, "Transport Costs and the Geography of Arbitrage in Eighteenth-Century China", American Economic Review 92(5): 1406-1419, December 2002 (author's copy) (https://spot.colorado.edu/~shiue/p1406_s.pdf)

What it is: A peer-reviewed economic-history paper using Qing archival grain-price lists to measure how far markets were integrated in eighteenth-century China, with a survey of what carriage cost by water and by land and how the major waterways connected the cities.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the size of the water-over-land cost advantage in premodern China from the scholarly literature, which is the ground for drawing a towpath and a wharf rather than a river road. Its limit is period and place: eighteenth-century China, with the figure taken from an earlier study the paper cites rather than measured afresh.

Used for: the nine- to tenfold cost advantage of junks over land carriage

kobayashi-2003-kasen-shuun

小林高英・苦瀬博仁・橋本一明, 江戸期の河川舟運における川舟の運航方法と河岸の立地に関する研究, 日本物流学会誌 11, May 2003 (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/logisticssociety1995/2003/11/2003_11_121/_pdf/-char/ja)

What it is: A peer-reviewed paper in the journal of the Japan Logistics Society on Edo-period river transport: how the river boats were worked, why bulk goods such as tribute rice went by water, and where the landings that served them stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states, from the logistics literature, that bulk went by river because boats carried more than the roads could, the Japanese half of the reason our river capital draws a wharf and a towpath. Its limit is that it is about how the boats and landings worked, not about whether roads followed rivers.

Used for: river boat transport carrying tribute rice in bulk to Edo

matsumura-1994-oigawa

松村博 (Hiroshi Matsumura), 大井川徒渉制を中心とする近世・東海道の渡河形態について, 土木史研究 14: 125-, June 1994 (refereed) (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/journalhs1990/14/0/14_0_125/_pdf/-char/ja)

What it is: A refereed civil-engineering-history paper on how the Tokaido crossed its rivers in the Edo period, centered on the Oi river, which travelers had to wade or be carried across because neither a bridge nor a ferry was allowed; it weighs the defensive, political, technical and economic explanations for that rule.

Why it applies, and its limits: It confirms the prohibition from the engineering-history literature and, unlike the popular account, sets the defensive explanation beside the others and doubts it, which is why our page states the motive as argued rather than settled. Its limit is that it is a paper on crossing forms, not on roads following rivers, which it does not address.

Used for: the Oi river's bridge and ferry prohibition and the competing explanations for it

oigawa-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 大井川 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A4%A7%E4%BA%95%E5%B7%9D)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Oi river, the Tokaido's most feared crossing, where in the Edo period neither bridge nor ferry was allowed and travelers were carried over: the crossing system, and the explanations given for the ban.

Why it applies, and its limits: It sets out the competing explanations for the ban - the defense of Edo and Sunpu, the river's own violence, the profits of the crossing towns - so that this page can state the motive as argued rather than certain. A tertiary summary used for that.

Used for: the Oi river crossing and the explanations for its bridge and ferry ban

fujian-tulou-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Fujian tulou (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujian_tulou)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Fujian tulou, the great earthen communal houses of the Hakka and Minnan mountain districts inscribed as World Heritage: their round and rectangular forms, the single clan under one roof, and the equal, unranked rooms.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes a famous East Asian fortress form built round, which this page uses to show that even there the square was as common, so that a curved wall is not the East Asian answer to the corner. A tertiary summary used with the Chinese article beside it, which states which form is the more widespread; and a tulou is a rural clan dwelling, one building, recruited here into an argument about castle baileys and city walls of a far larger order.

Used for: the clan under one roof, the equal rooms, and the round and rectangular forms

fujian-tulou-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 福建土楼 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A6%8F%E5%BB%BA%E5%9C%9F%E6%A5%BC)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Fujian tulou: the round and square earthen communal houses of the mountain districts of Longyan and Zhangzhou, their function as dwelling and defense in one, and which forms are the most common.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the square tulou is the most widespread form, the fact this page uses to show that the round fortress-house is the exception even where it is famous. A tertiary summary used for that ranking.

Used for: the square tulou as the most widespread form, and dwelling and defense combined

wheatbaku-asakusa-okura

気ままに江戸♪ 散歩・味・読書の記録 (an Edo-topography blog), 浅草御蔵（新江戸百景めぐり㊶） (https://wheatbaku.exblog.jp/30482848/)

What it is: A post on an Edo-topography enthusiast's blog on the Asakusa Okura, the shogunate's rice granary at Kuramae: its eight boat-entry channels for unloading the rice shipped from the shogunal lands, and the storehouses set on both sides of them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states plainly what the channels were for and where the storehouses stood, which is the arrangement our wharf granaries copy. Its limits are that it is an enthusiast's post, used beside the encyclopedia article it agrees with, and that its subject is the shogunate's central granary of sixty-seven storehouses, from which only the form and not the scale transfers to a provincial seat.

Used for: the boat-entry channels for unloading rice, with storehouses on both sides

kotobank-teramachi

Kotobank, 寺町 - 改訂新版 世界大百科事典, デジタル大辞泉 and ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 entries (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%AF%BA%E7%94%BA-101789)

What it is: The kotobank reference page for the teramachi, carrying side by side the entries of seven Japanese reference works, three of which are quoted here, on the temple district: its collective, continuous placement at the key points of a castle town's perimeter, and the military value of its large buildings and wide precincts in an emergency.

Why it applies, and its limits: Standard reference works on why a castle town's temples stood together at its edge, the rule our temple rim follows. Its limit is the encyclopedia's: it summarizes the planning intent without citing the town plans it rests on.

Used for: the collective placement of temples at the perimeter's key points for their military value

teramachi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 寺町 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%AF%BA%E7%94%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the teramachi, the temple district of a Japanese town: how castle towns gathered their temples and graveyards at the town's edge as a defensive line, and the surviving examples.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the defensive intent behind the temple district, which is why our capital draws its temple row at the rim. A tertiary summary used for that intent, beside the reference encyclopedias that say the same; the sentence quoted speaks of the time before the Edo period, which is earlier than most of what our capitals are drawn from.

Used for: temples gathered at the town's edge as a defensive line

pingyao-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Pingyao (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pingyao)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Pingyao, the walled county town in Shanxi: its position on the east bank of the Fen river in the Taiyuan basin, its Ming wall, and the 4 m moat outside the wall.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the town on its river. A tertiary summary used for the siting and the moat, and its 4 m moat is a measurement of the restored World Heritage site as it stands today, with no period source given for it.

Used for: Pingyao on the Fen's east bank, and the moat outside its wall

pingyao-chengqiang-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 平遥城墙 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E5%B9%B3%E9%81%A5%E5%9F%8E%E5%A2%99)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the city wall of Pingyao, the best-preserved Ming county wall: its circuit, its gates and towers, the 4 m moat outside it, and the southern side built along the Zhongdu river.

Why it applies, and its limits: It records that even this model Chinese walled town put one side of its wall along a river. A tertiary summary used for the wall's course and its moat, whose dimensions describe the wall as it survives after Ming rebuilds and modern conservation, not as first raised.

Used for: Pingyao's south wall along the Zhongdu river and its 4 m moat

hori-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 堀 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A0%80)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the moat: its types, the natural moat made of an existing river, the sogamae moat around a castle town, boats on river-fed moats, and the sectioning of a wet moat with earthen weirs into pools at different levels.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the vocabulary and the practices our moats are drawn with - the natural moat, the sectioned moat, the town moat. A tertiary summary used for those definitions.

Used for: the sectioned moat (mitochigai), the natural moat, and the town's sogamae moat

kojodan-mizubori

攻城団ブログ (Kojodan blog), 【お城の基礎講座】53. 水堀（みずぼり）, 2020-09-25 (https://blog.kojodan.jp/entry/2020/09/25/180000)

What it is: A numbered lesson in the castle-visiting community Kojodan's basics course, on the wet moat: how flatland castles drew water from rivers and how a dug moat often filled from below on its own.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the groundwater case in plain terms, the source our inner moat is written to hold. Its limit is that it is a hobbyist community's explainer.

Used for: water welling up in a dug moat

shirobito-906-mizubori

加藤理文 (Kato Masafumi), 【理文先生のお城がっこう】城歩き編 第18回 水堀と空堀, 城びと (Shirobito) (https://shirobito.jp/article/906)

What it is: An installment of the castle researcher Kato Masafumi's educational column, written as a teacher and a director of the Japan Castle Association, on the castle web magazine Shirobito, on wet and dry moats: where the water of a wet moat came from - groundwater, castle wastewater, rain, or a river, lake or sea it was deliberately drawn from - and why flatland castles so often have wet moats.

Why it applies, and its limits: It lists the sources a moat's water actually came from, from a specialist rather than a guidebook, which is what our capital's moat-filling rule is drawn from. Its limit is that it is a popular column and ranks none of the sources.

Used for: the sources of a wet moat's water

takamatsu-my-kagawa

うどん県旅ネット (Kagawa Prefecture Tourism Association), 城舟体験（史跡高松城跡 玉藻公園） (https://www.my-kagawa.jp/point/2840/)

What it is: The Kagawa prefectural tourism association's page on the castle-boat ride in the moat of Takamatsu Castle, the seaside castle whose moat is filled with the Inland Sea's own water and swum by sea fish.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the readable statement of the one plain case of a castle moat filled from the sea, which this page uses to show how wide the range of moat sources ran. Its limit is that it is a tourism page about the moat as it is today.

Used for: Takamatsu's moat of seawater and sea bream

imabarijo-blog

今治城 スタッフブログ (Imabari Castle staff blog), post of 2014-08-30 (http://imabarijo.blogspot.com/2014/08/blog-post_30.html)

What it is: The staff blog of Imabari Castle, run by the city museum that keeps the castle, describing the moat's exchange of seawater with the harbor and how its level rises and falls with the tide.

Why it applies, and its limits: The castle's own custodians on their own moat, for the tidal exchange our seaside capital's moat could show. Its limits are that it is a blog post describing the moat as it exchanges water with the modern port today, so that the Edo arrangement was the same is an inference, and that it says nothing about springs.

Used for: Imabari's moat exchanging tidewater with the sea

kotobank-monzenmachi-143199

Kotobank, 門前町 - 改訂新版 世界大百科事典, 日本大百科全書 and ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 entries (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%96%80%E5%89%8D%E7%94%BA-143199)

What it is: The kotobank reference page for the monzen-machi, the town before a great shrine or temple's gate, carrying the entries of three Japanese reference works: a street-village of inns, shops and craft workshops along both sides of the pilgrimage road, contrasted with the jinaicho, the temple town ringed by moat and rampart.

Why it applies, and its limits: Standard reference works on the open commercial form of the gate-front town, and on the enclosed temple town as a distinct type, which is why our capital's monzen is drawn as open machi. Its limit is the encyclopedia's summary form.

Used for: the monzen as an open street-village of inns and shops, and the moated jinaicho as a different type

kidoban-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 木戸番 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9C%A8%E6%88%B8%E7%95%AA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kido-ban, the keeper of a town's block gate: the gates installed in Edo and the castle towns, closed at the fourth hour of night, and the wicket by which those with business passed after inspection.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that block gates were the castle towns' night closure, not only Edo's, which is what lets this page say the monzen was barred like any block. A tertiary summary used for that.

Used for: block gates closed at night in Edo and the castle towns

cchfound-guqiandao

中国华夏文化遗产基金会 (China Huaxia Cultural Heritage Foundation), 古纤道 (https://www.cchfound.com/product/2934.html)

What it is: A heritage-item page from a Chinese cultural-heritage foundation on the ancient towpath at Shaoxing: its Tang date, its 7.5 km protected extent, and the dimensions of the stone-pier form - the deck's width, the piers' span, the slabs and the height above the water.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one readable page giving the towpath's measurements, which size the hauling path on our river capital. Its limits are that it is a foundation's summary page without its own citations, and that its figures describe the preserved central stretch as it stands today, whose fabric is later than the Tang institution it dates.

Used for: the towpath's 1.5 m width and its stone deck

todaiji-daibutsuden-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 東大寺大仏殿 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9D%B1%E5%A4%A7%E5%AF%BA%E5%A4%A7%E4%BB%8F%E6%AE%BF)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Great Buddha Hall of Todaiji in Nara, formally the temple's kondo: the dimensions of the standing eighteenth-century hall and of the far wider eighth-century original it replaced.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the two measurements that bound the largest Japanese temple hall, standing and lost, which is how this page keeps its hall-size ceiling honest about which it means. A tertiary summary used for the dimensions.

Used for: the Daibutsuden's 57.5 m front today and the original's 85.8 m

chion-in-mieido

浄土宗総本山知恩院 (Chion-in), 第6回 御影堂の建築様式 (1), 国宝・御影堂ものがたり (https://www.chion-in.or.jp/mieido/story/story_06.php)

What it is: The temple's own account of its National Treasure Mieido hall at Chion-in in Kyoto: its dimensions, 45 m across and 35 m deep, and its standing among the largest halls in Japan.

Why it applies, and its limits: A temple's own measurement of one of the largest standing Buddhist halls, the lower anchor of the hall-size band our temple glyphs are checked against. Its limit is that it is the temple describing itself.

Used for: the Mieido's 45 by 35 m

wako226-hairyo-yashiki

大江戸歴史散歩を楽しむ会 (an Edo history walking group), 大名の拝領江戸屋敷 (https://wako226.exblog.jp/239926652/)

What it is: A post on the blog of an Edo-history walking group setting out the shogunate's table of granted residence sizes for daimyo by stipend, from 2,500 tsubo for the smallest domains to 7,200 for the largest, and noting that the plots actually held ran larger.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one readable page that gives the whole table, which sizes the daimyo compounds on our capital. Its limits are real: it is an amateur group's summary with no citation of the regulation, so the table is used as a band. And the institution is a different one: the table is of plots the SHOGUNATE granted daimyo in Edo under alternate attendance, while a domain seat's compound was the lord's own ground, so the band transfers as a scale of what a house of a given stipend kept, not as a rule that applied there.

Used for: the bakufu's table of granted residence sizes by stipend

zuihoden-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 瑞鳳殿 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%91%9E%E9%B3%B3%E6%AE%BF)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Zuihoden, the mausoleum of Date Masamune at Sendai on the wooded hill of Kyogamine across the Hirose river from the castle, with the mausolea of his son and grandson and the lesser Date tombs around it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the one clear case of a ruling family's mortuary precinct standing on a wooded rise across the river from the castle, the form our capital's lineage precinct may take. A tertiary summary used for the site and its buildings; the Date were one of the greatest houses in the country, so the precinct is an upper case, and the buildings that stand are reconstructions after the fire of 1945, which leaves the siting untouched.

Used for: the Zuihoden across the Hirose meander from the honmaru, with the family's mausolea around it

jiangning-zhizao-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 江宁织造衙门 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E6%B1%9F%E5%AE%81%E7%BB%87%E9%80%A0%E8%A1%99%E9%97%A8)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Jiangning imperial weaving office at Nanjing, one of the three Jiangnan weaving offices that supplied the Qing court, with the wares each of the three was assigned.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the court's weaving was confined to three cities, which is why our capital gets a purveyor and not an imperial works. A tertiary summary used for the three cities and their wares; it gives no headcount, and the arrangement is the QING court's, so the negative drawn from it - no imperial works at a provincial seat - is one dynasty's organization of court supply carried across the period.

Used for: the three Jiangnan weaving offices and their assigned wares

nippon-com-kanda-konyacho

nippon.com, 『神田紺屋町』：浮世写真家 喜千也の名所江戸百景第20回 (https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu004020/)

What it is: An installment of a Nippon.com series pairing each of Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo with a photograph of the place today, here Kanda Konya-cho, the dyers' town: the indigo dyers who gave it its name and the bolts of cloth drying in rows that made the sight famous.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives Edo's dyers' quarter and the drying as its visible signature, which is what our dye-works row is drawn to show. Its limit is that it is a photographic feature rather than a trade history.

Used for: the Kanda dyers eave to eave, and the drying bolts ranged like banners

yk-kankou-konya

大和郡山市観光協会 (Yamatokoriyama Tourism Association), 箱本館紺屋 (https://www.yk-kankou.jp/spotDetail51.html)

What it is: The Yamatokoriyama tourism association's page on the Hakomotokan museum in the town's Konya-machi, the dyers' street of the castle town, with the channel down the middle of the street fed from the castle moat in which the dyed cloth and thread were rinsed.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a castle town's dyers' ward standing on water led from the castle moat, the siting our capital's dye works copy. Its limit is that it is a tourism page and gives no founding date.

Used for: the dyers' street on a channel off the castle moat

imado-yaki-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 今戸焼 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%BB%8A%E6%88%B8%E7%84%BC)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Imado ware, the unglazed and raku pottery fired at Imado and Hashiba northeast of Asakusa in Edo, with the count of some fifty producing households at the end of the shogunate.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the size of an Edo kiln quarter in households, which is what makes a kiln a quarter rather than a shop on our capital. A tertiary summary used for that count, which it attributes to a period source.

Used for: some fifty kiln households at Imado

kyoyaki-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 京焼 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%BA%AC%E7%84%BC)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Kyoto ware: the kilns of Higashiyama with the kiln houses concentrated at Sanjo Awataguchi, the other wares of the eastern hills, and the lesser kilns scattered in the east and north of the city.

Why it applies, and its limits: It shows the Kyoto kilns clustered on the city's eastern side, the pattern our capital's works district follows, and it also shows some scattered, which keeps this page from saying never. A tertiary summary used for that.

Used for: the kiln houses concentrated at Awataguchi, and the kilns scattered elsewhere

jsidre-bansui-2009

水田用水の番水技術の実態と論理, 農業農村工学会誌 (Journal of the Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering) 77(7): 559- (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjsidre/77/7/77_559/_article/-char/ja)

What it is: A four-page article by Tajima Masahiro, Ishii Atsushi and Miwa Isao in the 2009 volume of the journal of the Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering, on bansui, the rotation of paddy water: what it is, how blocks, intervals and order are set, and when it is used.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states from the engineering literature that rotation is the regime switched to in drought while normal supply is continuous. Its limits are that it describes modern irrigation districts, that only its abstract was read, and that the journal carries commissioned pieces beside refereed ones and the landing page does not say which this is.

Used for: rotation as the drought regime of paddy water supply

kiyosu-haisui-schedule

清須市 (Kiyosu City, Aichi), 令和8年度 水田の配水スケジュールについて (https://www.city.kiyosu.aichi.jp/kurashi_joho/seikatsu_kankyo/nogyo/tsusui_R7.html)

What it is: A municipal notice from Kiyosu in Aichi giving the year's paddy water-distribution schedule: the date supply opens in April, the days each block receives water through the summer, and the date it is shut off at the end of September.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a real irrigation calendar, which is the shape our field gates follow. Its limits are large and stated: it is present-day district practice in a machine-farmed landscape whose water comes by pressurized pipeline rather than by open ditch and field gate, not a premodern village's regime, and it is one district's year; only the season's SHAPE - an opening in spring, a shutoff before harvest - transfers, never a date.

Used for: a paddy water calendar from April to the end of September, delivered by block

kawagoe-gokashi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 川越五河岸 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B7%9D%E8%B6%8A%E4%BA%94%E6%B2%B3%E5%B2%B8)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Kawagoe Five Kashi, the five landings on the upper Shingashi river that served as the castle town's outer port, with the counts of their wholesale houses and boats.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a castle town's river landings were its outer port, the arrangement this page draws for a capital on a river. A tertiary summary used for that. It describes the same town as the company archive cited beside it, so the two are not independent corroboration, and the form is generalized to any river capital from one case.

Used for: the five landings as Kawagoe's outer port

smtrc-kawagoe-shuun

三井住友トラスト不動産 (Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Realty), このまちアーカイブス 3：川と舟運 ～ 川越 (https://smtrc.jp/town-archives/city/kawagoe/p03.html)

What it is: A sourced local-history page in a real-estate company's town archive series on Kawagoe's rivers and boat transport: the town's earlier outer port on the Irima river, the wet ground between the landings and the castle town, and the town's growth as a wholesale center.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the landings as an outer port separated from the castle town by low ground, which is the relation our river capital's wharf has to its wall. Its limit is that it is a company's popular archive rather than the town history it summarizes. It describes the same town as the encyclopedia article cited beside it, so the two are not independent corroboration.

Used for: the outer port and the wet ground between the landings and the town

kotobank-kashi

Kotobank, 河岸（かし） - 日本大百科全書 and other reference entries (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%B2%B3%E5%B2%B8-459508)

What it is: The kotobank reference page for the kashi, the Edo-period river landing, carrying the entries of Japanese reference encyclopedias: the bank where cargo was landed, the markets that formed there, its standing as a town or village, and the kashi wholesaler who ran the landing for fees.

Why it applies, and its limits: It shows that the landing was a place of business run by its wholesalers rather than a public quay, which is how this page describes it. Its limit is the encyclopedia's summary form.

Used for: the kashi wholesaler's loading, storage and fees

chuoku-nihonbashi-kashi

中央区まちかど展示館 (Chuo City machikado exhibition halls), 日本橋エリア特集 Part.5 (https://www.chuoku-machikadotenjikan.jp/feature/special09_nihonbashi05.html)

What it is: A local-history feature from Tokyo's Chuo ward on the Edo-period landings of the Nihonbashi district (the three named kashi stood on the Nishi-Horidome river), named by the cargo each handled - rice, small boats, salt.

Why it applies, and its limits: It names the cargo-specialized landings of one Edo river, the pattern our wharf district's specialized quays follow. Its limit is that it is a ward's heritage feature. And it is Edo, the largest city in the country, whose quay specialization a provincial seat would not match.

Used for: landings named by cargo along the Nihonbashi river

mizu-no-bunka-32-yanagawa

ミツカン 水の文化センター (Mizkan Water Culture Center), 堀の記憶が成し遂げた、柳川再生物語, 水の文化 32 (https://www.mizu.gr.jp/kikanshi/no32/07.html)

What it is: An article in the Mizkan Water Culture Center's periodical on the revival of Yanagawa's channels: the delta the town stands on, the tidal range of the Ariake sea beside it, the density of its waterways, and the tide barrier above which their water is drawn.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the ground Yanagawa's canals stand on and the fact that their water is deliberately kept above the tide, which corrects the reading that such channels are tidal. Its limit is that it is a water-culture magazine report rather than a hydrological survey. The tide barrier and the non-tidal regime are described in the present tense and undated, and the canal lengths are modern measurements of a modernized system, so what is attested is today's managed regime; the delta and the tidal range are geography and transfer freely.

Used for: Yanagawa's delta ground, the 6 m tide beside it, and the channels drawn above the tide barrier

nippon-com-matsue-horikawa

nippon.com, 『水の都・松江』の魅力が詰まった国宝・松江城と堀川めぐり (https://www.nippon.com/ja/guide-to-japan/gu900102/)

What it is: A travel and heritage feature on Nippon.com on Matsue, the castle town between Lake Shinji and Nakaumi whose waterways spread out from the castle moat through the town.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places Matsue's channel network on its lakeside ground and names it as the castle moat's own spread. Its limit is that it is a travel feature.

Used for: Matsue's waterways spreading from the castle moat, between two lakes

qiaokou-hanzheng-street

硚口区人民政府 (Qiaokou District People's Government, Wuhan), 两江淌出一条街, 2017-08-28 (https://www.qiaokou.gov.cn/qkgk/hghh/201708/t20170828_117732.shtml)

What it is: A local-history article on the Wuhan district government's site on how Hanzheng Street came to be: Hankou's first street the river street along the wharves, then the streets stepping inland from it, with merchant boats moored stern to bow along the bank.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes a Chinese city on a live river keeping its wharf on the bank and growing its commercial district up from it, which is the arrangement our river capital draws instead of a boat basin. Its limit is that it is a municipal history page rather than an urban-history study. Hankou was one of the empire's great river entrepots, not an ordinary provincial seat, so it shows the extreme of bankside commercial growth.

Used for: the river street first, the wharves in rows along the bank, and the streets stepping inland

hanzheng-jie-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 汉正街 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E6%B1%89%E6%AD%A3%E8%A1%97)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on Hanzheng Street in Wuhan, the ten-li commercial street that grew along the Han river's north bank in the Ming as the wharves of the new town of Hankou joined up into one street.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the growth of a Chinese river town's commercial street straight out of its line of wharves, the form our river capital's bankside district copies. A tertiary summary used for that. Hankou was one of the empire's great river entrepots, not an ordinary provincial seat, and most of the article's body is about the twentieth century; only its Ming paragraph is ours.

Used for: Hankou's wharves joining into a ten-li bankside street

rokudo-chinnoji-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 六道珍皇寺 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%85%AD%E9%81%93%E7%8F%8D%E7%9A%87%E5%AF%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Rokudō Chinnō-ji, the temple at the Rokudō crossroads in Kyoto held to stand at the entrance to the Toribeno cremation ground and at the boundary between this world and the next.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the gate-temple at the mouth of Toribeno and the tradition attached to it, the form our funerary complex's entrance follows. A tertiary summary used for that.

Used for: the Rokudō crossroads as Toribeno's entrance and the boundary of the worlds

fuso-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 風葬 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%A2%A8%E8%91%AC)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on exposure burial, the leaving of the dead in the open, naming the grounds outside Heian-kyō where it was practiced from the Heian period: Katabiragatsuji, Adashino, Toribeno and Rendaino.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests exposure at both of Kyoto's grounds this page discusses, the first of the three jobs a funerary field did. A tertiary summary used for that.

Used for: exposure burial at Toribeno and Rendaino

injoji-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 引接寺 (京都市) (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%BC%95%E6%8E%A5%E5%AF%BA_(%E4%BA%AC%E9%83%BD%E5%B8%82))

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Injō-ji, the Senbon Enmadō in Kyoto, the temple standing at the entrance of Rendaino, one of the old capital's three great funerary grounds.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the gate-temple at the mouth of the funerary ground, the arrangement our funerary complex copies. A tertiary summary used for that.

Used for: Injō-ji at the entrance of Rendaino

souda-kyoto-enmado

そうだ 京都、行こう。 (JR Tokai's Kyoto campaign site), 千本ゑんま堂［引接寺］ (https://souda-kyoto.jp/guide/spot/senbonenmado.html)

What it is: A temple guide page on JR Tokai's Kyoto tourism site for the Senbon Enmadō, Injō-ji: its position at the entrance of the Rendaino funerary ground and its standing as the hall where the spirits of the dead are welcomed back.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the gate-temple's own tradition of standing where the living pass to the other world, which is what this page uses the temple for. Its limit is that it is a tourism page, and it does not mention the Odoi rampart.

Used for: Injō-ji at the entrance of Rendaino as the place leading to the other world

imari-okawachiyama

伊万里鍋島焼協同組合 (Imari Nabeshima-yaki Cooperative Association), 大川内山の歴史 (https://imari-ookawachiyama.com/history/)

What it is: The kiln village's own trade association's history page for Okawachiyama, where the Nabeshima domain moved its kiln in 1675 and guarded it with a barrier so that its techniques and craftsmen could not leave.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the one plain case of a domain kiln set apart and guarded, the form our record keeps off-map as a prestige-ware kiln. Its limit is that it is the kiln village describing its own history, and it gives no distance from the castle town.

Used for: the Nabeshima kiln's move to Okawachiyama in 1675 and its barrier

liulichang-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 琉璃厂 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%90%89%E7%92%83%E5%8E%82)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on Liulichang in Beijing, the glazed-tile works of the Yuan and Ming that gave the later book and antiques street its name: its place among the Ministry of Works' five great works, its enlargement for the palaces, and its extent inside the city.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives an official works standing at the fringe of the capital, enlarged to serve the palace building, the case behind our capital's tile works. A tertiary summary used for that; it gives no distance from the palace. And it describes the imperial capital, whose Ministry-of-Works establishments and gate-signal apparatus a provincial seat had no counterpart of, so the form is stepped down two tiers by us.

Used for: the Liulichang as one of the five great works, enlarged for the palaces, and its extent

visitbeijing-wudachang

Visit Beijing (Beijing Municipal Culture and Tourism Bureau), 明代迁都北京时曾设'大五厂'，现如今都在哪儿？ (https://www.visitbeijing.com.cn/article/47yYgUFzCMj)

What it is: A popular history article on the Beijing tourism bureau's portal on the five great works the Ming set up when the capital moved to Beijing - the timber yards, the black-tile kiln, the glazed-tile works and the foundation-materials yard - and where each stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: It names the five works and the Liulichang's job of firing tile and vessels for the court, which is what our capital's fringe tile works is modeled on. Its limit is that it is a tourism bureau's feature rather than the Ming administrative records. And it describes the imperial capital, whose Ministry-of-Works establishments and gate-signal apparatus a provincial seat had no counterpart of, so the form is stepped down two tiers by us. Its period phrase is quoted with no source named.

Used for: the five great works and the Liulichang's function

bjd-zhonggulou

北京日报 (Beijing Daily), 北京钟鼓楼的奇妙数字 (https://xinwen.bjd.com.cn/content/s650bf36be4b0d5bd075f4be1.html)

What it is: A local-history feature in the Beijing Daily on the Bell and Drum Towers of Beijing: the order of drum and bell at the setting and lightening of the watch, and how the nine city gates closed and opened on their signal.

Why it applies, and its limits: It documents the job our bell-and-drum tower is drawn for - sounding the hour the gates shut and open. Its limit is that it is a newspaper feature and speaks of the city gates, not the lane palings. And it describes the imperial capital, whose Ministry-of-Works establishments and gate-signal apparatus a provincial seat had no counterpart of, so the form is stepped down two tiers by us.

Used for: the towers' signal for closing and opening the city gates

hirosakipark-tenshu

弘前公園 (Hirosaki Park official site), 弘前城 天守／御三階櫓 (https://www.hirosakipark.jp/707.html)

What it is: The official Hirosaki Park site's page on the castle's keep, formally its three-story turret: its first-floor plan of five by six ken and its ridge height.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the measured footprint of the keep, from the castle's own custodians on their own building. It is a visitor page rather than a survey report, and the standing building is the three-story turret of 1810, a deliberately modest late-Edo structure, not the five-story keep of 1611 that burned in 1627.

Used for: the keep's 5 by 6 ken plan

hirosaki-castle-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 弘前城 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%BC%98%E5%89%8D%E5%9F%8E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Hirosaki Castle: its original extent of 612 by 947 m and 385,200 square meters, and its surviving three-tier keep, the lowest of the extant three-tier keeps at about 14.4 m.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the castle's original area, against which the keep's footprint is measured on this page. A tertiary summary used for that figure. A 47,000-koku domain is a modest one, which makes it a good anchor; but the English article on the same castle, registered separately, quotes the same extent, so the two keys are one datum in two languages and do not corroborate one another.

Used for: Hirosaki's original 385,200 square meters

hirosakipark-outline

弘前公園 (Hirosaki Park official site), 弘前公園について (https://www.hirosakipark.jp/outline.html)

What it is: The official Hirosaki Park site's outline page, giving the park's total area of about 492,000 square meters.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source of the ~50 ha this page uses for the whole enceinte, which is the park's figure rather than the castle's original extent. Its limit is that a park boundary is not a castle boundary.

Used for: the park's 492,000 square meters

himeji-han-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 姫路藩 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A7%AB%E8%B7%AF%E8%97%A9)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Himeji domain: its founding in 1600 when Ikeda Terumasa was granted the whole of Harima at 520,000 koku, and its later reduction to 150,000.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the assessed yield of the domain whose castle is one of this page's scale anchors, and it dates that figure to the Ikeda enfeoffment so the anchor is not read as the domain's later size. A tertiary summary used for the figure.

Used for: Himeji's 520,000 koku under the Ikeda

kitsuki-castle-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 杵築城 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9D%B5%E7%AF%89%E5%9F%8E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Kitsuki Castle in Oita, built on the Daiyama promontory at the mouth of the Yasaka river, with the Takayama river to its north and Morie Bay to its east.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the castle on its promontory between the rivers and the bay, the flank position with water on two sides that this page cites it for. A tertiary summary used for the siting.

Used for: Kitsuki's promontory at the Yasaka mouth, the Takayama and Morie Bay

kyu-shokyoto-kitsuki

九州の小京都 (Kyushu Shokyoto, the Kyushu little-Kyoto towns' federation), 城下町のご案内（杵築） (https://www.kyu-shokyoto.org/kitsuki/jyouka/)

What it is: A regional tourism federation's description of the castle town of Kitsuki in Oita: the samurai quarters on the high ground north and south of the castle and the merchants' town in the valley between them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives Kitsuki's sandwich plan - warriors on the heights, merchants below - which is the arrangement this page cites the town for. Its limit is that it is a tourism federation's page. The page itself calls the arrangement unique to Kitsuki among castle towns, so the form is cited as one attested case and not as a norm.
