Used for: the samurai quarters on the heights and the merchants' town in the valley

kotobank-horokusei

Kotobank, 俸禄制 - 日本大百科全書 and 世界大百科事典 entries (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%BF%B8%E7%A6%84%E5%88%B6-1414874)

What it is: The kotobank reference page for the stipend system of the Edo domains, carrying the entries of two Japanese reference encyclopedias: retainers paid in warehouse rice out of the tax rice the domain collected into its own granary.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the domain granary's two-way job - tax rice in, stipends out - which is the whole function of the granary district on our capital. Its limit is the encyclopedia's summary form.

Used for: stipends paid from the domain granary out of the tax rice it collected

sina-neixiang-xianya

Sina News (repost), 河南内乡，有一座我国保存最完整的700年县衙 (https://k.sina.cn/article_6582636570_1885b101a00100t9j4.html)

What it is: A popular history article carried on the Sina news portal describing the Neixiang county yamen in Henan, the most complete surviving county government compound, room by room: the six boards' offices as side halls east and west of the courtyard before the great hall.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states where the six offices stood in a county yamen, which is why our county-scale seat draws them as rooms on the court rather than as buildings. Its limit is that it is a news portal's feature about one surviving yamen. The article has no named author and no citations, and the standing buildings are a late-Qing rebuild.

Used for: the six fang as side halls before the great hall, three east and three west

sina-pingyao-xianya

Sina News (repost), 平遥县衙博物馆，中国现存的明清时期县衙的典型建筑 (https://k.sina.cn/article_7072274192_p1a58a571000100kdl2.html)

What it is: A popular history article carried on the Sina news portal on the Pingyao county yamen museum, the typical surviving Ming-Qing county government compound: its area and its count of over two hundred rooms.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the room count of a county yamen, which sizes the seat of government on our maps. Its limit is that it is a news portal's feature. The article is credited to a personal self-media account rather than to the portal's own reporting, its figures are unattributed, and what they measure is the restored museum compound of an exceptionally wealthy county seat.

Used for: the Pingyao yamen's 26,000 square meters and over two hundred rooms

travelchinaguide-pingyao-yamen

TravelChinaGuide, Pingyao Ancient Government Office (https://www.travelchinaguide.com/attraction/shanxi/pingyao/ancient-government-office.htm)

What it is: A travel guide's page on the Pingyao county yamen, giving the compound's length, width and area.

Why it applies, and its limits: It corroborates the yamen's area from a second readable page. Its limit is that it is a travel guide. The page is a tour operator's promotional copy with no source for its dimensions, and it describes the restored museum; two weak pages agreeing is not verification.

Used for: the Pingyao yamen's 203 by 131 m and 26,000 square meters

edokara-yosuibaki

edo→tokyo (edokara.tokyo), 玉川上水の遺構-余水吐跡 (https://edokara.tokyo/conts/2020/06/12/1485)

What it is: A page on a site documenting Edo's surviving waterworks remains, on the spillway of the Tamagawa aqueduct at the Yotsuya gate: the facility that discharged surplus water to regulate the flow, and the valley and river it discharged into.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests that a real aqueduct carried a purpose-built spillway, which is why our capital's aqueduct is drawn with one. Its limit is that it is an enthusiast site, and its case discharged to a valley rather than a moat. The page gives no date for the spillway itself, so its Edo-period existence rests on the page's framing rather than on a dated statement.

Used for: the Tamagawa aqueduct's spillway and where its surplus went

beijing-chengchi-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 北京城池 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%8C%97%E4%BA%AC%E5%9F%8E%E6%B1%A0)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the walls and moats of Beijing: the moats of the palace city, the inner city and the Jiajing outer city, their widths, and the water system that fed them from the Jade Spring hills and drained them to the Tonghui river.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the ringed moats of the imperial capital and where their water came from and went, the Chinese anchor for our capital's engineered moat ring. A tertiary summary used for that. Beijing was the imperial capital, so its moat ring is a ceiling and not a norm, and the dimensions mix the period specification with a 1953 survey of a much-altered work.

Used for: Beijing's ringed moats, fed from the Jade Spring hills and draining to the Tonghui

ndl-crd-hikifune

National Diet Library of Japan, Collaborative Reference Database, 江戸時代、川の下流から上流へどのように舟を動かしていたか知りたい。 (https://crd.ndl.go.jp/reference/entry/index.php?id=1000279632&page=ref_view)

What it is: A librarian's sourced answer in the National Diet Library's Collaborative Reference Database to the question of how Edo-period river boats were moved upstream: by sail with a following wind, and otherwise by men hauling on a long rope from the bank.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states from the library's cited works that river transport depended on hauling from the bank, which is why our river capital draws a towpath. Its limit is that it is a reference answer summarizing published histories rather than the histories themselves.

Used for: upstream river boats hauled by rope from the bank

thepaper-dongjing-population

澎湃新闻 市政厅 (The Paper), 百万人口的北宋东京汴梁，与千万规模的北上广，哪个更拥挤？ (https://www.thepaper.cn/newsDetail_forward_1420523)

What it is: A history feature in The Paper's private-history section on the population of Northern Song Kaifeng, drawing on Li Hequn's doctoral study of the city's layout: the nine administrative wards outside the wall by 1021 and the population they held.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the extent of settlement outside the Song capital's wall in the historian's own figures, the case behind this page's reading of a capital's suburbs. Its limit is that it is a news feature reporting a thesis, and it speaks of population, not trade. Kaifeng was the empire's capital, a city of about a million, so extramural settlement on this scale is a ceiling and not a model for a provincial capital.

Used for: the nine wards outside Kaifeng's wall and their population

jokanji-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 浄閑寺 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B5%84%E9%96%91%E5%AF%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Jōkan-ji, the temple near the Yoshiwara quarter known as the throw-in temple for the courtesans buried there after the 1855 earthquake.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the temple's name, its origin and its position beside the quarter it served, the case this page uses for a burial ground standing near the wall. A tertiary summary; the distance is our own measurement. The page attests the temple's nearness to the pleasure quarter, not to any wall - Edo had none, so the wall is our frame - and the throw-in burials are one disaster episode of 1855 at the end of the period, not a standing practice.

Used for: the throw-in temple's name and its nearness to Yoshiwara

roving-bridge-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Roving bridge (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roving_bridge)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the roving bridge, the bridge that carries a canal towpath from one bank to the other, with the note that bridges were also needed at junctions and wherever a side arm interrupted the towpath.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests that a working towpath is carried over the channels that interrupt it, which is how our towpath is drawn where a drain meets the river. Its limits are large: it is British canal practice, not East Asian, and it speaks of junctions and side arms rather than field drains.

Used for: a towpath bridged where a side channel interrupts it

kawagoe-castle-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 川越城 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B7%9D%E8%B6%8A%E5%9F%8E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Kawagoe Castle: the lord's residence and the armaments office in the ninomaru until the fire of 1846, and the honmaru palace built in 1848 to replace them, which is the palace that survives.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a domain seat whose lord and offices sat in the second bailey, the arrangement this page uses for where a domain's council met. A tertiary summary used for that. The article does not say the domain's business was transacted in the second bailey, only that the lord's residence and the armaments office stood there; a 170,000-koku domain is a large one, and the arrangement is the one a fire ended in 1846.

Used for: Kawagoe's residence and armaments office in the ninomaru

nagoyajo-nawabari

名古屋城公式ウェブサイト (Nagoya Castle official website, City of Nagoya), 縄張 (https://www.nagoyajo.city.nagoya.jp/learn/construction/nawabari/)

What it is: The City of Nagoya's official castle site on the castle's layout: its rectangular, straight-lined enclosures set out in the teikaku manner, and how simple that is beside the Sengoku layouts built to be hard to storm.

Why it applies, and its limits: The castle's own keepers on the plan of the plains castle our capital most resembles, which is why its baileys are drawn as clean rectangles. Its limit is that it speaks of Nagoya alone. Nagoya was one of the largest castles in the country, laid out at one stroke on flat ground under a shogunate-ordered construction levy, which is why its plan is so regular; a smaller seat, or one grown on a hill, is a different case.

Used for: Nagoya's rectangular, straight-lined enclosures

kotobank-kurayashiki

Kotobank, 蔵屋敷 - 日本大百科全書 and 世界大百科事典 entries (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%94%B5%E5%B1%8B%E6%95%B7-58201)

What it is: The kotobank reference page for the kurayashiki, the domains' warehouse compounds at Osaka, carrying the entries of two Japanese reference encyclopedias: their concentration on Nakanoshima and the Tosabori and Edobori rivers for the convenience of water transport, and the sale of their rice through the Dojima brokers.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the waterside siting of the rice warehouses from standard reference works, which is why our granaries stand at the wharf. Its limit is the encyclopedia's summary form. The kurayashiki was an institution of the commercial capital, where domains sold their rice; that a domain seat's own granaries stood at its wharf in the same way is this page's inference.

Used for: the warehouse compounds concentrated on the rivers for water transport

tokyo-waterworks-tamagawa-rekishi

東京都水道局 (Tokyo Metropolitan Bureau of Waterworks), 玉川上水の歴史 (https://www.waterworks.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/kouhou/pr/tamagawa/rekishishiritai/rekishi)

What it is: The Tokyo waterworks bureau's own history page for the Tamagawa aqueduct: its digging as an open cut from Hamura to the Yotsuya gate and the stone and wooden mains laid under the city's streets the following year.

Why it applies, and its limits: The successor utility's own account of the aqueduct's two forms, open cut outside and buried conduit inside, which is the vocabulary our capital's water supply is drawn in. Its limit is that it is one system's history. And it is the shogun's own work in the largest city in the country, an upper bound a provincial seat would never match.

Used for: the buried stone and wooden mains under Edo

ashigaru-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 足軽 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B6%B3%E8%BB%BD)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the ashigaru, the foot soldiers of the warrior houses: their rise in the wars and their Edo-period standing, strictly set apart from full samurai status and often reckoned with the household servants.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that Edo ashigaru stood below samurai status. A tertiary summary used for that standing. The Edo-period section the quoted sentence sits in carries the encyclopedia's own insufficient-sources notice.

Used for: ashigaru set apart from samurai status in the Edo period

kanra-ashigaru-nagaya

甘楽町教育委員会 (Kanra Town Board of Education), 旧小幡藩武家屋敷足軽長屋 (https://www.town.kanra.lg.jp/kyouiku/bunkazai/bunkazai/20200722123543.html)

What it is: A municipal cultural-property page from Kanra in Gunma on a surviving Edo-period ashigaru row house of the former Obata domain: a terrace of identical minimal units, each two ken wide and three and a half deep, built for the domain's low-ranking retainers.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a measured surviving example of the uniform terrace for a domain's lowest retainers, the form this page weighs and declines for the capital. Its limit is that it is one small domain's terrace. The late-Edo date is the page's presumption, five of an estimated ten units survive, and the page names no survey for its dimensions.

Used for: a surviving ashigaru terrace of identical two-ken units

wugou-song-cremation-rujia

吴钩, 宋朝的土葬与火葬之争, 儒家网 (https://www.rujiazg.com/article/4066)

What it is: An essay by Wu Gou, a published writer on Song history, on the Confucian-studies portal 儒家网, on the Song dispute between burial and cremation: the edicts against cremation, the dozens of crematoria of the Southern Song capital and the order restoring fourteen of them, and the monks who kept the state's paupers' grounds under stipend.

Why it applies, and its limits: It quotes the Song administrative record on how many crematoria the capital had. Its limits are that it is a popular essay with a thesis, and that it quotes the record rather than being it. The essay names no edition or archive for the edict it quotes, so the quotation cannot be checked against a text.

Used for: Lin'an's several dozen crematoria and the edict restoring fourteen

guangdong-tongzhi-14

『廣東通志』卷十四 城池 (the Guangdong provincial gazetteer, Siku Quanshu recension), Chinese Wikisource transcription (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/廣東通志_(四庫全書本)/卷14)

What it is: The walls-and-moats chapter of the Guangdong provincial gazetteer in its Siku Quanshu recension, a primary administrative record listing each city's walls and moats and the officials who built, repaired and dredged them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a primary record of a Chinese city moat silting up and being dredged again and again by successive prefects, the maintenance cycle our moat's drawdown state stands for. Its limit is that it records the fact of each dredging and not the interval between them. It is read from a crowd-transcribed wiki copy rather than a critical edition, so a disputed character would have to be settled elsewhere, and the quoted case is Guangzhou, a great provincial capital and port, not an ordinary county seat.

Used for: Guangzhou's moat silting and being dredged again under successive officials

coastalwiki-siltation

Coastal Wiki (Flanders Marine Institute), "Siltation in harbors and fairways" (https://www.coastalwiki.org/wiki/Siltation_in_harbors_and_fairways)

What it is: A technical reference article in Coastal Wiki, the coastal-engineering encyclopedia maintained by the Flanders Marine Institute for the European coastal-science community, on why harbor basins and fairways silt up and what their maintenance costs.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the mechanism by which a still basin cut off a moving channel fills with sediment, which is why our river capital keeps its wharf on the bank. Its limit is that it is present-day harbor engineering, written for tidal ports rather than premodern river towns.

Used for: basin siltation from sediment exchange, and the dredging it forces

ujidera-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 氏寺 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B0%8F%E5%AF%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the ujidera, the clan temple: the Buddhist temples that powerful clans built from the Asuka period onward for the repose and benefit of their house, in place of the tombs they had raised before.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the clan temple to the Asuka period, which is what makes it older than the castle towns on this page. A tertiary summary used for the dating. The article carries a no-reliable-sources notice, cites only a dictionary, stops at the medieval period and says nothing of clan temples in castle towns, which is the comparison this page draws.

Used for: the clan temple from the Asuka period onward

homemate-karamete

ホームメイト・リサーチ 城・日本の城 (Homemate Research), 城郭用語辞典 搦手門（からめてもん） (https://www.homemate-research-castle.com/useful/glossary/castle/2125401/)

What it is: A castle-terms glossary entry on a Japanese commercial reference site for the karamete-mon, the rear gate of a castle: its pairing with the front gate and the siege tactic it served, drawing the enemy to the front while the garrison sortied from the rear.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the doctrine behind a castle's two gates, which is why our castle draws a front and a rear gate. Its limit is that it is a commercial hobby reference rather than a military-history source.

Used for: the sortie from the rear gate against attackers held at the front

jomai-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 城米 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9F%8E%E7%B1%B3)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on jōmai, castle rice: originally the tribute rice of the shogunal lands, later the rice the shogunate and the fudai domains stockpiled in their castles as military provision.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the rice stock kept inside a castle against siege, one of the two granaries our capital draws. A tertiary summary used for that. The article carries a notice that it shows no verifiable references, and the siege-store claim rests on it alone.

Used for: jōmai as military provision stockpiled in castles

bunka-kawashiri-komegura

文化遺産オンライン (Cultural Heritage Online, Agency for Cultural Affairs), 熊本藩川尻米蔵跡 (https://online.bunka.go.jp/heritages/detail/147327)

What it is: The national cultural-heritage database's record for the Kumamoto domain's Kawashiri rice-granary site, a historic site: the river-port granary where the domain's tribute rice was collected, which also served as a naval port.

Why it applies, and its limits: An official record of a domain's tribute-rice granary standing at its river port, the wharf granary our capital draws. Its limit is that the record says nothing of stipends.

Used for: the domain's tribute-rice granary at its river port

japanese-castle-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Japanese castle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_castle)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article surveying the Japanese castle: its baileys and their arrangements, its walls, moats and gates, and the yagura turrets set at the corners of the walls and over the gates.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the corner turret as a standard element, one of the three things this page says make a castle read as one. A tertiary summary used for that element.

Used for: yagura at the corners of the walls

manzello-2019-firebrand

Hedayati, Bahrani, Zhou, Quarles and Gorham, "A Framework to Facilitate Firebrand Characterization", Frontiers in Mechanical Engineering 5:43, 2019 (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/mechanical-engineering/articles/10.3389/fmech.2019.00043/full)

What it is: A peer-experimental studyed open-access review in Frontiers in Mechanical Engineering of how firebrands are generated, carried and start new fires, with the distance beyond which only a burning brand can do so.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the physics behind this page's judgment that a cremation ground's fire risk ends at its wall: the sixty-meter figure from the fire-science literature. Its limit is that it is a wildland and structure fire review, not a study of pyres. The 60 m figure is the paper's introductory framing of the wildland-fire literature rather than a result it measured, and the paper says nothing of pyres or of small contained fires.

Used for: the 60 m beyond which only burning firebrands start new fires

nwcg-spotting

National Wildfire Coordinating Group, "Crown Fire: Spotting Fire Behavior", Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide (PMS 437) (https://www.nwcg.gov/publications/pms437/crown-fire/spotting-fire-behavior)

What it is: The spotting chapter of the US interagency Fire Behavior Field Reference Guide: how firebrands are lofted by a crown fire's convection column and carried beyond the fire, and which fires generate them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the standards body's own statement that long-range spotting comes from crown fires, which is why a small pyre's brands cannot carry a city block. Its limit is that it is written for wildland fire in North America. The guide says nothing of small or contained fires and sets no minimum fire size, so that a pyre's brands cannot carry a city block is our inference from its silence.

Used for: long-range spotting from a crown fire's convection column

senbon-dori-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 千本通 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/千本通)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Senbon-dōri, the Kyoto street named for the thousand stupa-tablets once raised along the road to the funerary ground at the western foot of Funaoka-yama.

Why it applies, and its limits: It ties the street's name and course to the funerary ground at its head, which is how this page locates Rendaino. A tertiary summary used for that. The article gives two competing origins for the name, and the one this page uses carries no citation and no date while the other does.

Used for: Senbon-dōri as the road of tablets to the Funaoka-yama burial ground

kyototuu-rendaino

京都通百科事典 (Kyoto-tsu encyclopedia), 蓮台野 (https://www.kyototuu.jp/Geography/AreaRenndaino.html)

What it is: A privately compiled Kyoto topographical encyclopedia's entry on Rendaino, the valley from Funaoka-yama to the Kamiya river that was the old capital's northern funerary ground, and the road of a thousand stupa-tablets that led to it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the ground at the head of the road that became Senbon-dōri, corroborating the Wikipedia article on the street. Its limit is that it is an amateur reference.

Used for: Rendaino's extent and its road of tablets

yoritomo-rokudo

鎌倉手帳 (yoritomo-japan.com), 六道の辻 (https://www.yoritomo-japan.com/nara-kyoto/rokudonotuji.html)

What it is: A privately maintained Japanese history-sites reference's page on the Rokudō crossroads in Kyoto, on the road to the Toribeno funerary ground, where the dead were sent off.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the crossroads on the way to Toribeno, the siting this page uses; the temple's own article beside it carries the same. Its limit is that it is an amateur reference.

Used for: the Rokudō crossroads on the road to Toribeno

japanknowledge-jishibai

歌舞伎事典 (JapanKnowledge), 地方の歌舞伎 (https://japanknowledge.com/contents/kabuki/sousetsu/08chiho.html)

What it is: The article on provincial and village kabuki in the kabuki encyclopedia JapanKnowledge serves openly (the page was read in full on 2026-09-14 while the site around it is subscription-gated; a reader who meets a paywall should say so): the local plays performed by village youth at the tutelary shrine's festival and other rites, on stages that in many villages stood permanently in the shrine precinct.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests permanent stages on shrine ground, the origin of the shrine-ground theater our provincial towns carry. Its limit is that it describes the village, and a stage rather than a roofed playhouse. The article, signed by the kabuki scholar Hattori Yukio, puts village kabuki's peak in the late Edo period and into Meiji, later than most of what these maps draw from.

Used for: permanent stages in village shrine precincts for the local kabuki

kanamaruza-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 旧金毘羅大芝居 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/旧金毘羅大芝居)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Kanamaruza at Kotohira, the playhouse of 1835 in the town before the Kotohira shrine's gate, the oldest surviving playhouse in Japan.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a permanent roofed playhouse standing in a shrine town, the case nearest to the provincial-town theater this page draws. A tertiary summary; the article does not say the house stood on the shrine's own ground.

Used for: the Kanamaruza of 1835 in Kotohira's gate-front town

touken-world-edo-housing

刀剣ワールド (Token World), 江戸時代の住宅（家）とは (https://www.touken-world.jp/tips/51221/)

What it is: An article on a commercial Japanese reference site about swords and castles on Edo-period housing by status, giving the band of hatamoto residence sizes graded by stipend.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the size band of a hatamoto's residence, against which this page classes a compound. Its limit is real: a commercial hobby reference without citations, used for a band.

Used for: hatamoto residences of 500 to 2,300 tsubo by stipend

ginza-machidukuri-width

銀座街づくり会議・銀座デザイン協議会 (Ginza Machizukuri Council and Ginza Design Council), 銀座通りの幅はなぜ27mなのか (https://www.ginza-machidukuri.jp/column/26/)

What it is: A column by the Ginza street-planning councils on why Ginza-dori is 27 m wide, tracing the Meiji street back to the Edo-period Tokaido's 7 to 8 ken and showing the modern carriageway is exactly that width.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the width of the shogun's capital's grandest through-street in the Edo period, the ceiling this page sets a castle town's avenue under. Its limit is that it is a planning council's column, and one street. The column is unsigned and undated and cites nothing for its Edo figure, which it gives as background, so the number is a modern planning body's retrospective assertion about the busiest highway in the shogunal capital.

Used for: the Edo highway width of 7 to 8 ken, Ginza-dori included

sogamae-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 総構 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%B7%8F%E6%A7%8B)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the sōgamae, the outermost enclosure of a Japanese castle that took in the whole castle town within moats, stone walls and earthen ramparts, with Odawara's nine-kilometer circuit as the exemplar.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the form our single-rampart capital follows and gives its largest example. A tertiary summary used for the definition and the scale. The form is a late-Sengoku and Momoyama answer to a besieging army, systematized after the siege of Odawara, not an Edo-period peacetime norm - which bears on whether a capital of ours draws one rampart around its whole population.

Used for: the sōgamae enclosing the whole castle town, and Odawara's 9 km

jianghu-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 匠戶 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%8C%A0%E6%88%B6)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the jianghu, the hereditary registered artisan households of the Yuan and Ming, their separate register and their obligation to serve the government workshops.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that artisans were a registered hereditary class bound to the government's works, which is the organization this page's kiln quarter rests on. A tertiary summary used for the institution; it names no kilns or potters.

Used for: the registered hereditary artisan household

mizuarasoi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 水争い (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B0%B4%E4%BA%89%E3%81%84)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on irrigation-water disputes in Japan: their causes - weirs, conduits, the fairness of division works, the order and timing of intake - and their shift from violence to litigation under village self-government.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that irrigation water was held and allocated by village associations under customary practice and that the order of intake was itself fought over in the courts, which is why this page will not give a kawata quarter a headwater tap. A tertiary summary used for the institution; it is Japanese only. The article is a stub marked for expansion.

Used for: village associations holding and litigating irrigation intake

suiriken-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 水利権 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B0%B4%E5%88%A9%E6%A8%A9)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on water rights in Japan, including the customary rights the modern River Act recognizes for intakes that predate it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that intakes drawn since before 1896 hold customary right under the modern law, which is the durability of a village's water right this page rests on. A tertiary summary used for that continuity; it is about Japanese law and says nothing of China. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. The inference backward from a modern statute's recognition of old custom to the durability of a premodern village's right is this page's own.

Used for: customary water rights surviving into modern law

fao-29-salt-tolerance

R. S. Ayers and D. W. Westcot, Water Quality for Agriculture, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 29 Rev. 1, chapter 2 (https://www.fao.org/4/t0234e/T0234E03.htm)

What it is: The FAO's standard reference on irrigation water quality, whose second chapter tabulates the salt tolerance of crops as the soil and water salinity at which yield begins to fall, and groups the crops from sensitive to tolerant.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives rice's threshold and classes it moderately sensitive, which is the measured fact behind this page's rule that a tannery's brine must not reach the paddy. A modern agronomic table standing in for a physical bound that does not change with the century; its limits are that it is a soil-salinity table and does not draw the field-water distinction this page draws.

Used for: rice's salt tolerance threshold and class

tanning-leather-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Tanning (leather)" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanning_(leather))

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on tanning, the making of leather from hides: the ancient methods of soaking, liming, bating with dung and tanning in vats, and the trade's banishment to the edge of town for its smell.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the water soak, the unhairing with lime or urine, the bating with dog or pigeon dung, the salt curing of raw hides and the trade's place at the outskirts, which are the process and the siting this page's tanning yard draws. A tertiary summary of a general and largely Western history, used for the mechanism; it says nothing of Japan.

Used for: the tanning process and the trade's siting at the edge of town

noborigama-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 登り窯 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%99%BB%E3%82%8A%E7%AA%AF)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the noborigama, the multi-chamber climbing kiln of Japan: the firebox at the foot, the chambers stepping up the slope, the flue and chimney at the top.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the chambered tunnel climbing a slope with its firebox low and its chimney high, which is the kiln form these maps draw. A tertiary summary used for the form.

Used for: the climbing kiln's chambers, firebox and chimney

charcoal-kiln-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Charcoal kiln" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charcoal_kiln)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the charcoal kiln, from the traditional earth-covered pile to the masonry and steel kilns of later industry.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the traditional charcoal burn as a hemispherical pile sealed with earth, which is the low mound shape this page contrasts with the potter's tunnel kiln. A tertiary summary used for the form of the traditional pile. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. And the article is European throughout, German in its terms and examples; the earth-covered pile is a form East Asia also knew, but the page does not say so.

Used for: the charcoal burn as a low earth-sealed mound

anagama-kiln-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Anagama kiln" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anagama_kiln)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the anagama, the single-chamber tunnel kiln of East Asia built into a slope: its form, its firing of days stoked round the clock, and the cooling that follows.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the firing's length and its round-the-clock stoking, which is why this page keeps the potters living at the kiln, and the sloped tunnel form the kiln glyph draws. A tertiary summary used for the firing and the form; it does not name the noborigama. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. Its account of the firing blends historic Asian kilns with modern studio practice, so the days-long firing is a modern potter's as much as a premodern one's.

Used for: the days-long firing stoked round the clock; the sloped tunnel form

jingdezhen-porcelain-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Jingdezhen porcelain" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingdezhen_porcelain)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the porcelain of Jingdezhen, the Chinese kiln city: its siting on its clay deposits, its imperial and private kilns, and its workforce across the centuries.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the kiln city stood at its clay and that its imperial kilns sat at the city's center with the others four kilometers out, which is the kiln-at-the-clay siting this page follows. A tertiary summary; its one passage on where the workers lived describes seasonal migrants in sheds in 1905, not resident kiln households. The page gives no period for the arrangement of the imperial kilns at the center and the others four kilometers out, and Jingdezhen is the exceptional case - a national industry grown into a city - standing behind a county seat's single works.

Used for: the kiln city sited on its clay; imperial kilns at the center, others four kilometers out

stoneware-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Stoneware" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoneware)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on stoneware, the vitrified ceramic body fired between about 1,100 and 1,300 degrees, its history and its principal centers.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the firing range that sets fine stoneware apart from a county works' earthenware. A tertiary summary used for the range alone.

Used for: stoneware's firing range

earthenware-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Earthenware" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earthenware)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on earthenware, the low-fired porous ceramic body, its firing range and its place among the pottery types.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the firing range of the coarse ware a county works makes, beside the stoneware article's range for the finer body, which is the temperature gap this page argues from. A tertiary summary used for the range alone. The sentence carrying the firing range has no citation on the page.

Used for: earthenware's firing range

six-ancient-kilns-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Six Ancient Kilns" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Ancient_Kilns)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Six Ancient Kilns, the six medieval Japanese ceramic centers - Seto, Tokoname, Echizen, Shigaraki, Tamba and Bizen - and the wares named for them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It names the districts each known for one ware, which is this page's evidence that fine stoneware was a district's specialty rather than a county seat's. A tertiary summary used for the names; it does not say what an ordinary county seat did or did not fire. The grouping of six is a twentieth-century scholar's construct, devised after the war by Koyama Fujio; the districts are medieval, the canon is modern.

Used for: the districts each named for their one ware

cattle-crush-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Cattle crush" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle_crush)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the cattle crush or livestock crush, the frame that restrains a beast, with its history as the ox-shoeing frame of England, Spain and America.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the frame's old use was shoeing oxen, that it carries a belly sling, and that in Spain it was a village fixture, which is the standing frame this page's smithy apron carries. A tertiary summary used for the form and the fixture; it gives no dimension. And the frame is a Western fixture: the page names England, Spain and America and no East Asian use, while Japan's own hoof practice was straw, so the frame on these maps is a transplant the smithy sentence labels as this page's reading.

Used for: the ox shod slung in a standing shoeing frame

teitetsu-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 蹄鉄 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B9%84%E9%89%84)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the horseshoe, with a section on Japan: the straw umagutsu used from ancient times, the systematic adoption of Western metal shoes from Meiji, and straw sandals lingering in farming districts into Taisho.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that Japan protected hooves with straw until Meiji, which is why these maps give a courier station a sandal supply rather than a shoeing forge. A tertiary summary used for that one fact; it does not say nails were unknown before Meiji. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

Used for: straw umagutsu until Meiji; metal shoeing systematic only after

tatara-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Tatara (furnace)" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tatara_(furnace))

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the tatara, the Japanese ironsand smelting furnace: its construction, the three-day firing, the tonnages of sand and charcoal consumed and of steel produced.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the charcoal consumed against the steel produced, which is the fuel hunger this page argues from. A tertiary summary used for the tonnages; it ties the product to swords and says nothing of hooves. The tonnages are given with no date and no attribution to a period smelt; they describe the standardized run of the kind carried out today for swordsmiths, not an Edo ledger.

Used for: the tonnages of ironsand and charcoal per firing

tatara-seitetsu-jawiki

ja.wikipedia たたら製鉄 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%81%9F%E3%81%9F%E3%82%89%E8%A3%BD%E9%89%84)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on tatara ironmaking: the furnace, the iron sand and charcoal it consumed, the products it yielded and the two-stage refining that followed.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states what the iron was made into and how the refining hearth worked - pig iron reheated and its carbon burned down under the bellows - which is what this page's account of a smelting valley's works rests on. A tertiary summary used for the products and the refining sequence.

Used for: the products of tatara iron; the refining hearth's decarburizing

hoofcare-japanese-hoof-sandals

Fran Jurga, "Hoofcare History: Japanese Hoof Sandals Gave Horses Removable Traction", Hoofcare + Lameness blog, 2013 (https://hoofcare.blogspot.com/2013/02/hoofcare-history-japanese-hoof-sandals.html)

What it is: A post on a farriery trade publication's blog about the Japanese straw horse-sandal, drawing on two Western periodicals of the late nineteenth century - a farriers' journal correspondent's report of their price and a Scientific American piece on their cheapness and wear.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the sandals were cheap, quickly worn out and easily replaced, which is why a courier station on these maps stocks them. Its limits are that it is a trade blog retelling a traveler's account rather than scholarship, and that it gives no rate of wear per distance. The observations are of Meiji Japan in the 1890s, after the setting's period.

Used for: straw sandals as cheap consumables that wore out fast

burakumin-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Burakumin" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burakumin)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the burakumin, Japan's outcaste communities, their historical statuses (eta, hinin, kawaramono), their occupations in butchery and leatherwork, and where they lived.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the communities stood on riverbanks because tanning needed the water and that they were registered and settled apart, as separate villages or as parts of towns, which is the siting this page's tanning yard and outcaste quarter follow. A tertiary summary used for the siting and the segregation; it gives no siege rationale and no distance.

Used for: the outcaste communities on riverbanks for the tanning, settled apart

eta-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 穢多 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A9%A2%E5%A4%9A)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the eta, the hereditary outcaste status of pre-Meiji Japan: its occupations, its administration under the chori heads, and where its communities stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states where the communities stood - the village edge, beside a river - and what work the status carried: disposing of fallen cattle and horses, hide work, leather goods, sandals, lamp wicks, and the executioner's, constable's and watchman's duties. A tertiary summary used for the siting and the occupations; it is a national generalization and names no particular castle town. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

Used for: the outcaste quarter at the edge and by water; the caste's occupations

tsukurizakaya-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 造り酒屋 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%80%A0%E3%82%8A%E9%85%92%E5%B1%8B)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the sake-brewing house as a business and a social institution: its origins among families of wealth, its shop at the town center, its household of clerks, apprentices and guards.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the brewer's standing as local elite with a shop at the center of town, which is why this page keeps the brewery in town rather than at its edge. A tertiary summary used for that standing; it gives no count of brewers per town and no building sizes. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. The article runs down to the modern trade, so the shop at the center is read as the early-modern form.

Used for: brewers as town elite with a shop at the center

cangue-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Cangue" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cangue)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the cangue, the wooden collar worn as a public punishment in China and its neighbors, with its use in the Qing code and its later religious survivals.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the collar was worn continuously for up to several months and shows the magistrate's seal on the boards, which is the public half of the punishment this page draws. A tertiary summary used for the duration and the seal; it gives no statutory table of terms. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. The seal cited is read off a photograph of about 1870, a late-Qing object rather than a statute.

Used for: the cangue worn for months under the magistrate's seal

rekilabo-shokeijo

歴史文化探訪ラボ (rekilabo), 江戸時代の処刑場が人通りの多い街道沿いにわざわざ設置されたワケ (https://rekilabo.com/syokeijyo/)

What it is: A popular-history web article on why Edo's execution grounds were deliberately set along the busy highways into the city, naming Suzugamori on the Tokaido and Kozukappara on the Nikko road.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the siting and gives the shogunate's motive as deterrence, which is what this page's rule about the ground standing on the busiest way rests on. Its limits are that it is a popular site signed only with the site's name, with no citations a reader can follow (it names the 公事方御定書 of 1742 in its text), and that the motive is its reading of the record rather than a quoted ordinance.

Used for: the grounds at the highway entrances, passed by everyone entering, as a deterrent

tsuihokei-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 日本における追放刑 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AB%E3%81%8A%E3%81%91%E3%82%8B%E8%BF%BD%E6%94%BE%E5%88%91)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on banishment as a punishment in Japan, from the ancient codes through the Edo period, including the banishments a village imposed under its own law.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a village punished breaches of its own code by banishment, which is the ceiling this page gives village authority. A tertiary summary used for that one institution; it does not say that nothing heavier was ever available to a village. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

Used for: the village's own banishment, murabarai and tokorobarai

kawagoe-tokinokane-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 時の鐘 (川越市) (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%99%82%E3%81%AE%E9%90%98_(%E5%B7%9D%E8%B6%8A%E5%B8%82))

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Kawagoe's time-bell tower, the three-story wooden bell tower that has rung the hours over the old castle town since the seventeenth century and stands rebuilt after the fire of 1893.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the tower's height and its three stories, the one Japanese time-bell tower this page sizes against. A tertiary summary; it gives no base dimension and the town's population is not on it. The 16 m is the height of the 1894 rebuilding after the town fire, the fourth tower on the site, not a measured Edo tower.

Used for: the Kawagoe bell tower's 16 m and three stories

xingcheng-gucheng-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 兴城古城 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E5%85%B4%E5%9F%8E%E5%8F%A4%E5%9F%8E)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the old walled city of Xingcheng in Liaoning, the best-preserved Ming garrison city, with its walls, gates and the bell-and-drum tower at its central crossroads.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the tower's 21 m square platform pierced by a cross vault and the city's character as a Ming garrison, which is the street-arch tower type this page keeps off a small county seat. A tertiary summary used for the dimension and the type. The dimensions carry no citation on the page, whose one reference is the heritage listing, and they describe the platform after its repair of 1777.

Used for: Xingcheng's 21 m tower over the crossroads in a garrison city

idobata-kaigi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 井戸端会議 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%BA%95%E6%88%B8%E7%AB%AF%E4%BC%9A%E8%AD%B0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the idobata kaigi, the well-side gossip circle, as the gathering of tenement women at a communal well and as the idiom it became.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the circle was a tenement institution around a shared well, which is why this page counts the dense well pattern as urban rather than village density. A tertiary summary used for that setting; it gives no households-per-well figure. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. It dates the practice only as former.

Used for: the well-side circle as an urban tenement institution

kanda-josui-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 神田上水 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A5%9E%E7%94%B0%E4%B8%8A%E6%B0%B4)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Kanda aqueduct, Edo's first waterworks: its course from Inokashira pond, its wooden mains under the streets, the draw-wells it fed in the tenements, and the order in which it served the city's districts.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the tenements drew from shared aqueduct wells and that the samurai districts were supplied first with the remainder going to the townspeople, which is the shared-draw pattern and the status distinction this page's wells follow. A tertiary summary; it describes the shogunal capital, the largest system in the country.

Used for: tenement draw-wells shared in the alley; samurai districts served first

sekisho-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 関所 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%96%A2%E6%89%80)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the sekisho, the barrier stations of Japanese roads from antiquity through the Edo period: their military, policing and toll-levying functions and their siting at passes and river crossings.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the inspection-and-toll function and where the stations stood, which is the institution behind the tariff posts these maps place at the gates by the setting's canon. A tertiary summary; the historical stations stood on the roads rather than on a city's gates, a difference this page states.

Used for: barrier stations levying tolls, at passes and river crossings

shukuba-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 宿場 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%AE%BF%E5%A0%B4)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the shukuba, the post station of the Edo highways: its transport office, its inns for officials and for ordinary travelers, and the porters and horses it kept on hand for the relay.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a post station kept horses and porters permanently for the official relay beside its inns, which is the wayside facility with stabling this page names. A tertiary summary used for the institution; it says nothing of pasture.

Used for: the post station's inns and standing horses

fao-industrial-charcoal

FAO, Industrial charcoal making, FAO Forestry Paper 63, chapter 5, earth pits for charcoal making (https://www.fao.org/4/x5328e/x5328e06.htm)

What it is: The FAO's manual on charcoal production at industrial scale, whose chapter on the earth pit - the traditional method, documented at about thirty cubic meters gross with miniature village pits beside it - gives the fuelwood-to-charcoal ratio of that method.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the wood consumed per unit of charcoal - about four and a half to one by weight in a working pit - which is the ratio that sends the kiln to the wood on these maps. A modern technical manual standing in for a physical ratio that does not change with the century; the method it documents is the earth pit itself, close to a premodern burn; the ratio is a yield of one method at one size, so it bounds rather than measures a household's burn.

Used for: the fuelwood-to-charcoal ratio

edo-hantei-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 江戸藩邸 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B1%9F%E6%88%B8%E8%97%A9%E9%82%B8)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Edo domain residences, the upper, middle and lower estates each daimyo kept in the shogunal capital under alternate attendance: their siting relative to the castle, their sizes and their uses.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the lower residences were large garden estates in the outskirts used as villas and fire refuges while the working residence stood nearest the castle, which is the pattern of roomier estates outside this page draws. A tertiary summary; it describes daimyo under alternate attendance in Edo, an institution a domain seat's own samurai did not have. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

Used for: daimyo lower residences as roomy estates in the outskirts

equine-nutrition-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Equine nutrition" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equine_nutrition)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the feeding and watering of horses, with the daily water intake of an average horse and its increase under work, heat and dry forage.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a horse's daily water and the multiplier under hard work, which sizes the watering a courier or wagon yard must supply. A modern husbandry summary standing in for a physical requirement that does not change with the century. The figure is keyed to a modern horse of 450 kg; the horses of a premodern East Asian post road were far smaller, so the intake carried onto these maps is an upper figure.

Used for: a horse's daily water intake and its increase under work

water-buffalo-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Water buffalo" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_buffalo)

What it is: The English Wikipedia species article on the domestic water buffalo, its husbandry and its need of wallows in hot climates.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the buffalo's need to wallow to keep cool, which is why a livery yard on these maps offers a buffalo more than a trough. A tertiary summary used for that one behavior; its daily water intake is not on it.

Used for: the buffalo's need of a wallow

caravanserai-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Caravanserai" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caravanserai)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the caravanserai, the roadside inn of the Silk Road and the Islamic world, with its courtyard, its well or fountain, and its stabling for pack animals.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that whole trains were lodged and watered from a courtyard well or fountain, the relay-watering pattern this page's livery yard follows. A tertiary summary of a different region's tradition standing in for the pattern; it makes no comparison with multiplying basins.

Used for: watering a whole train from one courtyard well

mdfcta-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Metropolitan Drinking Fountain and Cattle Trough Association" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Drinking_Fountain_and_Cattle_Trough_Association)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Victorian London charity that built the city's public drinking fountains and granite cattle troughs, quoting Dickens's Dictionary of London of 1879 on their use.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the throughput of one busy street trough in a day, which is the turnover figure this page's relay watering rests on. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary of a guidebook's 1879 claim, and that Victorian London's horse traffic is a far larger case than a provincial livery yard. And a Victorian street trough was fed continuously from the water mains, while a yard basin on these maps is filled by bucket from a well, so the throughput does not carry across as a bound on how many animals one basin serves.

Used for: one trough serving 1,800 horses in a day

baidu-pingyao-city-tower

Baidu Baike, "Pingyao City Tower" (https://baike.baidu.com/en/item/Pingyao%20City%20Tower/84025)

What it is: The English-language Baidu Baike encyclopedia entry on Pingyao's Market Tower, the pavilion straddling South Street at the center of the walled county seat: its height, its position and its standing as the town's one tall building.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the tower's height and its singularity in the town, which is the county-tier anchor this page's tower glyph is sized to. A tertiary summary from a commercial encyclopedia used for those two facts. Pingyao was an unusually rich merchant town, so its tower is a generous county anchor; the height is the same figure the Chinese Wikipedia entry carries, so the two do not corroborate one another; and the English page is a machine rendering of the Chinese.

Used for: the Market Tower's 18.5 m and its being the only tall building

zhonggulou-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 鐘鼓樓 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%90%98%E9%BC%93%E6%A8%93)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the bell-and-drum towers of Chinese cities: the paired arrangement facing across an axis, the single combined building, and the morning-bell, evening-drum institution of announcing the hours.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the paired form as the usual arrangement, the combined single tower as a variant, and the towers' duty of announcing the time, which is the county-seat tower these maps draw. A tertiary summary; it gives no rule about how many towers a county seat had. The article is a stub carrying the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks references.

Used for: the paired and the combined tower forms; morning bell, evening drum

qiaolou-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 谯楼 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E8%B0%AF%E6%A5%BC)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia disambiguation page for the qiaolou, whose lead line defines it as the drum tower of an official compound where the drums and horns for announcing the hours and receiving guests were kept.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the form as the official compound's own timekeeping building, the variant this page names beside the freestanding tower. A tertiary summary used for the definition. The page carries no references at all and fixes no period.

Used for: the qiaolou defined

bianjinglou-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 边靖楼 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E8%BE%B9%E9%9D%96%E6%A5%BC)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Bianjing Lou, the Ming drum tower of Dai county in Shanxi, standing at the central crossroads of the county town.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places a county town's drum tower at the exact center of its crossroads, which is the siting these maps give the tower. A tertiary summary used for the siting.

Used for: a county drum tower at the central crossroads

yuanzhou-qiaolou-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 袁州谯楼 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E8%A2%81%E5%B7%9E%E8%B0%AF%E6%A5%BC)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Yuanzhou qiaolou in Jiangxi, the drum tower of a prefectural office founded in 944 under the Southern Tang and fitted out in 1219 as an observatory for measuring, keeping and announcing the time.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the qiaolou was part of the prefectural office compound, which is why this page calls it the compound's own tower rather than a poor seat's substitute. A tertiary summary; it does not say the tower stood over the compound's gate. The building is of the tenth to thirteenth centuries, several centuries before the Ming and Edo anchors these maps take.

Used for: the qiaolou as part of a prefectural office compound

kokucho-tokinokane-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 石町時の鐘 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%9F%B3%E7%94%BA%E6%99%82%E3%81%AE%E9%90%98)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Kokucho time bell, Edo's first and principal time bell: its founding, its public funding and the bell fee levied on the blocks within earshot, and the list of the city's other time bells.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the bell was run at public expense on a fee levied from the roughly four hundred blocks that could hear it, and lists the city's other time bells, all but this one at temples, which is the earshot anchor and the temple-bell pattern this page uses. A tertiary summary used for the fee district and the list; the fee is per ken of frontage, not per household.

Used for: the Kokucho bell's fee district of about 400 blocks; Edo's other time bells at temples

dageng-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 打更 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E6%89%93%E6%9B%B4)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on dageng, the night watch of Chinese towns: the five watches from seven in the evening, the watchmen who walked the streets striking clappers and gongs to call the hour, and the warnings against fire and theft they cried.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the watches were relayed through the streets by walking watchmen, which is how one tower's signal reached a whole city and why this page gives a capital no second tower. A tertiary summary used for the relay and the five watches. Much of the article documents modern survivals and regions outside the setting's Chinese core, so the imperial-era dating of the relayed watch rests on its general framing.

Used for: night watchmen relaying the hours through the streets

beijing-zhonggulou-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 北京钟鼓楼 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-hans/%E5%8C%97%E4%BA%AC%E9%92%9F%E9%BC%93%E6%A5%BC)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on Beijing's bell and drum towers, the paired Yuan-founded towers at the north end of the capital's axis, and the routine by which they struck the night watches.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the capital's one pair of towers timing the watches for the whole inner city, the China-first scaling answer this page sets against Edo's many bells. A tertiary summary; it describes the imperial capital, a ceiling rather than a norm.

Used for: Beijing's towers striking the watches for the whole city

kimon-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 鬼門 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%AC%BC%E9%96%80)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kimon, the northeast as the unlucky direction of Japanese geomancy, with the temples set to guard it in Kyoto and Edo.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the direction and Edo's guardian temple in it, which is the bearing this page reads the city's northern institutions against. A tertiary summary used for the direction; the alignment of execution ground, pleasure quarter and outcaste head's compound to it is this page's reading.

Used for: the kimon as the northeast

yoshiwara-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 吉原遊廓 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%90%89%E5%8E%9F%E9%81%8A%E5%BB%93)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Yoshiwara, Edo's licensed pleasure quarter, its founding, its 1656 removal to Nihon-zutsumi behind Senso-ji in Asakusa, and its later history.

Why it applies, and its limits: It records where the quarter was moved to, which is one of the three places this page aligns to Edo's northeast. A tertiary summary used for the relocation; it says nothing of the kimon or of direction. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. And the article gives its own reason for the move - the city had grown and daimyo residences had come up against the quarter - which competes with the northeast reading this page draws from the places.

Used for: the Yoshiwara's removal to Asakusa

kawaramono-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 河原者 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B2%B3%E5%8E%9F%E8%80%85)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kawaramono, the medieval and early-modern outcaste group of Kyoto named for the riverbeds they lived on, their trades in slaughter and leather, and the two explanations offered for the riverbed - untaxed ground, or the water the leather work needed.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the name, the trades and the riverbed siting with both reasons, which is the riverside outcaste quarter this page draws. A tertiary summary; the name is one they were called, not one they gave themselves. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources. Its subject is medieval Kyoto, earlier than most of what these maps draw from.

Used for: the kawaramono on the riverbeds, and why

danzaemon-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 弾左衛門 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%BC%BE%E5%B7%A6%E8%A1%9B%E9%96%80)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Danzaemon, the hereditary head of the eta of eastern Japan under the shogunate, and on his Asakusa Shinmachi compound: its enclosure, its buildings, its court and jail, and the officials housed there.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes an outcaste head's precinct standing inside the city as an enclosed block with residences, storehouses, a shrine, a court and a jail, which is the in-city outcaste quarter this page argues for. A tertiary summary used for the compound's contents; it does not say where the residents worked. And the compound was the headquarters of the man who administered every eta community in eastern Japan, inside the largest city in the country, with a court and a jail because it held delegated jurisdiction; an ordinary provincial seat's outcaste block is a far smaller and plainer thing.

Used for: the Danzaemon compound inside Edo and what stood in it

kosatsu-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Kōsatsu" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C5%8Dsatsu)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the kosatsu, the Edo-period official notice board, its contents and where it stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the boards stood where traffic was frequent - at post stations and barriers - which is the traffic siting this page's board follows. A tertiary summary used for that siting. The article is a few paragraphs on two references, one of them another wiki, and it says what the Japanese article cited beside it says, so the two are not independent.

Used for: the notice board sited where traffic was frequent

shoya-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 庄屋 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%BA%84%E5%B1%8B)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the shoya, the Edo-period village headman (nanushi, kimoiri): the duties of the office, the documents it signed and relayed, and the literacy it required.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the headman copied and relayed the lord's circulars and needed reading, writing and the abacus for the office, which is the one reader per settlement this page's notice board depends on. A tertiary summary used for the duties. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks sufficient sources.

Used for: the headman relaying circulars and required to be literate

kawarabuki-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 瓦葺き (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%93%A6%E8%91%BA%E3%81%8D)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on tile roofing in Japan, its forms and its use on houses, with the ease of replacing a single broken tile.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a kawara roof is repaired tile by tile, which is why this page counts a tiled roof as a lasting one. A tertiary summary; it gives no lifespan. The article carries the encyclopedia's own notice that it lacks citations and may hold original research.

Used for: tile roofs repaired in patches

sonraku-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 村落 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9D%91%E8%90%BD)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the village as a settlement form, with its classification of village shapes and the ground each was sited on.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that line villages follow natural levees and the spring line at the foot of the hills, the easy-water ground this page's dispersed households sit on. A tertiary summary used for the siting. The passage dates nothing and its examples are present-day villages, so it establishes the landform logic rather than that premodern villages were sited so.

Used for: villages strung along levees and spring lines

kotobank-genroku-kuniezu

kotobank 元禄国絵図 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%85%83%E7%A6%84%E5%9B%BD%E7%B5%B5%E5%9B%B3)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the reference-encyclopedia entry on the Genroku provincial maps, the shogunate's 1697 survey of every province: its policy for drawing boundaries and recording village yields, and how disputes and variances from the older maps were settled.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the district boundaries within a province - not domain borders - were to be drawn clearly and variances settled by inquiry before the map was made up, which is the authenticity this page claims for a drawn line. A tertiary summary of a published reference work, used for the survey's policy.

Used for: the Genroku survey's boundary policy

tamahagane-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 玉鋼 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%8E%89%E9%8B%BC)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on tamahagane, the steel of the tatara: how the kera lump was broken and sorted from the 1750s, and how its fractions were finished into steel or into wrought iron at the smithy.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the crushing and sorting of the kera and the finishing of part of it into wrought iron, the sequence this page's smelting valley follows. A tertiary summary used for that sequence. The crushing and sorting is dated to the 1750s, while the finishing of fractions at the smithy into wrought iron sits in the article's account of the modern Yasukuni tatara, so the sequence's seventeenth-century date rests on the paper cited beside it.

Used for: the kera crushed, sorted and part refined to wrought iron

chouara-tannery-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Chouara Tannery" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouara_Tannery)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Chouara tannery of Fez, the medieval tannery still worked by hand in stone vats of lime, urine and pigeon dung.

Why it applies, and its limits: It shows one other tradition soaking hides in standing vats rather than a current, the pit-soaking form a ditch-fed yard on these maps falls back to. A tertiary summary of one Moroccan case; it does not speak for every other tradition.

Used for: the standing-vat soak at Fez

tokoname-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 常滑焼 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%B8%B8%E6%BB%91%E7%84%BC)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Tokoname ware, the stoneware of the Chita peninsula, with its medieval kiln-site counts and its later history.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the scale of a medieval kiln district in kiln sites, which is the real size this page's one drawn works stands down from. A tertiary summary used for the count; it does not give distribution or workers' residence.

Used for: the thousands of medieval Tokoname kiln sites

edo-no-kaji-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 江戸の火事 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B1%9F%E6%88%B8%E3%81%AE%E7%81%AB%E4%BA%8B)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the fires of Edo and the shogunate's fire-prevention measures: the great fires, the firebreaks, and the ordinances restricting bathhouse hours, fireworks and refuse burning.

Why it applies, and its limits: It records fire ordinances restricting fire-using trades inside the dense town, the fire law this page's kiln siting rests on. A tertiary summary; no passage names kilns.

Used for: Edo's fire ordinances on trades and open burning

hinin-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 非人 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%9D%9E%E4%BA%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the hinin, the Edo-period outcaste status below the eta: who fell into it and what its members did.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the status and lists its occupations, none of them a craft, which is what this page's separation of the potter from the outcaste rests on. A tertiary summary used for the definition. That potters were not of the status is drawn from the list's silence, not stated on the page.

Used for: the hinin status and its occupations

sueki-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 須恵器 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%A0%88%E6%81%B5%E5%99%A8)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Sue ware, the gray stoneware of ancient Japan: its kilns, its high reducing firing, and the tile-and-ware kiln sites of the Nara period.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that ware kilns were built beside tile kilns at the same sites, which is why these maps draw one works for both. A tertiary summary used for that pairing; it is ancient, not Edo, and speaks of kilns side by side rather than one kiln firing both.

Used for: tile kilns and ware kilns built together

pottery-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Pottery" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pottery)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on pottery as a craft and a material, including its durability and its standing as the commonest artifact of archaeology.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that fired clay survives where organic goods rot, which is why this page treats every settlement's ceramics as a steady demand a works must meet. A tertiary summary used for that one fact.

Used for: pottery's survival and ubiquity in the archaeological record

alfred-weber-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Alfred Weber" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Weber)

What it is: The English Wikipedia biography of Alfred Weber, carrying his least-cost theory of industrial location and its material index.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the rule by which heavy, cheap goods are made near their market, which this page applies to storage jars. A modern economic theory standing in for a transport constraint that does not change with the century; the application to ceramics is this page's own.

Used for: the material-index rule of location

farrier-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Farrier" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrier)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the farrier, the hoof-care and shoeing trade, its history and its traditional premises.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that farriers traditionally worked from a forge with a yard for hot-shoeing, which is the premises this page's smith apron draws. A tertiary summary about Europe; it carries no size.

Used for: the farrier's forge with a yard

blacksmith-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Blacksmith" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blacksmith)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the blacksmith, the trade and its premises; the sentence quoted sits under the article's medieval heading, so it describes medieval Europe.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that smiths worked in small shops, often at the center of a village or town, which is the modest premises this page gives a town smith. A tertiary summary; it carries no measurement.

Used for: the smith's small shop at the center of town

yizhan-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 驿站 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%A9%BF%E7%AB%99)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the yizhan, the imperial post-relay stations of China, with the Tang network's count and staffing and the Han's thirty-li spacing.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the Tang network's 1,639 stations and the Han's spacing of a station every thirty li, the comparison figure for the setting's own denser courier network. A tertiary summary used for those two numbers; the setting's road mileage and courier counts are the GM's canon. The count and the spacing come from different dynasties, the count cited to the 大唐六典 and the spacing given for the Han.

Used for: the Tang post network's count and the Han spacing

horseshoe-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Horseshoe" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the horseshoe: its history from wrapped hooves in ancient Asia through the nailed iron shoe of medieval Europe and the iron shoes of Yuan China.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that iron shoes became common in China only from the Yuan and that earlier hoof protection was wrapped or strapped, which is why this page does not rest its argument on Chinese practice. A tertiary summary; it does not say whether the Yuan shoes were nailed.

Used for: hoof protection before and after the Yuan

hipposandal-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Hipposandal" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hipposandal)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the hipposandal, the Roman iron hoof-boot fastened with clips and laces.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the Roman device was strapped on rather than nailed, one of the two comparisons this page considered and set aside. A tertiary summary; it does not mention the imperial post.

Used for: the Roman strap-on hoof-boot

kotobank-tsukigomeya

kotobank 搗米屋 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%90%97%E7%B1%B3%E5%B1%8B)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the reference-encyclopedia entries on the tsukigomeya, the Edo rice-hulling retailer that bought brown rice from the brokers, polished it and sold it white to consumers.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the hulling and polishing was the shop's own work, which is why the rice dealer draws as an ordinary shop with no separate mill. A tertiary summary of published reference works, used for that one fact.

Used for: the rice dealer polishing in-shop

karausu-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 唐臼 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%94%90%E8%87%BC)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the karausu or fumi-usu, the treadle mortar in which a foot-worked pestle pounds grain.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the treadle pestle this page puts in a rice dealer's shop. A tertiary summary used for the tool; it does not say where the tool stood. The article is a stub carrying the encyclopedia's own notice that it needs sources, and it dates and locates the tool nowhere.

Used for: the treadle mortar

senju-shuku-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 千住宿 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%8D%83%E4%BD%8F%E5%AE%BF)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Senju-juku, the first post station north of Edo on the Nikko and Oshu highways: its distance from Nihonbashi, its bridge over the Arakawa, and the Kozukappara execution ground in the town just south of it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It places the northern execution ground about two ri, five miles, out along the highway, which is the distance behind this page's rule that a ground hugs a road rather than a gate. A tertiary summary used for the distance and the placement. The two ri is the page's distance to the post town; that the ground in the town just south of it stood about as far out is this page's reading of two sentences.

Used for: Kozukappara two ri out along the highway

wulin-jiushi-wikisource

周密 (Zhou Mi), 武林舊事 (Wulin jiushi), 卷六 瓦子勾欄, Chinese Wikisource transcription (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%AD%A6%E6%9E%97%E8%88%8A%E4%BA%8B/%E5%8D%B7%E5%85%AD)

What it is: The late thirteenth-century memoir of Southern Song Hangzhou, whose sixth chapter lists the city's pleasure precincts (wazi) inside and outside the wall by name, twenty-three of them, and the goulan of the most flourishing.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the primary list of a Song capital's pleasure precincts, the count this page sets against a provincial city's touring players. A primary text read from a crowd-transcribed wiki copy; it gives a goulan count for one precinct only, and the other Hangzhou memoir counts the precincts differently.

Used for: Hangzhou's twenty-three wazi and the North Wa's thirteen goulan

dongjing-menghualu-juan2

孟元老 (Meng Yuanlao), 東京夢華錄 (Dongjing meng Hua lu), 卷二, the chapter on the streets east of the corner tower (Dongjiaolou jiexiang), Chinese Wikisource transcription (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9D%B1%E4%BA%AC%E5%A4%A2%E8%8F%AF%E9%8C%84/%E5%8D%B7%E4%BA%8C)

What it is: The second chapter of the memoir of Northern Song Kaifeng written about 1147, on the streets east of the Eastern Corner Tower: the three pleasure precincts there, the fifty-odd goulan within them and the great sheds that held thousands.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the primary count of a Song capital's theater sheds, the figure this page sets against a provincial city's touring players. A primary text read from a crowd-transcribed wiki copy; it describes the imperial capital, a ceiling rather than a norm, and it counts one district's precincts.

Used for: Kaifeng's fifty-odd goulan and the largest shed holding several thousand

mengliang-lu-wikisource

吳自牧 (Wu Zimu), 夢粱錄 (Mengliang lu), 卷十九 瓦舍, Chinese Wikisource transcription (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%A4%A2%E7%B2%B1%E9%8C%84/%E5%8D%B719)

What it is: The memoir of Southern Song Hangzhou of about 1274, whose nineteenth chapter gives the city's pleasure precincts as no fewer than seventeen inside and outside the wall and their founding for the garrison's northern soldiers.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the second primary count of Hangzhou's precincts, read beside the first so that the page carries the range the record gives rather than one figure. A primary text read from a crowd-transcribed wiki copy.

Used for: Hangzhou's seventeen or more wazi

nihon-no-shiro-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 日本の城 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC%E3%81%AE%E5%9F%8E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia survey article on the castles of Japan: their history, their parts and their layouts, including the gate-mouths and which way the front of an early-modern castle usually faced.
