Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the main gate of an early-modern castle stood at the front, usually the south, with the rear gate opposite, which is the pair and the aspect our capital's castle draws. A tertiary summary used for the convention; it gives no reason for the aspect and nothing on divination.

Used for: the ote-mon at the front, usually south, the karamete-mon at the rear

kotobank-kawazarae

kotobank 川浚 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%B7%9D%E6%B5%9A)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the dictionary entries on kawazarae, the periodic dredging of a river bed, with Edo-period usages.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the sarae this page names as a moat's maintenance and attests the practice in the Edo period, for rivers. A dictionary reference used for the term; it says nothing of moats.

Used for: the word sarae for periodic dredging

matsue-bukeyashiki-about

Matsue Buke Yashiki (Shiomi Nawate), Buke yashiki ni tsuite (About the samurai residence), the residence's own account of the house and its households (https://www.matsue-bukeyashiki.jp/about/)

What it is: The about page of the preserved samurai residence on Matsue's Shiomi Nawate, run by the San-in Chuo Shimpo newspaper company, whose credit the page carries: the house's size in tsubo, its rebuilding after the fire of 1733, the division of its front and private halves, and the rank of the retainers who lived in it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the measured size of a surviving domain-seat samurai residence and the stipend band of its households, the anchor this page checks its detached samurai house against. A custodian's visitor page rather than a survey report; its households were retainers of 500 to 1,000 koku, an upper case beside the poor samurai our terrace houses.

Used for: the residence's 67 tsubo and the 500-to-1,000-koku band of its households

chenghuangmiao-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 城隍廟 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9F%8E%E9%9A%8D%E5%BB%9F)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the City God temple, the shrine of a walled city's tutelary deity, with the Ming edict of 1369 that ranked the City Gods by the administrative rank of their cities and set off temple-building across the empire.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the ranking of City God temples down to the county, which is why a county seat on these maps carries one beside its yamen. A tertiary summary used for the edict and its date.

Used for: the 1369 edict ranking City God temples to the county

tonami-heiya-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 砺波平野 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A0%BA%E6%B3%A2%E5%B9%B3%E9%87%8E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Tonami plain, the alluvial fan in Toyama whose dispersed farmsteads are Japan's best-known case, with the Kaga domain's reclamation policy held to explain the scattering.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the tenure arrangement thought to be a major cause of the dispersed pattern, the reason this page gives for its dispersed hamlets. A tertiary summary; the arrangement is a cultivation right rather than a land grant, and the reclamation runs from the late Sengoku into mid-Edo.

Used for: the Kaga tenure arrangement behind the scattered farmsteads

kotobank-warazuka

kotobank 藁塚 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%97%81%E5%A1%9A)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the dictionary entries on the warazuka, the straw rick piled in the reaped field after threshing, an autumn season-word.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states what the rick is and when it stood, the seasonal feature these maps leave undrawn. A dictionary reference; it gives no standing duration and does not use the Toyama word waraguro.

Used for: the straw rick after the harvest

kaison-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 塊村 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A1%8A%E6%9D%91)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the kaison, the clustered village, the commonest form a village took of itself, with the ground it arose on and the row village it is set against.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states where a clustered village arose - the foot of a hill, a river terrace, a crossroads - and describes the houses gathered in an irregular lump, the knoll cluster these maps draw. A tertiary summary used for the siting and the form.

Used for: the clustered village on narrow dry ground where water could be got

wang-2023-sw-zhejiang

Wang and colleagues, "Spatial Morphological Characteristics and Evolution of Traditional Villages in the Mountainous Area of Southwest Zhejiang", ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information 12(8):317, 2023, the abstract as indexed by DOAJ (https://doaj.org/api/search/articles/doi%3A10.3390%2Fijgi12080317)

What it is: A peer-reviewed open-access study of the forms of traditional villages in Lishui, southwest Zhejiang, finding them clustered and banded and growing along rivers and roads; the abstract is read from the open-access directory's record, the publisher refusing an automated fetch.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the elongated river- and road-following village form in the Chinese literature, the form this page's linear hamlets take. A study of one mountainous district's traditional villages.

Used for: villages in southwest Zhejiang expanding along rivers and roads

reihendorf-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Reihendorf" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reihendorf)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Reihendorf, the German row village of farmsteads along a street with each holding's land adjacent to it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the row form and its reason - the farmland beside the dwelling saves transport - which is the linear settlement category this page places its strung-out hamlets in. A tertiary summary of a German form used as the documented type; the setting's villages are not German.

Used for: the row village and why its land lies beside its houses

boso-no-mura-kazusa

Chiba Prefectural Boso no Mura, 上総の農家, the museum's page on its Kazusa farmhouse (https://www.chiba-muse.or.jp/MURA/facility/page-1521181891660/page-1521294570333/)

What it is: The open-air museum's own page on its reconstructed Kazusa farmhouse, a village-headman-class compound of eight buildings rebuilt by traditional methods from nineteenth-century models.

Why it applies, and its limits: It lists the eight buildings of a headman's compound, the top of the farmstead ladder these maps draw the typical plot below. A custodian's page on a reconstruction; it describes one class of farmhouse in one province.

Used for: the eight buildings of a headman-class farm compound

kotobank-minka

kotobank 民家 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%B0%91%E5%AE%B6)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the Nipponica encyclopedia's entry on the minka, the Japanese folk house, with its plan types - the three-room hall type, the four-room type - and how the complex plans grew from them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a complex farmhouse plan is the standard type with rooms added, the growth by addition these maps' varied houses follow. A tertiary summary of a published reference work; it gives no proportions and no direction of growth.

Used for: the minka plan growing by added rooms from a standard type

naya-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 納屋 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%B4%8D%E5%B1%8B)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the naya, the separate storage shed of a farm or a fishing village.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the shed a farm kept its crop and tools in, the commoner outbuilding these maps draw beside the rarer storehouse. A tertiary summary used for the definition.

Used for: the naya as the farm's crop and tool shed

doma-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 土間 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9C%9F%E9%96%93)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the doma, the earth-floored part of a Japanese house, and what a farmhouse did in it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the doma's uses - meals after work, drying the crop, weaving sandals, tending tools - the working floor this page gives a household without a shed. A tertiary summary; it does not call the doma a store.

Used for: the doma as the farmhouse's working floor

kotobank-dozo

kotobank 土蔵 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%9C%9F%E8%94%B5)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the reference-encyclopedia entries on the dozo, the plastered earthen storehouse: its construction and what townhouses and farmhouses kept in it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the labor the walls took and what a farmhouse stored, the construction behind this page's reading of the kura as a wealth marker. A tertiary summary of published reference works; it does not price the building.

Used for: the dozo's construction and contents

fengshui-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 風水 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%A2%A8%E6%B0%B4)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on fengshui, the geomancy of siting, with the classic formula of the good seat - mountains behind, the sun before, water in front.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the seat principle a dwelling was sited by, the hill behind and water before that this page's clusters answer to. A tertiary summary; its water is a watercourse or pond, not paddy.

Used for: the fengshui seat: mountains behind, water before

sanson-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 散村 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%95%A3%E6%9D%91)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the dispersed village, sanson, the settlement form of farmhouses scattered among their fields, with the Toyama name sankyoson for the Tonami case.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the dispersed form and gives both its names and readings, the form and the words this page uses for its dispersed hamlets. A tertiary summary; it does not say how a steading was reached.

Used for: the dispersed village and its two names

back-lane-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Back lane" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_lane)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the back lane, the service way behind houses, with its origin in the planned medieval village running parallel to the main street at the far end of the plots.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the back lane and the main street together framed the planned village and that the lane divided the village from its fields, which is the field-ward edge this page draws. A tertiary summary of the English planned village, stated as such; it is not evidence for East Asia.

Used for: the back lane as a planned-village device and the village's edge toward the fields

nucleated-village-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Nucleated village" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nucleated_village)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the nucleated village, the clustered settlement form, with the planned English village's plots and back lane.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a back lane at the far end of the plots gives a planned village its regular layout, the device this page's back lane reproduces. A tertiary summary of the English medieval case, which the page cites as such.

Used for: the back lane giving a planned village its regular layout

lilong-shanghai-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Lilong, Shanghai" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilong,_Shanghai)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Shanghai's lilong lane housing, the dense terraces of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries whose lanes became the residents' shared living space.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the lanes were the public space all the houses faced and used, the socially live lane this page draws in a village. A tertiary summary of a modern urban form standing in for a village's; the scale and the century both differ.

Used for: lanes as the residents' shared space

fao-farm-structures-ch14

FAO, Farm structures in tropical climates, chapter 14, Rural water supply and sanitation (https://www.fao.org/4/s1250e/s1250e1d.htm)

What it is: A chapter of the FAO and SIDA manual on farm buildings for the tropics, on siting and protecting a rural well against the pollution of animal yards and privies.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the modern sanitary rule that a well stands uphill and some twenty meters from an animal yard, the contamination this page's byre-and-well spacing answers. A modern engineering manual for the tropics standing in for a physical hazard that does not change with the century.

Used for: the well kept twenty meters up grade from animal yards

watering-trough-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Watering trough" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watering_trough)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the watering trough, the basin set at a rural or urban watering place for animals and, as the abreuvoir, for humans too.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a community's watering place served its beasts and its humans alike, which is why a village well on these maps may have a trough beside it. A tertiary summary of a largely Western institution; it names springs, not wells, as where troughs stood.

Used for: the shared watering place for humans and animals

pig-toilet-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Pig toilet" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pig_toilet)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the pig toilet, the privy set over a pigsty, once common in rural China and attested from Han-dynasty tomb models.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the privy-and-pigsty grouping and its antiquity, the manure economy behind this page's siting of the animal facilities with the latrine. A tertiary summary; it speaks of pigsties, not of cattle sheds or chicken houses.

Used for: the privy over the pigsty, attested from the Han

hatake-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 畑 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%95%91)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the hatake, the dry field, and the grains, vegetables, beans, tubers and fruit grown on it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines where a household's bulk vegetables and dry crops were grown, which is why the dooryard bed on these maps is small. A tertiary summary used for the definition; it draws no line between a field and a kitchen garden.

Used for: the dry field as the place of bulk vegetables and dry crops

inekari-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 稲刈り (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A8%B2%E5%88%88%E3%82%8A)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the rice harvest: cutting in autumn, rack-drying in the field and threshing once the ears have dried.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that rice is cut in autumn and dried on racks in the field before threshing, which is why a paddy household's yard needs less threshing floor than a dry-grain one and why its season is the autumn. A tertiary summary; it gives no drying time and names no month for threshing.

Used for: rice cut in autumn and field-dried on racks before threshing

kurita-2019-igune

栗田英治・重岡徹・武元将忠 (Kurita Hideharu, Shigeoka Toru and Takemoto Masatada), on conserving the igune landscape of the Osaki Koudo world agricultural heritage area, 農業農村工学会誌 87(10) (2019), 825-828, J-STAGE PDF (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jjsidre/87/10/87_825/_pdf/-char/ja)

What it is: A report in the irrigation and rural engineering society's journal on conserving the homestead-grove landscape of the Osaki agricultural heritage area in Miyagi, with heights of six groves measured on the ground and from the air.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives measured heights of Tohoku homestead groves, the anchor for the tall end of this page's grove band. A present-day survey of surviving groves in one district.

Used for: measured igune heights at six points in Osaki

minami-2024-igune

南健斗・水田瑛人・米澤千夏・大風翼 (Minami Kento, Mizuta Eito, Yonezawa Chinatsu and Okaze Tsubasa), on the windbreak effect of homestead groves set in rows across the prevailing wind, 風工学研究論文集 28 (2024), J-STAGE PDF (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/windengresearch/28/0/28_J14/_pdf/-char/ja)

What it is: A peer-reviewed wind-engineering paper on the windbreak effect of homestead groves set in rows across the prevailing wind in an Osaki settlement, with a survey of the groves' composition and heights.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the surveyed height band of a settlement's igune, 9 to 16 m with tall trees and 3 to 6 m without, the band this page's grove heights are drawn within. A modern engineering study of a present-day settlement; its groves are what survives, not the period's.

Used for: the surveyed height band of Osaki's igune

daikon-jawiki

ja.wikipedia ダイコン (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%80%E3%82%A4%E3%82%B3%E3%83%B3)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the daikon radish, its varieties and its sowing and harvest seasons.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the autumn-sown daikon's season, standing in the ground from early autumn into winter, which puts the kitchen bed's binding season in the same month as the rice drying. A tertiary summary used for the season.

Used for: the daikon in the ground through the autumn

gassho-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 合掌造り (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%90%88%E6%8E%8C%E9%80%A0%E3%82%8A)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the gassho-zukuri farmhouse of the Sho river valleys: its steep thatched roof of 45 to 60 degrees, the king-post-free loft of two to four levels it yields, and the snow and the silkworms behind both.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a steep thatched roof yields a large loft, the loft these maps' farmhouses carry. A tertiary summary of one regional house type; its reasons for the pitch are snow and rain rather than thatch, and it does not call the loft dark.

Used for: the steep roof and the large loft it gives

kotobank-momisuri

kotobank 籾摺り (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%B1%BE%E6%91%BA%E3%82%8A)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the Nipponica encyclopedia's entry on hulling, the removal of the husk from paddy rice, with the hulling ratio by weight and by volume.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the hulling yield, 80% by weight, the conversion between paddy and brown rice this page's yard sizing runs through. A tertiary summary of a published reference work.

Used for: the hulling ratio of paddy to brown rice

chang-jiang-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 长江 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%95%BF%E6%B1%9F)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Yangtze, with the names its reaches carry from Yibin to the sea.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the reach names of the great river in one sentence, the one-river-many-names pattern this page's rivers follow. A tertiary summary used for the names.

Used for: the Yangtze's reach names

kasenho-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 河川法 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B2%B3%E5%B7%9D%E6%B3%95)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the River Law, the statute of 1896 and its replacement of 1964 that put whole river systems under unified state and prefectural management.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the two statutes under which Japan's rivers were named and managed as single systems, the modern one-name-per-river this page sets against the old per-reach names. A tertiary summary used for the dates.

Used for: the River Laws of 1896 and 1964

kaya-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 茅 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%8C%85)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on kaya, the thatching grasses, and the kayaba, the ground around a settlement burned each year and harvested for them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a settlement kept a harvested, yearly burned kaya ground, the village-commons reed bed this page draws. A tertiary summary; it does not name the iriai tenure.

Used for: the kayaba burned yearly and harvested

yoshi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia ヨシ (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%83%A8%E3%82%B7)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the common reed, its uses for thatch and for the yoshizu screen.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the reed's uses for roofing and screens, the harvest this page's reed beds yield. A tertiary summary used for the uses.

Used for: reed for thatch and screens

isawa-senjochi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 胆沢扇状地 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%83%86%E6%B2%A2%E6%89%87%E7%8A%B6%E5%9C%B0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Isawa alluvial fan in Iwate, one of Japan's largest, with its size and the canals that water it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the fan's area and standing, the case this page uses for radial canals at fan scale. A tertiary summary used for the size.

Used for: the Isawa fan's area

juan-zeki-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 寿庵堰 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%AF%BF%E5%BA%B5%E5%A0%B0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Juan weirs, the seventeenth-century irrigation canals drawn from the Isawa river that opened the Isawa fan to paddy.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the canals' lengths and the ground they watered, the weir-canal irrigation of a fan this page describes. A tertiary summary; it does not say where on the fan the intake stood.

Used for: the Juan weir canals of the Isawa fan

songshi-273-wikisource

宋史 (History of Song), 卷二七三, the biography of He Jiyun with He Chengju appended, Chinese Wikisource transcription (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E5%AE%8B%E5%8F%B2/%E5%8D%B7273)

What it is: The Yuan-compiled official history of the Song, whose chapter 273 carries He Chengju's memorial proposing the dike-and-marsh belt across the Hebei frontier to stop the Khitan cavalry.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the primary record of a state deliberately making wet ground as anti-cavalry terrain, the defensive inundation this page names. A primary text read from a crowd-transcribed wiki copy; the passage carries no date.

Used for: He Chengju's proposal of the Hebei marsh belt against cavalry

kotobank-shimogoe

kotobank 下肥 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E4%B8%8B%E8%82%A5-154033)

What it is: The Kotobank page reprinting the reference-encyclopedia entries on shimogoe, night soil as fertilizer, and its use by the farm villages around the early-modern cities.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the villages supplying a city's greens took its night soil in bulk, the suburban vegetable belt this page draws around a town. A tertiary summary of published reference works.

Used for: the night-soil-fed vegetable belt around a city

shinden-kaihatsu-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 新田開発 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%96%B0%E7%94%B0%E9%96%8B%E7%99%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on new-field development, the reclamation of lakes, shallows and wastes for paddy under the shogunate and the domains, with the merchant-financed fields of the Kinai.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the Edo-period reclamation waves around Osaka, the intensive working of a city's outskirts this page describes. A tertiary summary; it names the shogunate as sponsor and no wave around Edo itself.

Used for: reclamation waves around Osaka

yusuichi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 遊水地 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%81%8A%E6%B0%B4%E5%9C%B0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the yusuichi, the retarding basin that holds a river's flood water for the sake of the ground downstream.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the flood basin as purposed wet ground, one of the bounded forms wetness took near a city on these maps. A tertiary summary used for the definition.

Used for: the flood basin as purposed wet ground

yodogawa-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 淀川 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%B7%80%E5%B7%9D)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Yodo river system, from Lake Biwa to Osaka bay, with the names its reaches carry.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the river's three names and where each begins - at a border and at a confluence - the per-reach renaming this page's rivers follow. A tertiary summary used for the names.

Used for: the Seta, Uji and Yodo names and where they change

ankyo-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 暗渠 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9A%97%E6%B8%A0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the culvert, the covered watercourse, and the covering of urban streams as cities grew.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that watercourses inside a growing city disappear from the surface under building, the reason no relic of a diverted stream's old bed is drawn through a city. A tertiary summary of a modern process.

Used for: urban watercourses vanishing under buildup

endorheic-basin-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Endorheic basin" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endorheic_basin)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the endorheic basin, the closed drainage whose water leaves only by evaporation and seepage, and where such basins occur.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a closed water body is characteristically a desert arrangement, which is why a terminal moat with no outlet belongs to an arid site and not to rice country. A tertiary summary of a physical-geography concept.

Used for: the closed basin as a desert form

standard-step-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Standard step method" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_step_method)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the standard step method for computing a channel's water-surface profile, with a worked example of the backwater above a sluice gate returning to normal depth upstream.

Why it applies, and its limits: It shows that an impoundment lifts the surface upstream only for a finite reach before the channel returns to its own depth, which is why raising a moat cannot lift its whole feeder. A modern hydraulics text on a canal gate, standing in for the physics.

Used for: the finite backwater above a gate

nanjing-chengqiang-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 南京城墙 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%8D%97%E4%BA%AC%E5%9F%8E%E5%A2%99)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Ming city wall of Nanjing, its gates and the water gates and conduits by which the Qinhuai and the lake water passed the wall.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that water crossed the wall at gates and through conduits laid in the wall's foundation, the culvert-through-the-wall this page draws for a city drain. A tertiary summary of the imperial capital's wall.

Used for: water passing a city wall by gate and conduit

contour-canal-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Contour canal" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contour_canal)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the contour canal, the canal dug to follow the contour of the land it crosses, with its characteristic meandering course.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a dug canal follows the contour, which is why a channel on these maps may run across the fall of the ground rather than down it. A tertiary summary of the British canal tradition; it gives no gradient figure.

Used for: a dug canal following the contour

weir-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Weir" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weir)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the weir, the low dam across a river that impounds water and lets it flow over its crest, with its uses in flood control, measurement and milling.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a weir impounds water, slows the river above it and passes the flow over its crest, the ponding and overflow behavior this page's sluice-fed reaches and set-level moats rest on. A tertiary summary; it does not describe a head-race's width or say in so many words that a weir holds a level.

Used for: water impounded and slowed above a weir, passing over the crest

mill-race-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Mill race" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_race)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the mill race, the channel that leads water from a pond or weir to a wheel and away again.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the race is narrow and swift against the broad pond, the distinction this page draws between the ponded reach above a sluice and the race below it. A tertiary summary.

Used for: the race as the narrow swift member beside the broad pond

himeji-castle-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 姫路城 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A7%AB%E8%B7%AF%E5%9F%8E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Himeji castle, with the lengths and widths of its three moat circuits.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the moat widths of the great provincial castle these maps take as their provincial-city moat anchor. A tertiary summary; the widths are the moats as they survive, and no average is stated.

Used for: the three moats' widths

aichi-yosui-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 愛知用水 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%84%9B%E7%9F%A5%E7%94%A8%E6%B0%B4)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Aichi canal, the postwar irrigation scheme from the Kiso river to the Chita peninsula, with its trunk and branch canals.

Why it applies, and its limits: It shows a real scheme naming its trunk and branch canals, the tiered vocabulary this page's channel hierarchy uses. A tertiary summary of a modern scheme.

Used for: the trunk and branch canals of one scheme

kangai-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 灌漑 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%81%8C%E6%BC%91)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on irrigation, its methods and history in Japan, including plot-to-plot watering.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines plot-to-plot irrigation, the cascade from paddy to paddy that lets interior plots on these maps stand without a ditch of their own. A tertiary summary used for the term.

Used for: plot-to-plot irrigation defined

contour-trenching-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Contour trenching" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contour_trenching)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on contour trenching, the soil-conservation technique of digging trenches along the contour to catch runoff.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a trench dug along the contour catches the water flowing down the slope, the interceptor form this page's field-toe ditch takes. A modern conservation technique; its purpose is infiltration rather than protection.

Used for: a trench along the contour catching downhill water

fao-irrigation-canals-ch5

FAO, Irrigation water management: introduction to irrigation, training manual 1, chapter 5, Irrigation canals (https://www.fao.org/4/r4082e/r4082e06.htm)

What it is: A chapter of the FAO's introductory irrigation training manual on canal cross-sections, side slopes, freeboard and earthen construction.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the dug earthen trapezoidal section and the convention for its side slope and freeboard, the shape this page's ditch widths are computed from. A modern extension manual standing in for a physical form; it gives no slope for a particular soil.

Used for: the dug earthen canal's trapezoidal section

aze-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 畦 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%95%A6)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the aze, the paddy bund of heaped mud that divides the fields and holds their water, with the named bund along an open channel.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the bund's purpose - that the water not leak out - and names the bund on the ditch side, which is why a basin on these maps is sealed on every side. A tertiary summary used for the definitions.

Used for: the bund holding the paddy's water on every side

environmental-impact-irrigation-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Environmental impact of irrigation" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_of_irrigation)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the environmental effects of irrigation schemes: the deep percolation that recharges groundwater, the rising water table, waterlogging and salinity.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a scheme's percolation losses recharge the groundwater and waterlog land, which is the mechanism behind the wet ground below a ditch on these maps. A modern engineering summary standing in for a physical relation.

Used for: irrigation seepage and waterlogging

soil-salinity-control-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Soil salinity control" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soil_salinity_control)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on controlling soil salinity in irrigated land, with the percolation losses that raise the water table and waterlog the ground.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that irrigation water the aquifer cannot carry away raises the water table and waterlogs the land, the seepage-below-a-command relationship this page draws. A modern engineering summary; it does not localize the waterlogging below the command.

Used for: percolation losses raising the water table to waterlogging

kisodani-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 木曽谷 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9C%A8%E6%9B%BD%E8%B0%B7)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Kiso valley, the mountain corridor of the Nakasendo highway; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that steep mountain land leaves cultivated ground scarce, confined to narrow flats along the river, which is the terrain limit this page names. It speaks of the valley, not of the post towns' own acreage.

Used for: the terrain-limited low end of tract size (fields)

mu-land-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Mu (land)" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mu_(land))

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the mu, the Chinese unit of land area, with its statutory values by period; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the 1915 mu of 614.4 m2 fixed on the Qing definitions and the 1930 metric mu of 666 2/3 m2 (0.1647 acre), which convert this page's figures. It gives no Ming value and nothing about parcel sizes, so it supports nothing about holdings.

Used for: the size of a mu (fields)

kokumori-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 石盛 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%9F%B3%E7%9B%9B)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on kokumori, the assessed standard yield per tan set for each grade of paddy, dry field and house plot in the early-modern cadastral surveys; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the Taiko-survey ladder (upper paddy 1.5 koku, middle 1.3, lower 1.1 per tan; upper dry field 1.2) and its derivation from an assumed harvest at a five-tenths milling. These are tax-assessment rates for land grades, not measured yields, which is the limit stated beside the figure.

Used for: the 1.3 koku/tan figure and the paddy-over-dry-field value ladder (fields)

jori-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 条里制 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9D%A1%E9%87%8C%E5%88%B6)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the jori system, the ancient square land division whose grid of about 109 m survives across Japan's old plains; an encyclopedia article listing the plains and basins where its remains are found.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supports the surviving regular grid on long-settled plains and that western Japan's jori parcels were regular enough to need no later readjustment. It describes land division, not how a village's paddies read at village scale.

Used for: gridded paddies in ancient core provinces (fields)

cultivator-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Cultivator" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivator)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the cultivator, the implement drawn between crop rows to break the soil and kill weeds; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the row-crop cultivator's purpose - weed control between the rows - and that hoe weeding between rows is ancient, which is why ruled rows paid on dry land. A general article on dry-field tools with nothing on paddy.

Used for: why rows pay on dry fields (fields)

tauchiguruma-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 田打車 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%94%B0%E6%89%93%E8%BB%8A)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the tauchiguruma, the hand-pushed rotary paddy weeder of the Meiji period; a short encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests that paddy weeding before the weeder was by hand or by hand claw, crouching, and that the weeder is walked between the rice hills - the between-rows tool for mud this page's argument turns on. It gives no dates for the tool's spread.

Used for: hand weeding before the rotary weeder (fields)

genge-jawiki

ja.wikipedia ゲンゲ (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%B2%E3%83%B3%E3%82%B2)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on genge (Chinese milk vetch, Astragalus sinicus), the legume sown among the standing rice in autumn and turned in as green manure in spring; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the winter green-manure practice in the paddy itself, its root-nodule nitrogen fixation with a quantity, and its disappearance under chemical fertilizer and earlier planting. It says nothing of night soil, ash or oil cake and does not describe the plowing-under.

Used for: renge as the paddy's winter green manure (fields)

alluvial-fan-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Alluvial fan" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alluvial_fan)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the alluvial fan, the cone of sediment that spreads out from a canyon mouth; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: Read for the landform's shape alone - narrowest at its apex and widening outward - which is the opposite of the drawn irrigation fan this page describes and keeps the two from being confused. It says nothing of paddy or canals.

Used for: the direction an alluvial fan widens (fields)

fengshui-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Feng shui" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feng_shui)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on feng shui, the Chinese practice of siting buildings and graves by landform and orientation; an encyclopedia article with references, read for its sentence on where southern Chinese villages put their graves.

Why it applies, and its limits: Its statement that graves went on the highest hills, far from water and on otherwise unvaluable farmland, is the grave half of this page's per-archetype matrix. It is a tertiary summary of southern China with no period given, and it says nothing of terraces, outcrops or ponds.

Used for: grave siting on the slope rather than in the wet paddy (fields)

temple-of-confucius-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Temple of Confucius" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temple_of_Confucius)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Confucian temple, the school-temple every prefectural and county school carried; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the Tang decree of 630 that put a Confucian temple in every province's and county's school and the temple's siting at the school, which is the state character of the school-temple this page relies on; it is a tertiary summary and dates the requirement to the Tang, not the Ming.

Used for: the Confucian school-temple as a state foundation (religion and death)

chenghuang-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 城隍 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/城隍)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the City God, the tutelary deity of a walled city and its official cult; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the Ming founder's enfeoffment of city gods at the capital, prefecture, department and county levels with the local official leading the sacrifice, which is the state character of the City God temple this page relies on; a tertiary summary, and it does not order the foundations of a county seat.

Used for: the City God temple as a state foundation (religion and death)

fushimi-inari-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Fushimi Inari-taisha" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fushimi_Inari-taisha)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Fushimi Inari Taisha at Kyoto; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the count of about 800 gates along the main path and the ten thousand in total, which are the figures this page's dense regime rests on; it gives neither the run length nor the arrangement in rows.

Used for: the Senbon Torii count (religion and death)

bunkotsu-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 分骨 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%88%86%E9%AA%A8)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on bunkotsu, the division of one person's cremated remains between two or more places of interment, and the law around it; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the practice and its procedure, which is what the divided remains on this page rest on; it is written for the present day and says nothing of a portion going to a head temple.

Used for: divided remains (religion and death)

osaka-nanabaka-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 大阪七墓 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A4%A7%E9%98%AA%E4%B8%83%E5%A2%93)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Osaka's seven graveyards, the Edo-period burial grounds on the city's rim and the 2017 excavation of the Umeda ground; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the consolidation of the city's scattered graveyards onto its outer rim for military reasons and the excavation's counts of skeletons and ossuaries; it says nothing of how the graves lay, so it carries the density of use and not the plan.

Used for: Edo-period urban burial at Osaka (religion and death)

sanuki-kokubunji-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 讃岐国分寺 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%AE%83%E5%B2%90%E5%9B%BD%E5%88%86%E5%AF%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Sanuki provincial temple, citing its excavation reports; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the excavated Nara-period precinct as 240 by 220 m, the one instance this page's ~218 m figure rests on, and it is the small end of the range the other provincial temples read give; one site, and nothing on shrines.

Used for: the size of a provincial temple precinct (religion and death)

shimotsuke-kokubunji-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 下野国分寺跡 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%B8%8B%E9%87%8E%E5%9B%BD%E5%88%86%E5%AF%BA%E8%B7%A1)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Shimotsuke provincial temple site, citing its excavation reports; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the excavated precinct's dimensions, which set the large end of the kokubunji range against Sanuki's small one; one site, and nothing on shrines.

Used for: the size of a provincial temple precinct (religion and death)

fushimi-inari-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 伏見稲荷大社 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%BC%8F%E8%A6%8B%E7%A8%B2%E8%8D%B7%E5%A4%A7%E7%A4%BE)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on Fushimi Inari Taisha, the head shrine of the Inari cult at Kyoto, with its Senbon Torii; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the custom of dedicating torii to the Edo period, puts the donated gates at about ten thousand on the mountain and describes the dense rows; a tertiary summary of one shrine, from which this page generalizes the donation row.

Used for: the Inari donation row (religion and death)

torii-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Torii" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torii)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the torii, the Shinto gate, its forms, names and uses; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the naming of ranked gates along an approach (ichi-, ni-, san-no-torii) and the donor's name on each of Fushimi's gates, which are the two regimes this page draws; it gives no spacing figure and does not date the votive custom.

Used for: ranked torii and donated torii (religion and death)

hokora-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 祠 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A5%A0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the hokora, the small wayside god-shelf below the shrine tier; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a hokora has no torii or only a very small one and stands inside the human sphere - at a settlement's entrance, a crossroads, the fields - which is the tier below the shrine on this page; it gives no count against shrines.

Used for: the hokora tier without a torii (religion and death)

kotobank-kyodo-bochi

Kaitei Shinpan Sekai Dai-hyakka Jiten (Heibonsha) and Digital Daijisen (Shogakukan), s.v. 共同墓地, on kotobank (https://kotobank.jp/word/共同墓地)

What it is: Kotobank's reproduction of the encyclopedia and dictionary entries on the communal graveyard, the burial ground a settlement holds in common.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that a settled community forms its graveyard apart from its dwellings, which is the siting this page relies on; dictionary entries of a few lines, with no figures and nothing on how many foundations draw on one ground.

Used for: the communal graveyard outside the built area (religion and death)

sodo-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 僧堂 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%83%A7%E5%A0%82)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the sodo, the communal hall of a Zen temple where the monks meditate, eat and sleep; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests that celibate clergy lived communally in a hall that is one of the compound's own buildings, which is the housing this page implies within the wall; a Japanese Zen institution, not a Chinese urban monastery, and it gives no numbers.

Used for: monks housed inside the temple wall (religion and death)

shake-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 社家 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A4%BE%E5%AE%B6)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the shake, the hereditary priestly families of a shrine; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that the office passed within a family for generations and that the families' houses stood near the shrine, clustering into a named quarter, which is the householder clergy this page relies on; it gives no generation count and speaks of Japanese shrines, not Chinese temples.

Used for: hereditary shrine priesthoods and where they lived (religion and death)

danka-system-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Danka system" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danka_system)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the danka system, the Edo-period affiliation of every household to a Buddhist temple that buries it and that it supports; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the relation between a temple and its patron households and the sects a household might be registered to, which is the patronage this page's temple count rests on; it says nothing of how many temples a place has or how the number scales.

Used for: each temple as a separate foundation with its own patrons (religion and death)

hongwu-emperor-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Hongwu Emperor" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hongwu_Emperor)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Hongwu Emperor, founder of the Ming; an encyclopedia article, read for its sentence on the 1390s restriction of monasteries.

Why it applies, and its limits: Its statement that each county was limited to one monastery with a maximum of two monks is the one readable figure for the size of an ordinary Ming temple, and it points to a very small median; it is a tertiary summary of one edict, and it says nothing of the great urban monasteries.

Used for: the size of the median Ming temple (religion and death)

demographic-transition-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Demographic transition" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_transition)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the demographic transition, the model of mortality and fertility before and after industrialization; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: Its band for pre-transition death rates brackets the rate this page's sizing arithmetic uses; its worked examples are colonial North America, and it names no figure for premodern China or Japan.

Used for: the crude death rate behind the burial-ground sizing (religion and death)

kegare-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Kegare" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kegare)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on kegare, the Shinto concept of ritual defilement; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states that death is the primary source of defilement, that the kami are kept from it and that priests must avoid it, which is the real-world rule this setting's shrines depart from; a tertiary summary.

Used for: Shinto's avoidance of death pollution (religion and death)

chinju-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 鎮守神 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%8E%AE%E5%AE%88%E7%A5%9E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the chinju, the tutelary deity guarding a building or a tract of land, and its shrine; a short encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the tutelary this page sets beside the Chinese earth god; it does not itself say the deity guards a village, and the comparison is this page's.

Used for: the tutelary chinju in its grove (religion and death)

fao-ac264e-ch4

FAO/NACA, Integrated Fish Farming in China, ch. 4 "Rearing of fry and fingerlings" (https://www.fao.org/4/ac264e/AC264E04.htm)

What it is: Chapter 4 of the FAO and Network of Aquaculture Centers in Asia manual on Chinese integrated fish farming, on the nursery chain from fry to fingerling to grow-out pond.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the sizes of fry and fingerling ponds and the stocking chain, which is this page's warrant for small nursery parcels in a pond block; a twentieth-century design manual, so its figures are prescriptions rather than a premodern survey.

Used for: nursery ponds in a dike-pond block (archetypes)

polder-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Polder" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polder)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the polder, the diked tract below the surrounding water level; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives full enclosure by dikes, the floor below the surrounding water some or all of the time, exchange through sluices and the permanent flood risk, which is the enclosure rule this page states; a general and largely Dutch article, not the Jiangnan case.

Used for: why a polder is enclosed on every side (archetypes)

dongting-lake-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Dongting Lake" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dongting_Lake)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Dongting Lake, the Yangtze flood-basin lake whose shores were poldered; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the lake's seasonal range of level and area and names the polders made in its basin, which is the fluctuating water outside this page's polder; it says nothing of what the exposed bed carries.

Used for: the seasonal water outside a polder (archetypes)

morus-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Morus (plant)" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morus_(plant))

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the mulberry genus, with its cultivation for silkworm leaf; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the yearly pruning of leaf mulberry to 1.5 to 1.8 m, the bush height this page draws; it says nothing of crown width, spacing or fruiting under leaf harvest.

Used for: the height of coppiced silkworm mulberry (archetypes)

pollarding-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Pollarding" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pollarding)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on pollarding, the pruning system that keeps a tree at a set height and harvests its shoots; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the withy harvest, the held height and the low stub form, which is why this page's dike willows stand low; it names no dike or waterway, and its examples are European.

Used for: pollarded dike willows (archetypes)

waju-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 輪中 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%BC%AA%E4%B8%AD)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the waju, the ring-diked polder settlements of the Nobi plain; an encyclopedia article citing prefectural and academic works.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the continuous ring dike and the homestead's own windbreak and flood groves sited by the winter wind and the flood direction, which is this page's evidence that a polder village kept its house groves; it says nothing of planting on the dikes themselves.

Used for: homestead groves inside a polder (archetypes)

willow-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Willow" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the willow genus, its habitat, its uses in basketry and its planting on stream banks; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives willow's wet-ground habit, its interlacing roots protecting a bank against the water and the withies grown in pollards, which is the bank-planting mechanism this page's dike rows rest on; a general article with nothing on Chinese dikes or dates.

Used for: willow on the dike's water face (archetypes)

willow-palisade-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Willow Palisade" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willow_Palisade)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Willow Palisade, the Qing border earthwork of Manchuria planted with willow rows; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the rows of willow planted on the levees and the levees' dimensions, which is the row-on-embankment form this page borrows as an analog; a border work, not a polder dike, and it carries no in-row spacing.

Used for: willow rows on an embankment (archetypes)

hojo-seibi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 圃場整備 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9C%83%E5%A0%B4%E6%95%B4%E5%82%99)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on hojo seibi, the postwar consolidation of paddy plots into machine-sized rectangles; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the standard plot sizes of the mechanization era and the rectangle as the basic shape, which is the modern look this page tells the reader to avoid; it carries no dates for the program's standards.

Used for: the machine-era plot as an anachronism (archetypes)

tanada-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 棚田 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%A3%9A%E7%94%B0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the tanada, the terraced paddy, its small cells and its stone retaining banks; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the small area of each terraced cell and the stone-walled banks that hold the steps, which is the terrace form this page draws; it does not say what sets the cell's size.

Used for: terraced paddy cells (archetypes)

nelumbo-nucifera-enwiki

en.wikipedia "Nelumbo nucifera" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelumbo_nucifera)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the sacred lotus, with a section on its cultivation as a root crop; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the species' water depth, the deep and the shallow (adlittoral) cultivar classes and the rotation of lotus with rice in one field, which is the agronomy this page's lotus overlay rests on; it is a general article, not a description of any premodern village.

Used for: lotus depth classes and the rice rotation (archetypes)

dojo-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 道場 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/道場)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the dojo, the martial-arts practice hall, with its history from private and outdoor practice to the built hall; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests practice at a private residence, outdoors or on an earthen floor before the mid-Edo boarded hall, and the great enrolled dojos of Edo, which is the ladder this page's county and city tiers rest on; it frames the change by period, not by town and country, and gives no floor areas.

Used for: where samurai trained (buildings)

nishimawari-koro-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 西廻り航路 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/西廻り航路)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the western sea route, the Edo-period shipping route round Japan and Kawamura Zuiken's reform of the tax-rice shipping on it; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests that the tax rice moved on commoner hulls the shogunate contracted and then hired directly, under officials, pennants and inspection rather than ownership, which is the documentary control this page describes; the actor is the bakufu's route administration, not a county office.

Used for: hired hulls for the tax rice (buildings)

kakoimai-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 囲米 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/囲米)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on kakoimai, the Edo-period reserve of grain stored against famine by the shogunate, domains and villages; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the reserve and its names, one of which is reserved unhulled rice, which is the corner of unhulled grain this page keeps; it does not compare the keeping qualities of hulled and unhulled rice.

Used for: the famine reserve of unhulled rice (buildings)

kureki-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 榑木 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/榑木)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on kureki, split timber, and the Edo-period upland villages that paid their land tax in it; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests a mountain district's tax arriving as a local good in place of rice and later as cash, which is the upland tax this page describes; it draws no consequence for the storehouse.

Used for: the upland tax in timber and cash (buildings)

kotobank-katteguchi

Digital Daijisen (Shogakukan), s.v. 勝手口, on kotobank (https://kotobank.jp/word/勝手口)

What it is: Kotobank's reproduction of the dictionary entry on the katteguchi, the kitchen door of a Japanese house and the host's door of a tea room.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the kitchen door as a named entrance set against the guests', which is the service circulation this page inverts; a dictionary line with nothing on what the door opens onto.

Used for: the kitchen door as the service entrance (buildings)

gokura-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 郷蔵 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/郷蔵)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the gokura, the Edo-period village granary that held the tax rice awaiting shipment; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the village granary as a temporary store for the tax rice and, in places, a famine reserve, which is the first link of the chain this page draws; it says nothing of the office's own storehouse.

Used for: the tax rice's passage from village to store (buildings)

tsuijibei-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 築地塀 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/築地塀)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the tsuijibei, the rammed-earth wall with its own tiled roof; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the wall's construction and the roof set on top of it, which is why this page draws a compound wall as a roofed thickness; it states neither the roof's purpose nor the wall's cost.

Used for: the roofed earthen compound wall (buildings)

xuli-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 胥吏 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/胥吏)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the xuli, the sub-official clerks of imperial Chinese government, quoting Song to Qing memoirs and memorials; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the clerks as entrenched local staff, the official's dependence on their knowledge and their enrichment out of the revenue they handled, which is the clerk this page's county runs on; a Chinese picture, and it says nothing of the Japanese tedai.

Used for: the permanent local clerk (buildings)

machi-bugyo-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 町奉行 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/町奉行)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the machi-bugyo, the Edo-period urban magistrate, his office and its jurisdiction; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It defines the office as the administration and justice of the urban districts and puts the magistrate's residence inside the magistracy, which is the co-location this page's compound rests on; it gives no layout.

Used for: the urban magistracy as a model (buildings)

kuramai-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 蔵米 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/蔵米)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on kuramai, the rice received as land tax and held in the authorities' storehouses, and the stipends reckoned from it; an encyclopedia article.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests that the tax rice the authorities held was brown rice reckoned in bales, which is the form this page's granary carries; it describes the stipend's reckoning rather than the villages' delivery, so the delivery form itself is on no page read.

Used for: the tax rice as brown rice in bales (buildings)

Attested instances (anchors, not works)

Named real-world cases the rules are calibrated against. They are evidence, but they are measurements rather than publications, so they are listed separately and cited inline by name.

Anchor What it anchors
Suzugamori 74 x 16.2 m (~243 x 53 ft), serving Edo for 220 years - the execution-ground size anchor
Pingyao Market Tower attested at 133.4 m2 plan (~38 ft square); ~60 m mamian tower spacing - the wealthy-county-seat anchor
Xi'an mamian bastions ~20 m wide projecting ~12 m; ~120 m tower spacing (the peaceful tier)
Himeji moats averaging ~20 m (max 34.5 m) - the provincial-city moat tier
Osaka outer moat ~70-90 m - the grand-city moat tier, deliberately ABOVE our range
Fushimi Inari Senbon Torii: ~800 gates over ~400 m - the donation-row regime
Kasuga Taisha / Meiji Jingu / Nagao ranked ichi/ni/san-no-torii 200 m-1.3 km apart - the other regime
Northampton largest excavated urban tannery at 36-37 pits - far past anything in this pool
Longsheng largest terrace 0.62 mu (~0.10 acre); 15,862 terraces in one village
Edo Kokucho time bell billed ~400-410 blocks 'within earshot' - the bell-audibility anchor
Shunde county ~4.6% dike-pond in 1581 while containing townships already over 50% - the scatter was normal

kanazawa-teramachi

VISIT KANAZAWA official travel guide, Teramachi Temple Area (https://visitkanazawa.jp/en/spot/detail_10182.html)

What it is: A visitor attraction listing on VISIT KANAZAWA, the official travel guide published by the Kanazawa City Tourism Association, describing the Teramachi temple district - one of three quarters of the old castle town into which the ruling Maeda family gathered temples when the town was laid out.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the scale a castle town's temple district could reach - some seventy temples close together in one of Kanazawa's three - which is the top of the range our temple quarters are measured against. Its limits are that it is a tourist board's page with no sources; that the seventy is a present-day count of what stands, not a period census; that Kanazawa was the seat of the largest domain in the country and one of its largest castle towns, so its temple stock is a ceiling and not a norm; and that it was three districts, not one.

Used for: ~70 temples clustered in one castle-town temple district

takada-teramachi

Takada Teramachi tourism site / Joetsu Stories (https://joetsu-stories.jp/2025/02/03/takada-teramachi-part-1/)

What it is: An English-language local history article on Joetsu Stories, a bilingual site about the city of Joetsu in Niigata Prefecture, telling how the temple quarter (teramachi) of the castle town of Takada came into being after Matsudaira Tadateru moved his seat there in 1614. It describes the ground west of the castle that was set aside for temples, the first wave of temples that moved in, and what the domain expected of them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives one dated case of a temple quarter made by a lord's decree - about twenty-five temples moved to ground west of the castle at Takada in 1614 - which sets the size of a castle town's temple quarter on our maps and the reading that it doubled as a defensive belt quartering foot soldiers. Its limits are that it is an anonymous local-history blog post that cites nothing; that its count is hedged by its own writer ("probably about 25"); that it is one town in one province at one date, a point in a range and not a rule; and that the reading of "protection" as spiritual support plus billets for soldiers is the writer's interpretation, unattributed.

Used for: ~25 temples relocated to Takada in the 1614 wave

takayama-teramachi

Japan Travel, "Takayama's historic 'Temple Town'" (https://en.japantravel.com/gifu/takayama-s-teramachi-gifu/13893)

What it is: "Takayama's historic 'Temple Town'", a visitor's guide article by Sandra Isaka on Japan Travel, a community travel site written by contributors, walking the reader through the temple quarter on the eastern edge of Takayama and noting who founded most of its temples.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a size-matched low anchor for a town's temple quarter - Takayama's, with more than ten temples and shrines - which bounds the bottom of the range our town maps draw. Its limits are that it is community travel writing, a visitor's walk-through with no sourcing; that its count mixes Buddhist temples with Shinto shrines, so it is not a temple count; that it counts the quarter as it stands today rather than at any period; and that Takayama, its castle pulled down after 1692 and the town run from the intendancy office thereafter, is a particular kind of town.

Used for: "over 10 temples and shrines" in a SMALL castle town - the size-matched anchor for the city tier

jokamachi-wiki

Japanese Wiki Corpus, Jokamachi (https://www.japanesewiki.com/history/Jokamachi.html)

What it is: The English rendering of the Japanese Wikipedia castle-town article published in the Japanese Wiki Corpus, a collection of translated Japanese encyclopedia articles on history and culture. The passage we use covers the temple district placed at the town's outer rim, whose walled precincts were counted as part of the town's defenses.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives, in English, the temple quarter at the rim of the castle town with its precincts counted as part of the defenses, which is what puts the teramachi where our maps put it. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary at one further remove: the English is a machine-translation research corpus (the bilingual corpus of Wikipedia's Kyoto-topic articles made by NICT, Japan's National Institute of Information and Communications Technology), a frozen snapshot rather than the maintained article, which is why it reads as it does; and that two other entries in this registry point at the same article and at the Japanese original it translates, so the three cannot corroborate one another.

Used for: the teramachi sited at the jokamachi's outer rim, its precincts forming part of the city defenses

pingyao-chenghuangmiao

Wikipedia, City God Temple of Pingyao (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_God_Temple_of_Pingyao)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the City God Temple of Pingyao, the Chenghuang temple in the walled county town of Pingyao in Shanxi, which describes the site as three separate temples standing together on one complex of more than 7,300 square meters and lists them individually.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the shape of a county seat's civic temple - not a single hall but a compound holding several cults side by side, the City God's own temple among them - which is how our town maps compose a precinct rather than dropping one building. It is a tertiary summary used for what stands on the site rather than for a measurement, the surviving buildings are later rebuildings of a much older foundation, and Pingyao was a wealthy town whose temple is a generous example rather than an average county one.

Used for: the City God temple as a complex of three distinct temples on one county-seat site

chinaknowledge-tang-econ

chinaknowledge.de, Tang-period economy (http://www.chinaknowledge.de/History/Tang/tang-econ.html)

What it is: Ulrich Theobald's survey of the Tang-period economy on ChinaKnowledge.de, a single-author sinological reference site, covering land tenure, the great estates and the place of the monasteries in them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries in one sentence all three things this record asserts about monastic wealth - that manors were owned by monasteries among others, that they held oil mills, spinneries and breweries, and that the labor on them was slaves, craftsmen and tenant farmers - which is what puts productive enterprise inside a temple's economy on these maps rather than leaving a precinct as a place of worship only. Its limits are that it is a serious single-author reference rather than primary or peer-reviewed scholarship, and that its own authorities for this material, Gernet and Twitchett, could not be read.

Used for: monastic manors carrying oil mills, spinneries and breweries, worked by dependent labor; monastic estates outside the state's tax reach

inexhaustible-treasuries

Studies in Chinese Religions 5(2), "Giving while keeping: inexhaustible treasuries and inalienable wealth in medieval China" (https://doi.org/10.1080/23729988.2019.1639463)

Not cited: no publicly readable page carries the passage the record relied on.

Used for: the wu-jin-zang interest-earning endowment; Xuanzong's 713 liquidation

tontine-monastery-lending

The Tontine Coffee-House, "Buddhist Monastery Lending" (https://tontinecoffeehouse.com/2024/02/26/buddhist-monastery-lending/)

What it is: A post, "Buddhist Monastery Lending," written by Daniel DeMatos in February 2024 for The Tontine Coffee-House, a financial-history blog running since 2018 that covers the history of financial institutions and innovations. It traces how Buddhist monasteries in China served as lenders and pawnbrokers from the arrival of Buddhism down to the nineteenth century, and closes with a short reading list that includes Jacques Gernet's Buddhism in Chinese Society.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the institutional facts behind a temple that lends - the monastery as the great pawnbroker, and pledged goods held in an associated warehouse or granary for the life of the loan - which is why a temple compound on our maps can reasonably carry a strongroom rather than only a hall. It is a secondary blog summary rather than a scholarly work, so we take from it only what its own cited literature supports, and it is about China; we apply it to a Japanese-flavored setting on the strength of the monastic economy the two shared, not as a statement about any particular Japanese temple.

Used for: monasteries as pawnbrokers; the 1202 Song lay-partnership pawnshop ju

pawnbroking-history

Wikipedia, History of pawnbroking (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_pawnbroking)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "History of pawnbroking", a tertiary summary of lending against pledged goods from antiquity to the present, with a short section on China that runs from the earliest monastic pawnshops through the Song.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use its statement that the earliest Chinese pawnbrokers were established and run by Buddhist monasteries, and its note that Southern Song laypeople formed partnerships with monasteries to open pawnshops, when deciding where a lending house belongs on a map - inside or beside a temple precinct rather than in a market row. It is a tertiary summary whose claims we accept only where its own references support them, and China occupies a few sentences of a global survey, so we take the institutional association it describes and not a chronology or a count.

Used for: pawnbroking limited to Buddhist monasteries prior to the Tang

zhengyi-householder-priests

Patheos Religion Library, "Taoism: Ethics and Community - Leadership" (https://www.patheos.com/library/taoism/ethics-morality-community/leadershipclergy)

What it is: The leadership-and-clergy article of the Patheos Religion Library’s Taoism section, a general-audience reference on the world religions, describing who Daoist clergy are and how the Zhengyi and Quanzhen traditions differ in how they live.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the statement behind this project’s householder clergy: a priest of the Zhengyi tradition marries, marriage is required at the highest rank, and the role is often passed down in a family - which is what puts families rather than celibates inside a temple precinct on these maps. Its limits are that it is a tertiary religion-portal article, written in the present tense about clergy in China and Taiwan TODAY rather than about any premodern century, and it names no sources of its own.

Used for: married priests, marriage required at the highest rank, the role passed down in a family

kannushi-wiki

Wikipedia, Shinto priest / Kannushi (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kannushi)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the kannushi, the priest who tends a Shinto shrine, covering the office, its duties, and the way it has been passed down within families.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one structural fact that shapes who lives beside a shrine on our maps - that the office was hereditary, held by a married priest whose children succeeded him, so a shrine implies a resident priestly household rather than a celibate community. It is a tertiary summary and we take its figures only where its own references support them; note too that its most concrete statements are about the modern era, including the abolition of hereditary appointment in 1871, which is well after the period our setting is modeled on and which we use only as evidence of how deeply rooted the practice was before it.

Used for: hereditary shrine office, up to 100 generations; abolished 1871, persists by local preference

jodo-shinshu-marriage

Seattle Betsuin, "Jodo Shinshu and Marriage" (https://seattlebetsuin.org/jodo-shinshu-and-marriage/)

Used for: the Tokugawa exemption permitting a married temple head to keep priestly status

tricycle-temple-wives

Tricycle, "Temple Wives of Japan" (https://tricycle.org/magazine/japan-temple-wives/)

What it is: "Temple Wives of Japan," an interview by Karen Jensen with the scholar Jessica Starling, published in the Spring 2022 issue of Tricycle: The Buddhist Review, a long-running nonprofit Buddhist magazine. It explains the bomori - literally the guardian or protector of the temple, in practice the wife of a Jodo Shinshu resident priest - and the household that a temple in that tradition actually is.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us what a rural temple contains as a domestic institution: a married clergy exempted by the Tokugawa government so a temple head could be married and still hold priestly status, a wife who runs the temple, and succession from father to eldest son - which is why our temple compounds carry a priest's family dwelling rather than a celibate dormitory. It is a magazine interview rather than a study, and it describes one tradition, Jodo Shinshu, whose married clergy was the exception in the Edo period rather than the rule, so we use it for the shape of a temple household and not as a claim about every sect.

Used for: the bomori institution and eldest-son succession

nishikori-tsunaba

Kotobank, Nishikori tsunaba site entry; Yaotsu town history pages (yaotsu-mall.com) (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%8C%A6%E7%B9%94%E7%B6%B1%E5%A0%B4%E8%B7%A1-3061429)

What it is: A Kotobank reprint of the entry on the Nishikori tsunaba from the Heibonsha historical place-name gazetteer 日本歴史地名大系, a scholarly reference compiled from local records. It describes the rope catch across the Kiso river at Nishikori, where the logs floated down from the Kiso forests were stopped at the mouth of the gorge and made up into rafts, and says that when the practice began is not known.

Why it applies, and its limits: It tells us that a full-river catch stood at the gorge mouth where the loose-log drive ended and the rafting began, which is what puts a boom and a timber yard at that point on our river maps. Its limits are that it is a gazetteer entry reprinted by an aggregator, read in extract, so it supports the site and its position and nothing more; that a yearly log count, the season, the size of the timber magistracy and an origin in the 1340s are on no page we could read, and the entry itself says the origin is unknown, so they stand as guesses; and that one exceptional domain-run river stands in for the ordinary timber trade.

Used for: the full-river rope catch at the gorge mouth (the entry says when it began is unknown; a yearly log count, the season, a 138-official magistracy and a 1340s origin are on no readable page and stand as guesses)

kiso-unzaihou

Rinya-cho (Japan Forestry Agency), Kiso-style felling and transport method pages (https://www.rinya.maff.go.jp/chubu/kiso/morigatari/unzaihou.html)

What it is: A page published by the Chubu Regional Forest Office of Japan's Forestry Agency, part of a public-history series on the Kiso forests, describing the Kiso-style felling and timber transport method - axe felling, the sledge and chute haul down to the water, loose-log drives, and rafting - as it was practiced from the late sixteenth century until 1920. The page notes that its illustrated guide is what the office supposes to be a Meiji-era copy of late-Edo originals, and gives no author.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for how timber reached a town, and it describes that chain in order: the loose-log drive handed off to rafts at the tying station, three men riding each raft, and the run down to the timber storage yard at Nagoya and the bay port beyond, which is what puts a log yard where we put it. It is a government agency's explanatory page rather than a study, and it describes one valley's system, so the crew size and the yard locations are a worked example of how such a trade ran and not a national standard.

Used for: the loose-log drive (the page's terms are kotari-gari and okawa-gari) handing off to rafts at the tsunaba; three-man raft crews; onward transport to the Nagoya and bay-port storage yards

susquehanna-boom

Wikipedia, Susquehanna Boom; PA Conservation Heritage; Lumber Heritage Region (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susquehanna_Boom)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Susquehanna Boom at Williamsport, Pennsylvania, the seven-mile log boom that ran from 1851 to 1909: some 350 to 400 stone-filled timber cribs, 22 feet high, stretched diagonally across the river, holding as much as 300 million board feet of logs at once.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the anatomy of the largest kind of boom - fixed cribs of stone-filled timber, the enclosure they make, the volume it held - from which the physics of anchoring and enclosure on our timber rivers is taken. Its limits are that it is industrial North America, not premodern East Asia, so the arrangement transfers and the scale does not; that it is a tertiary summary whose figures are only as good as its own references; and that a lifetime total of logs is not on the page at all and is not used.

Used for: seven miles of boom stretched diagonally across the river; ~350-400 stone-filled cribs 22 ft high; 300 million board feet held at once (the lifetime log total is not on the page)

stcroix-boom-nps

NPS, "The St. Croix Boom" (https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/stcroixboom.htm)

What it is: A public-history article by Dan Ott, written in 2013 for the National Park Service's St. Croix National Scenic Riverway, on the log-handling works of the St. Croix river between Minnesota and Wisconsin from 1856 to 1914: the river divided lengthwise into log channels and holding pens beside a maintained navigation channel, the hinged sheer boom, and the lawsuits and negligence rulings the works drew.
