Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary, and the flood count we quote from it carries no citation on the page, so it is an uncited encyclopedia statement, with the peer-reviewed frequency in the peer-reviewed flood study cited beside it the better anchor; that Kaifeng under a perched, silt-choked river is the worst case of river-city danger and not the average; and that it is the Chinese half of a setting also modeled on Japan.

Used for: Kaifeng's flood count (cities/river-cities.html).

fao-ac180e-rice-fish

FAO, Fish Culture in Rice Fields, chapter 7 "Culture Operations" (https://www.fao.org/4/ac180e/AC180E07.htm) - "the height of the dry bund should be at least 25 cm, but a height of 60 cm is recommended".

What it is: A chapter of Fish Culture in Rice Fields, a technical manual published by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization on raising fish in flooded rice paddies. The "Culture Operations" chapter covers how such a field is prepared and managed, including the earth bund that holds the water in, which it says should stand at least 25 cm high and better still 60 cm.

Why it applies, and its limits: A paddy bund is a wall of piled mud whose height is set by how deep the water must stand, which has nothing to do with modern machinery, so the figure carries back to a premodern field. The honest limits are that this is a present-day extension manual rather than a historical record - the same chapter assumes modern fertilizer, pesticides and bred varieties; that it was written for tropical fish-farming projects in Africa and Southeast Asia rather than for a Chinese or Japanese paddy; and that a bund built to keep fish in is taller than one built only to keep water in, so we treat its 60 cm as the upper end of the range a paddy bund occupies rather than as a measured premodern height.

Used for: the permanent dry bund and its height, as quoted in the bund entry (homesteads.html); the chapter's name is corrected here and flagged for the GM.

minka-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 民家 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/民家) - a general page on commoner dwellings; no roof pitch and no ridge height on it

Used for: the negative the record states beside kayabuki-jawiki: neither the 45-degree pitch nor the 6-7 m ridge is on the pages read (homesteads.html).

fengshui-woodland-enwiki

en.wikipedia Fengshui woodland (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fengshui_woodland) - the concept ("A Fengshui woodland, Fungshui woodland, or Fengshui forest, known in Chinese as 風水林"), regional totals and the 57-village survey mentioned;

What it is: The English Wikipedia article "Fengshui woodland", a short encyclopedia entry on the patches of woodland kept behind and around villages in southern China and Hong Kong for geomantic reasons, giving the Chinese term 風水林 and some regional totals.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one thing only - that the village grove is a recognized, named class of woodland rather than a decoration we invented. It is a tertiary summary whose figures we take only where its own references support them, and it carries no count of groves per village and no grove area at all, so the sizes and numbers on our maps come from the survey papers and, where those run out, are marked as guesses.

Used for: the fengshui forest as a named village-woodland class (vegetation.html); not for its count or size.

hu-2011-fengshui-patches

Hu, Li, Guo et al., "Values of village fengshui forest patches in biodiversity conservation in the Pearl River Delta, China", Biological Conservation 144 (2011) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0006320711000450; the full text is paywalled: doi 10.1016/j.biocon.2011.01.023; unsupported by any readable page until then) - the ABSTRACT is public on that page and was read - 3403 plants/ha, 49.1 m2/ha, 32 well-protected patches, one 1200 m² transect each

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Hu, Li, Guo and colleagues, "Values of village fengshui forest patches in biodiversity conservation in the Pearl River Delta, China", in Biological Conservation volume 144 (2011). The authors surveyed thirty-two well-protected village fengshui forest patches, sampling one 1,200 square meter transect in each, and report the species richness, stem density and basal area they found.

Why it applies, and its limits: A fengshui forest is the protected wood a village keeps at its back, which is exactly the feature our homestead and village groves are modeled on, and this is a direct measurement of how thickly such a grove actually stands (about 3,400 stems and 49.1 square meters of basal area per hectare, which the authors themselves put on a level with well developed evergreen broadleaf forest). Its limits: only the abstract is on a public page, so we take nothing beyond the figures the abstract states; the survey is of patches that survive in one region of southern China in the twenty-first century, and choosing the well-protected ones means these are the healthiest examples rather than an average grove; and southern China is not Japan.

Used for: the stem-density and basal-area figures of intact fengshui groves (abstract); the record's 'closed canopy' gloss was replaced by the authors' own comparison to well-developed evergreen broadleaved forests

afcd-ncsc-9-06

Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (Hong Kong), "Fung Shui Woods in Hong Kong", Advisory Council on the Environment, Nature Conservation Subcommittee paper NCSC 9/06, December 2006 - with an Annex listing all 115 surveyed woods by species richness and GIS-measured area in m² (https://www.epd.gov.hk/epd/sites/default/files/epd/english/boards/advisory_council/files/ncsc-paper-06-09.pdf)

What it is: A December 2006 paper by Hong Kong's Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department to the Nature Conservation Subcommittee of the Advisory Council on the Environment, reporting a 2002 to 2004 survey of 115 fung shui woods - the native forest patches behind villages that villagers preserved, with fruit trees and useful plants at their edges - each wood's boundary drawn on a survey map and its area computed by GIS, listed in an annex.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one large measured set of village grove areas the record could read - the annex over which our median, mean and spread of grove sizes are computed - and so it is what sizes the groves on our maps. Its limits are that the 115 woods were chosen as the most representative sites and the paper says the survey was not exhaustive, so our figures are statistics over a selected sample that plausibly drops the smallest and most degraded woods; that the paper scopes the feature to southern China, so its standing in for the wider East Asian practice is our assumption rather than its claim, made because no comparable Japanese survey could be read; that it is a modern survey of the woods that survived; and that the boundaries were drawn by judgment where a wood merged into secondary forest, so each area carries a convention.

Used for: the one large measured area distribution of village fengshui groves - the record's arithmetic over the Annex: median 9,866 m², mean 11,026 m², 58 of 115 under 1 ha, 45 between 1 and 2 ha, 12 at 2 ha or more, range 606-53,170 m²

hk-herbarium-fsw

Hong Kong Herbarium (AFCD), "An Overview of Fung Shui Woods in Hong Kong" (https://www.herbarium.gov.hk/en/special-topics/fung-shui-woods/an-overview-of-fung-shui-woods-in-hong-kong/index.html)

What it is: "An Overview of Fung Shui Woods in Hong Kong", a page published by the Hong Kong Herbarium of the government's Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department. Fung shui woods are the patches of trees traditionally kept standing behind a village for the good fortune they were held to bring, and the page summarizes a field survey begun in 2002: about 116 such woods, averaging a hectare, ranging from 600 square meters at the smallest to 6 hectares at the largest, with 80% of them lying below 100 m elevation.

Why it applies, and its limits: The village grove is a feature we draw on nearly every map, and this gives the one thing hardest to guess - how big it actually is, and how much the sizes vary. We use a Hong Kong survey because no comparable measured survey of Japanese homestead or village groves could be read on a public page; it is southern China rather than Japan, and subtropical, so the tree species differ, and that the siting custom is the same is our assumption rather than the page's finding. It is a modern survey of the woods that have survived to be counted, not of what once stood; and the page rounds its figures and cites no study of its own, so where it disagrees with the underlying 2006 paper we follow the paper.

Used for: the survey summary - 116 woods, average 1 ha, 600 m² to 6 ha, 80% below 100 m; the 2006 paper's GIS table is primary where the two differ

afcd-hkbio-8

Yip, Ngar, Yip, Liu and Lai, "AFCD Survey of Local Fung Shui Woods", Hong Kong Biodiversity 8 (March 2005) 2-5 (https://www.afcd.gov.hk/english/publications/publications_con/files/hkbonewsletter8.pdf)

What it is: An article by Yip, Ngar, Yip, Liu and Lai reporting the Hong Kong government's survey of local fung shui woods, published in the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department's newsletter Hong Kong Biodiversity, issue 8 (March 2005). It describes what these village woods are, notes that they typically form a crescent behind a village, and explains how the surveyors drew each wood's boundary.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a government field survey of the actual feature we draw - the planted or protected belt of trees standing behind a village - by the people who measured it, which is why we take the crescent form and the boundary convention from it. The woods surveyed are in Hong Kong, in subtropical southern China rather than Japan, and they are the twenty-first-century remnants of a much older practice, so the form is better attested by this source than any historical extent is; the surveyors themselves note that boundaries were drawn when there were significantly fewer large trees than the wood once held.

Used for: the form - a crescent behind the village - and the boundary rule the area survey used

yuan-liu-2009

Yuan Juanwen and Liu Jinlong, "Fengshui forest management by the Buyi ethnic minority in China", Forest Ecology and Management 257(9) (2009) 2002-2009 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0378112709000632; the full text is paywalled: DOI 10.1016/j.foreco.2009.01.040)

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Yuan Juanwen and Liu Jinlong, "Fengshui forest management by the Buyi ethnic minority in China", published in Forest Ecology and Management in 2009, on how Buyi villages in Guizhou province hold and manage the sacred groves kept for a settlement's fengshui.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the shape of a village's sacred forest holdings in a real case - two fengshui parcels per village in the two villages studied - which is what sets how many groves a village on our maps keeps. Its limits are that it is two villages of one ethnic minority in one southwestern province, so a shape and its extremes rather than an average; that it is a count of what survived in the 2000s, after a century in which collectivization and forestry law reshaped village forests; and that the 133-hectare lineage forest the record quotes as the large tail of the range is not this paper's own measurement - it is a Han lineage's forest in Fujian, cited secondhand in the paper's introduction from another author - so the outlier comes from a different province and a different community.

Used for: two fengshui parcels per village in two Buyi villages (Guizhou); the 133 ha Letu lineage forest as the large tail

park-2013-maeulsup

Park Mee Jeong, Kim Sang Bum, Jang Choul Soon, Shin Min Ji and Kim Eun Ja, 「A study on the construction of a GIS database of traditional village groves and on the analysis of their distribution characteristics」 (translated from the Korean by this project; original: 「전통마을 숲의 GIS-DB구축 및 분포 특성 분석에 관한 연구」), 농촌계획 (Journal of Korean Society of Rural Planning) 19(1) (2013) 149-164 (https://koreascience.kr/article/JAKO201311637857073.pdf) - Korean analogue

What it is: A peer-reviewed Korean study by Park Mee Jeong, Kim Sang Bum, Jang Choul Soon, Shin Min Ji and Kim Eun Ja in the Journal of the Korean Society of Rural Planning (2013), which assembles a mapped database of 462 traditional village groves and field-surveys 100 of them, reporting each grove's area, its distance from the village and the kind of place it stands in.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the only publicly readable survey we found that actually measures the planted grove at a village's mouth, and its numbers are what our maps size that belt of trees by - most groves under a hectare, and the village-entrance grove, the sugumagi that blocks the water mouth, averaging around seven tenths of a hectare and accounting for 42 of the 100 surveyed. Two limits stated plainly: it is Korean rather than Japanese or Chinese, cited because no comparable public survey of Japanese village groves could be read, and Korea is offered as a fair analogue because it shares the region's geomantic siting tradition and its village scale; and the groves measured are the ones that survive today, so a present-day area is only an approximation of the original planting.

Used for: the 462-grove GIS census (national mean the paper's own national mean of 10,375 m² - which is the unweighted mean of its eight PROVINCIAL means and not the per-grove mean of the census, that being about 10,223 m²; 356 of the 462 under 10,000 m²) and the 100-grove field survey by location type: the village-entrance grove (동구숲, the sugumagi water-mouth blocker) mean 7,149 m², 42 of 100

kweon-youn-2021

Kweon Deogkyu and Youn Yeo-Chang, "Factors influencing sustainability of traditional village groves (Maeulsoop) in Korea", Forest Policy and Economics 128 (2021) 102477 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1389934121000836; open access) - Korean analogue

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Kweon Deogkyu and Youn Yeo-Chang, "Factors influencing sustainability of traditional village groves (Maeulsoop) in Korea", published open access in Forest Policy and Economics in 2021. It surveys twenty-four red pine village groves around Mt. Jiri in Namwon, South Korea, reporting each grove's area and how many trees it holds along with the social conditions that keep such groves alive.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the closest thing to a measured answer we could read on a public page to the question of how big a village's planted grove actually is and how many trees stand in it, so it sets the size band our groves are drawn to. Two honest limits: it is Korean, standing in for Japan and China because no comparable open survey of Japanese or Chinese village groves could be read, though village grove planting is a shared regional practice; and it measures groves as they survive today, which records what has lasted rather than what was originally planted.

Used for: 24 red-pine village groves around Mt. Jiri: mean 2,197 m², range 250-6,330 m²; "less than 10 to more than 100" trees per grove

ma-2017-fengshui-carbon

Ma Lei, Shen Chunyu, Lou Duo, Fu Shenglei and Guan Dongsheng, "Patterns of ecosystem carbon density in edge-affected fengshui forests", Ecological Engineering 107 (2017) (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0925857417304548; the full text is paywalled: DOI 10.1016/j.ecoleng.2017.07.037)

What it is: A peer-reviewed article by Ma Lei, Shen Chunyu, Lou Duo, Fu Shenglei and Guan Dongsheng, "Patterns of ecosystem carbon density in edge-affected fengshui forests", published in Ecological Engineering in 2017. It measures forty-five plots of 40 by 40 m across five surviving fengshui forest fragments around Guangzhou in southern China, reporting among other things how much tree trunk area each hectare of grove carries.

Why it applies, and its limits: The basal area it reports is our best readable measure of how densely a village's protective grove actually stands, which is what decides whether a grove is drawn as scattered trees or as a solid canopy. Its limits are real: the full text is behind a paywall, so we use only the abstract and the publicly visible passages; it measures subtropical Guangdong fragments as they survive today, so it is a modern measurement of the remains of an old practice, and a southern Chinese figure applied to a setting that leans Japanese.

Used for: basal area 30.0-52.5 m²/ha in five Guangzhou fengshui fragments (45 plots of 40 x 40 m)

zhongshan-fsw-2016

孙红梅、张冬冬、修小娟 (Sun Hongmei and Xiu Xiaojuan of the Guangdong Zhongshan State-owned Forest Resource Protection Center, 广东省中山市国有森林资源保护中心; Zhang Dongdong, the corresponding author, of the Fuxin City Forestry Bureau, Liaoning, 辽宁省阜新市林业局), 「The medicinal plant resources of the fengshui groves of Zhongshan City」 (translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「中山市风水林的药用植物资源」), 热带生物学报 (Journal of Tropical Biology) 7(3) (2016) 368-372 (https://rdswxb.hainanu.edu.cn/cn/article/doi/10.15886/j.cnki.rdswxb.2016.03.016; DOI 10.15886/j.cnki.rdswxb.2016.03.016)

What it is: A peer-reviewed survey by Sun Hongmei, Zhang Dongdong and Xiu Xiaojuan, "The medicinal plant resources of the fengshui groves of Zhongshan City" (中山市风水林的药用植物资源), published in 热带生物学报 (Journal of Tropical Biology) in 2016; the authors work for the state forest resource protection center of Zhongshan in Guangdong and for the forestry bureau of Fuxin in Liaoning, and the fieldwork behind it covers that one municipality's fengshui groves.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it not for its botany but for the count it had to make first: 66 groves in 66 natural villages totaling 269.85 hectares, which works out at about four hectares a village and gives us a typical grove to draw against the very large outliers other studies report. Its limits are place and era - the Pearl River Delta is subtropical southern China, warmer and wetter than the setting's Japanese model, and the groves were measured as they stand now, so the figure describes the survivors of a century of clearing around them rather than what a village once held.

Used for: a Pearl River Delta municipal census of fengshui groves - 66 groves in 66 natural villages, 269.85 ha in total (about 4.1 ha each, the record's arithmetic)

huangshan-daily-jiekou

黄山日报 (Huangshan Daily), 「Huangshan's exploration of the forest-chief system」 (translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「林长制的黄山探索」), 2022-01-01, mirrored by the Yangtze River Delta CPC news site (http://www.yrdcpcn.org.cn/c189/20240913/i238685.phtml; journalism, not scholarship) - read in machine translation and the Chinese original was not read

What it is: A newspaper article from 黄山日报 (the Huangshan Daily), "林长制的黄山探索" ("Huangshan's exploration of the forest-chief system"), dated 1 January 2022 and mirrored on a Yangtze River Delta party news site. It reports on a modern forest-stewardship program in Anhui province, and in passing describes the water-mouth grove standing at the entrance to Jiekou village in Shexian.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one concrete measure of a water-mouth grove - over a hundred mu (roughly seven hectares), nearly a thousand old trees, and fifty-six yews more than five centuries old - and the record treats that as the extreme end of the range rather than the ordinary case; a stand that has been kept at a village mouth for that long is evidence about the form even though the article around it is current news. Its limits: it is journalism rather than scholarship and it is promotional about a government program; the numbers are the reporter's, unsourced; the article is in Chinese and we read it in machine translation, so the wording is not the newspaper's own English; and it describes the largest example anyone in the region can name, so nothing in it should be read as typical.

Used for: the Jiekou (Shexian) water-mouth grove - over a hundred mu with nearly a thousand ancient trees and 56 yews over 500 years old, described as the largest in East China: the tail, not the type

meander-enwiki

Wikipedia, "Meander" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meander)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on meanders - the bends a channel makes as it winds across its own floodplain. It gives the geometry of a bend (its radius against the channel's width, its wavelength, its sinuosity) and the erosion and deposition that cut one, and it credits the radius figure to Leopold and Langbein's 1966 Scientific American article on river meanders.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the one number our ditches are drawn from - how tight a turn running water makes, measured against the channel's own width - together with the bank behavior that produces it. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia article rather than the survey work behind it; that the radius it gives is the curvature a FREE channel settles into over years by cutting its own outer bank, while a farm ditch is dug and kept to a line, so its curve is set by whoever dug it and by the field boundary it runs along rather than by the water; and that it gives no figure for a maintained earthen ditch at all, so the step from a river's bend to a ditch's is this project's reasoning and not the article's.

Used for: how far a natural channel's bend swings against its own width - a bend radius of two to three channel widths - and what a turn does to the two banks

watersa-junction-angle

Water SA, "Numerical study of junction-angle effects on flow pattern in a river confluence located in a river bend" (https://scielo.org.za/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S1816-79502016000100006)

What it is: A 2016 paper in Water SA, the journal of South Africa's Water Research Commission, reporting a three-dimensional numerical model of a river confluence that sits inside a river bend. It runs the model across junction angles from 30 to 115 degrees and reports what each angle does to the zone of separated flow at the mouth, to the streamwise velocity near the inner wall, to the strength of the secondary spiral flow, and to the bed shear stress inside the junction.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one thing: the DIRECTION in which a junction's angle changes the way a side channel enters a larger one, which is what sets the two feet of a river-fed moat where it meets its river. Its limits are worth stating plainly - it models a confluence located in a bend, so its figures (a 59% rise in peak bed shear between 30 and 115 degrees) belong to that geometry rather than to a straight reach; it is a numerical model rather than a survey of a real waterway; it is modern hydraulics, so it describes what water does and says nothing about what a premodern builder intended or achieved; and the slack water behind the mouth and the attack on the far bank that our record reads from it are not among its findings. One limit deserves to be spelled out, because it bears on whether the direction we take from the paper carries at all: the model holds the tributary's width and its share of the discharge fixed, at the proportions of a laboratory channel, whereas the offtake that feeds a moat draws a share of its river's flow smaller by orders of magnitude - a trickle beside a current rather than one stream meeting another - so we cannot be sure even the direction of the effect survives the change of scale.

Used for: the direction in which a junction's angle changes the way a side channel enters a larger one: a wider angle enlarging the separation zone at the mouth and raising the bed shear inside the junction

daihachiguruma-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 大八車 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/大八車)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the daihachiguruma, the large two-wheeled hand cart of Edo-period Japan - a tertiary encyclopedia entry covering what the cart was, who was allowed to use it, where it was allowed, and the smaller beka-guruma of the Kamigata region.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one thing only, the legal confinement of the freight hand cart to Edo, Owari and Sunpu, which is what makes a cart the exception rather than the norm on a country lane, and for the article's note that freight carts were not permitted on the Tokaido until the Meiji period. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary rather than a document or a study; that it speaks for Japan alone, one half of this setting; and that it is about the regulated cities and highways, so it tells us what was forbidden outside them and nothing about what an ordinary village lane looked like.

Used for: the Edo hand cart, and the three places the shogunate allowed it: Edo, Owari and Sunpu

stone-routes-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Stone routes (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_routes)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the stone routes, the stone-paved ox-cart roads laid in Japan to carry goods and building materials into Kyoto - the stone is the road's surface, not its cargo - a tertiary entry that gives the road's construction: its width, the two rows of laid stones the wheels ran on and the earth track between them for the beasts.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the one measured wheeled way we could read for premodern Japan, 2.7 m of route with a 90 cm center for the bulls, which sets the upper bound our village lanes are kept under: if a purpose-built cart road was nine feet across, an ordinary farm track was not wider. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia article citing no survey in the passage we quote; that a paved road built to carry freight into the capital is the most exceptional kind of way there is and is not evidence of what an ordinary lane measured; and that it is Japanese, while China is this setting's leading reference.

Used for: the width of a purpose-built ox-cart route - 2.7 m overall, with a 90 cm walking center between two rows of laid stones

lowtech-chinese-wheelbarrow

Low-Tech Magazine, "The Chinese wheelbarrow" (https://solar.lowtechmagazine.com/2011/12/the-chinese-wheelbarrow/)

What it is: A long illustrated article from Low-Tech Magazine, an independent magazine on pre-industrial and low-energy technology, on the Chinese one-wheeled barrow - what it carried, how it was built, and the road network that grew up around it rather than around the cart. It quotes and credits its two main authorities by name, Rudolf Hommel's 1937 fieldwork on Chinese hand tools and Joseph Needham's history of Chinese technology.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is what our whole picture of a Chinese country lane rests on - narrow paths wide enough for a walker and a barrow, cart tracks only on the eastern plains, and paths built for pedestrians, carrying-pole porters, barrow-pushers and litter-bearers - which decides the vehicle we draw a lane for. Its limits are that it is a popular magazine article rather than a peer-reviewed study, so it is a readable route to Hommel and Needham rather than a primary source itself; that it is an advocacy publication whose standing thesis is that pre-industrial transport was more capable than it is remembered to be, so it reads its evidence in that direction; that it carries no width measurement at all - the paths it describes are 「scarcely wide enough for foot passengers and wheelbarrows」, which is a description and not a figure, so the width we draw a lane at is ours and not the article's; that its observations are early twentieth-century fieldwork used as a witness to a much older practice; and that its cart-track sentence speaks for the eastern plains, not for the rice-growing south our settlements are modeled on.

Used for: what the Chinese rural network was built for and who used it - narrow paths for foot passengers and wheelbarrows, with rough cart tracks only on the eastern plains

itabashi-kotobank

Encyclopedia entry s.v. 板橋, aggregated at kotobank (https://kotobank.jp/word/板橋)

What it is: The dictionary and encyclopedia entry for 板橋 (itabashi) at kotobank, which aggregates the major Japanese reference works, giving the word's plain sense: a bridge made of boards.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it to fix the name of the small crossing our maps draw over a farm ditch, so that the glyph and the word a reader clicks mean the same object - a planked deck and not an earthen one. Its limits are that it is a dictionary definition and nothing more: it gives no construction, no size, no period and no picture of how such a bridge was used, so everything else our entry says about the plank comes from elsewhere.

Used for: what an itabashi is: a bridge made of boards

dobashi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 土橋 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/土橋)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the dobashi, the earthen-decked bridge - a tertiary entry describing how one is built, logs laid side by side and earth thrown over and trodden down until the surface is level, and noting that in the Edo period plank bridges were limited to an important few while earthen bridges were the great majority.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the other half of the naming question: it tells us what a dobashi actually is, which is what lets our record say that the plank bridge and the earthen bridge are two different objects rather than two words for one. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary with no measurements and no dating of the technique, and that it is Japanese, so it names the Japanese form of a thing our maps place in a setting drawn from both China and Japan.

Used for: how an earthen bridge deck is built - earth thrown over side-by-side logs and trodden down until it fills the hollows

shakkanho-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 尺貫法 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/尺貫法)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the shakkanho, the traditional Japanese system of weights and measures, a tertiary entry that tabulates each unit against the metric system - among them the tsubo at 400/121 square meters, the se at thirty tsubo, and the tan at ten se.

Why it applies, and its limits: Every area a Japanese source states in tsubo, se or tan has to be turned into square meters before it can be drawn, and this is the conversion we use; the figures are exact definitions rather than measurements, so there is little for a source to be wrong about. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia article; that the article's own values are the legally fixed modern definitions of units whose local sizes varied before they were standardized, so a premodern document's tsubo may not be exactly this tsubo; and - the one that can put a figure badly wrong rather than slightly - that the tan was redefined in the course of Hideyoshi's cadastral survey, from 360 bu to the 300 bu this page's tan assumes, so an area a pre-1590s document states in tan and we convert with this table comes out about a fifth too small. The tsubo itself is stable across that change, so an area given in tsubo is safe.

Used for: the shakkanho land measures the record converts from: the tsubo, the se and the tan in square meters

kateisaien-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 家庭菜園 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/家庭菜園)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the household kitchen garden, a tertiary entry which records that ground a Japanese household cultivates to feed itself is called yashikibatake, the homestead field. It also gives the plot a short history: its origin can be traced as far back as the Yayoi period, and by the Edo period such a plot stood inside the residences of the warrior class as well as those of farmers.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the object and its name - the bed beside the house that grows a household's own food, as distinct from the fields it farms for the tax and the market - which is what the garden on our homesteads is, and its two dates are what tell us the plot is far older than the modern gardening the rest of the article is about. Its limits are sharp and worth stating: the article gives no area and no count, so it cannot support the size band our maps hold a garden to, and that band is labeled a guess on the page; its history is two sentences rather than an account, so it fixes that the plot existed early and nothing about what it looked like; and it says such cultivation is often done on odd scraps of ground away from the residence as well, so it does not by itself put the bed against the house.

Used for: the name of the household's own cultivated ground, the yashikibatake

fao-farm-structures-cattle

FAO, Farm structures in tropical climates, chapter 10, Cattle housing (https://www.fao.org/4/s1250e/s1250e11.htm)

What it is: The cattle-housing chapter of Farm structures in tropical climates, a design manual published by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations for builders and extension workers in the tropics. It gives the space a beast needs - a shade structure at 2.5 to 3 square meters per animal, a free stall 2.2 m long by 1.2 m wide for a milking cow of 500 to 600 kg, a bull pen with 12 to 15 square meters of shaded rest and 20 to 30 of exercise yard.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the readable answer to a question the historical record was silent on - how much room one large draft animal takes under a roof - and it is what keeps our byre shed sized against a stated figure rather than guessed at. Its limits are three, and the first two are stated on the page beside the figure. It is a MODERN standard, written for modern stock and modern welfare expectations, and a twentieth-century dairy cow is not an Edo-period ox or a water buffalo. It is written for a different part of the world - the manual addresses builders and extension workers in tropical Africa, so nothing in it is a record of East Asian practice, and the animals it sizes for are the ones kept there. And the third is a matter of DIRECTION: these are welfare minimums, what a builder today is told to provide, not measurements of what anyone built, so treating them as a target makes the shed we draw generous rather than accurate, and the error runs one way.

Used for: a modern standard the drawn byre is measured against: the stall length and width for a milking cow, and the shaded area a beast is allowed

tnau-cattle-housing

TNAU Agritech Portal, Animal Husbandry, housing space for cattle (https://agritech.tnau.ac.in/animal_husbandry/animhus_cb_housing_space.html)

What it is: A page of the Agritech Portal of Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, an Indian agricultural extension resource, tabulating the floor space livestock housing should allow by class of animal - for adult cattle, 3.5 square meters under cover and 7.0 square meters of open area, with a manger 60 to 75 cm.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a second modern figure for the room one adult beast needs, and it is what we check the FAO manual against: the two come out on the same order of size, which tells us neither is idiosyncratic. Its limits are the manual's and two more. The agreement is NOT independent corroboration of anything premodern - both pages are normative housing standards saying what a keeper ought to provide for modern stock, so both may be generous for the same reason, and two such standards agreeing says they share a convention rather than that an old byre measured what they recommend. The page is also unsigned and carries no references, so no figure on it can be traced back to a study. And it is a recommendation rather than a survey of what exists, written for southern Indian husbandry, so it stands in for East Asian practice on the strength of the animal rather than the place.

Used for: a second modern standard for the same question: the covered and open space an adult beast is given, and the width of its manger

hinomi-yagura-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 火の見櫓 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%81%AB%E3%81%AE%E8%A6%8B%E6%AB%93)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the 火の見櫓 (hinomi-yagura), the fire-watch tower of Japanese towns and villages: a raised lookout platform used to spot a fire early, summon the fire brigade and sound the alarm to the neighborhood, generally carrying a hansho bell at its top. It covers how the towers developed alongside the firefighting system from Edo-period Edo, how far across the country they had spread by the early Showa era, and the town-by-town code by which the bell was rung.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the plain definition of the structure our city maps draw and of what the watch on it was for, and it is the only source in the record that dates the institution and its spread, which is what settles whether a small unwalled seat would carry one. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary rather than a study; that it describes Japan alone; that much of the article is about the surviving steel towers and the modern volunteer companies, so the premodern form has to be taken from its historical passages and not from what it shows standing today; and that its two datings do different work and must not be run together - it puts the ORIGIN of the tower in Edo-period Edo, the shogunal capital, but the SPREAD of the form across the country in the early Showa era, which is the twentieth century, so the fact that such towers became common everywhere cannot be used to put one in a small premodern settlement.

Used for: what a fire-watch tower was for, the watch house beneath it with its permanently stationed watchman, and the dating of the institution and of its spread across the country

hansho-kotobank

kotobank 半鐘 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%8D%8A%E9%90%98-118280)

What it is: Kotobank's entry for 半鐘 (hansho), aggregating standard Japanese reference dictionaries: the small bronze hanging bell hung on a fire-watch tower, and the code by which the number of strokes told a hearer what kind of incident had happened - for a fire, a continuous peal for a near one, fewer strokes the further off it was. The entries also date the usage: one of the dictionaries puts the hanging of the bell on a fire-watch tower from the Edo period onward, and the historical dictionary among them carries an attestation of the word from 1686.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the one thing our fire-tower explanation needs beyond the tower itself: that the bell carried information by its cadence rather than simply making a noise, which is why a watchman on a tower is worth drawing, and it puts that bell on a tower within the period our settlements are pitched in rather than leaving it undated. Its limits are that it is a short tertiary dictionary entry with no citations; that its 1686 attestation is of the WORD in another of its senses, the bell of a striking clock, the earliest example it gives for the fire-alarm sense being dated 1706; and that it describes Japan only.

Used for: the alarm bell hung on a fire-watch tower and the code its strokes carried - a continuous peal for a near fire, fewer strokes the further off it was - and the bell's dating to the Edo period

machibikeshi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 町火消 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%94%BA%E7%81%AB%E6%B6%88)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the 町火消 (machi-bikeshi), the townsman fire companies of Edo: the ordinance establishing them, issued in 1718 by the South Town Magistrate Ooka Tadasuke on the advice of the block headmen and of Ogyu Sorai; the 1720 revision into forty-seven iroha companies west of the Sumida and sixteen more for Honjo and Fukagawa, one company to about twenty blocks; and the arrangement by which the companies stood under the town magistrate's command while each block bore their cost.

Why it applies, and its limits: It tells us who actually manned, paid for and commanded an urban fire watch, which is the point our setting departs from deliberately, and it shows that the departure is narrower than it looks, since command sat with the magistrate historically as well. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary; that it is about Edo alone, the largest city in the country; and that it describes an institution of the long Tokugawa peace, so its scale and its politics do not transfer to a provincial city of the earlier, more martial period these maps are pitched in.

Used for: who manned, paid for and commanded a townsman fire company, and the block-by-block scale of the arrangement - which is what our setting's fire watch is measured against

dongjing-menghualu-wikisource

孟元老, 東京夢華錄 卷三 (Chinese Wikisource) (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E6%9D%B1%E4%BA%AC%E5%A4%A2%E8%8F%AF%E9%8C%84/%E5%8D%B7%E4%B8%89)

What it is: The third chapter of 東京夢華錄 (Dreams of Splendor of the Eastern Capital), Meng Yuanlao's recollection of daily life in Kaifeng, the Northern Song capital, written in the twelfth century after the city had fallen, given here in the original literary Chinese on Chinese Wikisource. The passage we use describes the military patrol posts set through the wards and lanes and the brick-built 望火樓 fire-watch tower, with its lookouts above and its quartered soldiers and firefighting gear below.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a primary account, by someone who lived in the city, of exactly the institution our city maps draw - a permanent fire-watch tower with a manned station under it - in a dense premodern East Asian capital, which is the strongest kind of evidence the record can have for it. Its limits are that it describes one imperial capital at the very top of the urban hierarchy and not a provincial seat; that it is a nostalgic memoir composed from memory after the city was lost, so its figures are recollection rather than record; and that it says nothing about smaller towns, so it cannot be read either way on what an ordinary market town kept.

Used for: the Song capital's brick-built fire-watch tower, with lookouts above and soldiers and firefighting gear below, and the military patrol posts set through its wards and lanes

omamori-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Omamori (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omamori)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the omamori, the amulet a Japanese shrine or temple gives out - what it is, how it is made and carried, and how it is understood by the people who receive one.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the transaction rather than the object: the amulet comes from the shrine or temple itself, and what the recipient gives back is understood as a donation to it, which is why our maps show no third-party stall selling charms at a temple gate. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary; that the word the article itself uses for the exchange is "sold", so "bestowed" is our own gloss on it and not the page's; that our conclusion goes one step further than anything the page states - it never says that nobody else sold charms at a gate, and we are reading that from its silence; that the passages about factory manufacture and shop-sold versions describe MODERN commercialism, not the premodern practice our maps depict, so they cannot be read back into the setting; and that it describes Japan alone.

Used for: the amulet as a donation to the shrine or temple that issues it

monzenmachi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 門前町 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%96%80%E5%89%8D%E7%94%BA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the monzen-machi, the town that grows in front of a large shrine or temple: how it forms when tradesmen and craftsmen dealing with the institution and its pilgrims gather at the gate, and how its trades changed over time.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our evidence that the approach to a great temple carries a settlement of its own, which is what puts shops, inns and lodging on a city map beside a temple rather than scattered anywhere. Its limits matter to how we read it: the article attributes the eating houses and souvenir shops a modern visitor pictures to the RAILWAY era, and names inns (hatago) as the premodern trade, so the crowded food-and-souvenir street is later than the period we draw; and it is a tertiary summary describing Japan.

Used for: who gathers before a great temple's gate, and how the trades there shifted

qingming-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Qingming Festival (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qingming_Festival)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Qingming, the Chinese tomb-sweeping festival: the visit to the ancestors' graves, the cleaning and maintenance of the ground, and the offerings burned there - incense, joss paper, spirit money and paper replicas of goods.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives us what actually happens at a Chinese grave, which is what makes a burial ground a tended place on our maps rather than waste ground, and it names the paper goods whose makers we put among the funeral trades. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary; that it describes the festival as practiced rather than a historical period, so it cannot date anything; and that it says nothing about where the goods were made or sold, nor how far from a mound the tending reached, which is the figure our drawn collar would need.

Used for: the spirit money and paper replicas a family burns for its dead, and the tomb-sweeping and groundskeeping at a grave

tudigong-enwiki

en.wikipedia, Tudigong (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tudigong)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on Tudigong, the Chinese earth god, and the small shrines kept for him - in villages, in the countryside, and inside larger temples and houses.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the shrine's PLACE: the article shows such a shrine standing within a village's entrance gate, which is what puts the village shrine at the way in on our maps rather than at its center. Its limits are sharp: the instance it shows is a photograph caption of one walled village in Hong Kong, not a general statement; the article's own PROSE gives a different typical placement, describing such shrines as commonly located beneath the main altar of a temple or below the door of a house, so a reader of the page would come away with the household and temple shrine rather than the village gate; and nothing on it connects the earth-god shrine to the water-mouth specifically, so the join our record makes between the two is our own reading and is labeled as such.

Used for: the earth-god shrine standing inside a walled village's entrance gate

cssn-citang-panyu

中国社会科学网, 漫谈番禺广府祠堂 (https://www.cssn.cn/ztzl/jzz/rwln/wh/whcy/202209/t20220923_5541419.shtml)

What it is: An article by 朱光文 (Zhu Guangwen), published in the magazine 人文岭南 (Renwen Lingnan) number 98 and dated 2019-11-27 where it is reposted on the website of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, about the Cantonese (Guangfu) ancestral halls of Panyu, in Guangdong: how such a hall is laid out on its axis, with a pond or pan-pool and an open plaza before its front gate, and what the plaza is used for.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our evidence that a hall of this kind fronts a hard open plaza where the lineage gathers and holds its ceremonies, which is why our maps keep swept open ground before a religious building instead of packing houses to its door. Its limits are that it describes the Cantonese ancestral HALL of one southern county, not the earth-god shrine we pair it with and not northern practice; that it is a popular article on an institutional site rather than a survey; that it is written about halls that are still standing, and where it does sort them by period it is dating the BUILDINGS, while every sentence it gives about the plaza carries no period at all - so it says what such a forecourt is for and nothing about when the arrangement began or how old the one we draw would be; and that it says nothing about grain-drying, markets or opera on that ground.

Used for: the pool and the open plaza in front of a Cantonese ancestral hall, and the reasons given for them - fengshui, drainage and fire

ryobosei-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 両墓制 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E4%B8%A1%E5%A2%93%E5%88%B6)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on ryobosei, the two-grave system: the burial place where the body is interred, often in mountain forest away from habitation, and the separate visiting-grave with its stone pagoda, frequently inside a temple precinct, which holds neither body nor bone.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the practice that lets our maps put a settlement's burial ground at the edge of the fields while the stone that a family visits stands at the district's temple - two places for one dead person, which is otherwise hard to credit. Its limits are stated on the page and we keep them: the custom is concentrated in the Kinki region and merely scattered elsewhere, so it is a regional form rather than a national norm, and the article is a tertiary summary.

Used for: the two-grave system - the burial place away from habitation and the separate visiting-grave that holds neither body nor bone - which is what lets a settlement's burial ground stand out at the edge of the fields while the stone a family visits stands at a temple

chinju-no-mori-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 鎮守の森 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%8E%AE%E5%AE%88%E3%81%AE%E6%A3%AE)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the chinju no mori, the forest attached to a Shinto shrine: a wood established and maintained within the precinct and around it so that it surrounds the sanctuary, the approach and the place of worship.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is why the ground around a shrine is drawn swept but the trees around it are drawn standing: the grove is deliberately KEPT, the opposite of cleared, so our sweeping rule touches only the loose scatter and never the wood. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary with no measurements - no depth, no species count, no distance from the hall - so it gives the principle and none of the numbers, and that it describes Japan.

Used for: the kept grove around a shrine, established and maintained so as to surround the precinct

kofukuroman-sanmai

福井県伝承浪漫, 県内各地サンマイ写真（火葬場・土葬地）【福井県の葬送Ⅳ】 (https://kofukuroman.com/sousou4-sanmai/)

What it is: A page of 福井県伝承浪漫, one enthusiast's folklore website about Fukui prefecture, on the sanmai - the burial and cremation ground of a Fukui hamlet - with field photographs, the local names, and the observation that the sanmai stands at the edge of the settlement while the visiting-grave is at the temple within it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is our readable witness that ordinary hamlets buried their own dead at their own fringe, which is what sets a burial ground at the edge of a settlement on our maps, and it describes the cremation site as a dug pit with no building, which is what keeps our drawn cremation ground bare. Its limits are considerable and worth naming: it is one person's compilation with photographs rather than a survey, written and published without editorial review, so nothing on it has been checked by anyone but its author; it gives no areas or distances at all; the grounds it photographs are twentieth-century survivals rather than sites dated to any premodern century, so they witness a custom that lasted into living memory rather than one we can date; and it speaks for one prefecture.

Used for: a worked instance of the two-grave system: the sanmai standing at the edge of the hamlet while the visiting graves stand at temples inside it

bochi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 墓地 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A2%93%E5%9C%B0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the graveyard as a category, which distinguishes the kinds - among them the village graveyard, held in common and managed by the inhabitants of a settlement - and notes that new graveyards of that kind are no longer permitted under present-day Japanese law.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one fact: the village graveyard held in common by its own inhabitants is a recognized kind of place, which is what justifies drawing one ground for a settlement rather than scattered family plots. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary largely concerned with modern regulation, that it gives no size, no siting rule and no period for the village form, and that it gives no household threshold and nothing on the disused grounds left standing.

Used for: the village graveyard held in common and managed by the settlement's own inhabitants

tanigawa-1992

Tanigawa Akio, "Excavating Edo's Cemeteries: Graves as Indicators of Status and Class", Japanese Journal of Religious Studies 19/2-3 (1992) (https://nirc.nanzan-u.ac.jp/journal/6/article/832/pdf/download)

What it is: A peer-reviewed article in the Japanese Journal of Religious Studies, freely readable in full, reporting the archaeology of Edo-period cemeteries excavated in Tokyo. It sorts the graves into categories by construction - stone chambers, wooden coffin graves, jar burials in wooden chambers, plain jar burials and coffins - and gives the major axis of each kind, from 65 cm to 2.4 m.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the only measured evidence our record has for how much ground one grave takes, which is what our burial-ground sizes are built up from. Its limits must be stated wherever it is used: the paper gives the size of a GRAVE PIT and no area per burial, no density and no cemetery area - the one large figure in it is the excavation trench, not a graveyard - so the step from a pit's width to a ground's acreage is this project's arithmetic; and it is Edo-period Japan, so it says nothing about Chinese full-body burial.

Used for: the sizes of excavated Edo commoner graves

tokyohakuzen-yoyogi

東京博善, 設立前の歴史 (https://www.tokyohakuzen.co.jp/anniversary/history02/)

What it is: The institutional history page of Tokyo Hakuzen, a Japanese crematory operator, on the cremation grounds that preceded it. It quotes the Edo-period gazetteer Shinpen Musashi Fudoki-ko for the Yoyogi cremation ground: 900 tsubo in extent, with three houses of those who worked there.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one readable figure we have for the size of a cremation ground serving a great city, and it is what our drawn grounds are scaled against. Its limits are worth being plain about: it is a company's own history quoting a gazetteer rather than the gazetteer itself (and it misprints the title), so the figure reaches us at one remove; it is a single ground serving metropolitan Edo, the largest city in the country, so it is an upper anchor and not a typical one.

Used for: the Musashi gazetteer's 900 tsubo for a cremation ground, and the three households of those who worked it

ritter-timber-bridges

Michael A. Ritter, Timber Bridges: Design, Construction, Inspection, and Maintenance, USDA Forest Service EM 7700-8 (1990), 944 pp (https://www.ltrc.la.gov/ltap/pdf/timber_bridges_design_construction_inspection_maintenance.pdf)

What it is: The United States Forest Service's standard manual for timber bridges, written by a Forest Service engineer: the timber itself, the design of beams, decks and railings, the kinds of abutment, and inspection and maintenance, with worked design examples running to 944 pages.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for the one thing our own record had only reasoned about, what a timber beam actually needs to bear on, and for what an abutment is there to do, which is to hold the roadway embankment. Its limits are large, and they are why it settles only half of the question it was fetched for: it is a modern manual, and its worked examples are highway-loaded glulam beams on spans up to about 94 feet, far heavier and longer than a plank over a farm ditch, so its bearing lengths are an upper bound and not a premodern measurement; and in 944 pages it never gives a distance from the water's edge to the abutment, which is the figure our maps actually draw.

Used for: the bearing length of a timber beam - 10 to 24 inches in the manual's own worked designs - and the abutment as the thing that contains the roadway embankment. NOT for the landing distance, which it does not give and which stays a GUESS

nrcs-ts14q-abutments

United States Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service, "Technical Supplement 14Q: Abutment Design for Small Bridges", National Engineering Handbook Part 654 (2007) (https://directives.nrcs.usda.gov/sites/default/files2/1712931168/7375.pdf)

What it is: A design supplement in the United States Department of Agriculture's engineering handbook covering the abutments of small rural bridges - the single-span, single-lane kind carried on timber stringers and simple strip footings - with the loads, the footing, the slope and what to do about scour.

Why it applies, and its limits: It describes the bridge our maps draw, and it states the mechanism that sets an abutment back from the water: a shallow strip footing cannot be sunk below the depth the current will scour, so the bank is armored instead and the footing kept clear of it. Its limits are that it is modern engineering guidance written for modern materials, loads and construction; that the only distance in it is an illustrative worked example rather than a rule, and is measured from the crest of the bank slope rather than from the water; and that it is American, standing in for a practice no premodern East Asian source we could read describes.

Used for: the scour reason for setting a bridge's bearing back from the channel edge, and the description of the small single-span timber bridge our plank glyph stands for. NOT for a landing distance

toyama-1988-road-undevelopment

外山科夫, 二宮公紀 and 馬場俊介, "我が国の道路未整備の背景 - 江戸から昭和初期まで -" (The background to the undeveloped state of our country's roads, from Edo to the early Showa), 日本土木史研究発表会論文集 8 (1988) 96-103 (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/journalhs1981/8/0/8_0_96/_pdf)

What it is: A refereed paper in the proceedings of Japan's civil engineering history conference asking why Japan built no roads for wheeled vehicles between the Edo period and the early twentieth century: what moved on the roads, what was forbidden on them, and what the prohibition was protecting.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the direct evidence for the countryside our lanes are drawn for - no horse-drawn carriage at all before Meiji, inhabitants on foot or on horseback, goods on a horse's back - It is also precise where the general account is loose: the highway cart prohibition was to keep the post-horse system supplied with horses, not to spare the road surface, and the causes it names include the kind of horse rather than the size of one. Its limits are that it speaks for Japan alone, one half of this setting; that it is a short conference paper rather than a monograph; and that it gives no road widths and no lane dimensions of any kind.

Used for: the absence of the cart from the Japanese countryside; the highway prohibition and its motive; the light city cart doing the road little damage; terrain, climate and the kind of horse as the causes named

ctie-michi-nazenaze

株式会社建設技術研究所 (CTI Engineering Co., Ltd.), 道のなぜなぜ 1-4, "江戸時代の道路はどのようなものだったのですか？" (https://www.ctie.co.jp/service/publishing/img/michi-nazenaze/1-4.pdf)

What it is: A short explanatory sheet on Edo-period roads from a question-and-answer series published by a large Japanese civil engineering consultancy, covering the Five Highways, their construction and their width.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the width of the trunk highways in ken, and it is careful in exactly the way that mattered to us: it states the ordinary figure with mountain roads expressly excluded, so the two are not to be confused. Its limits are that it is a company's popular publication and cites no survey behind the number; that it is Japanese; that it gives no figure at all for the mountain roads it excludes, so that narrowing remains unsourced; and that a second readable account of the same highways gives a wider ordinary width, so the two bracket the figure rather than confirm it.

Used for: the Five Highways at 3 to 4 ken (about 5.4 to 7.2 m) excluding mountain roads, and 5 ken (about 9 m) where they ran close to Edo

nippon-com-gokaido

nippon.com, 大名行列が通った道: 五街道と脇往還 (https://www.nippon.com/ja/japan-topics/c08604/)

What it is: A general-audience article from nippon.com, the news and culture site of a Japanese public-interest foundation, on the Five Highways and the secondary routes beside them, and on the daimyo processions that traveled them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the second readable account of a trunk highway's width, and it disagrees with the first - 4 ken as the ordinary width, rising to 7 or 8 ken in places - which is why our record brackets the figure instead of stating one. Its limits are that it is journalism with no survey cited; that the explanation it offers for the width is a military one, which suits the greatest highways and not an ordinary road; and that it says nothing about mountain roads or about the barriers.

Used for: the second, wider account of the Five Highways' width (4 ken, rising to 7 or 8 ken in places)

chinaknowledge-caoyun

ChinaKnowledge.de, "caoyun 漕運, tribute grain transport" (http://www.chinaknowledge.de/History/Terms/caoyun.html)

What it is: A reference page on caoyun, the imperial tribute-grain transport, from ChinaKnowledge.de, a scholar-run encyclopedia of Chinese history: what the grain was, which provinces produced it, the canal system that carried it, and the fleet and troops that worked it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the fact our lanes depend on - that bulk goods in Ming China moved by water, in quantities no road could have taken - with the 1472 decree of four million shi a year to the canal terminal outside Beijing and the abandonment of the sea route. Its limits are that it is a tertiary reference page rather than a study, so its figures reach us without the gazetteer or archive behind them; that it describes the state's own grain traffic rather than ordinary trade; and that it does not characterize the feeder canals as a dense net; and that it says nothing about Japan, whose water freight stays uncited.

Used for: tribute rice moving by canal and river boat; the 1472 four-million-shi decree and the Tongzhou terminal; sea transport replaced by canal transport

kyoto-machiya-isan

京都市 (City of Kyoto), 京都遺産, 京町家とその暮らしの文化 (https://kyoto-bunkaisan.city.kyoto.lg.jp/kyotoisan/nintei-theme/kyoumachiya.html)

What it is: The City of Kyoto's own heritage description of the Kyo-machiya, the Kyoto townhouse: the earth-floored passage running from the street to the back of the plot, the working front where customers are received, the cooking place behind it, and named surviving houses of the type.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states as a principle the thing our shop-house bands are built on, work and dwelling in one building, and it says which part of the plan is shop and which is home, so a merchant family living behind its own storefront is no longer general reading. Its limits are that it is a municipal heritage page rather than a study; that the Kyo-machiya is the most developed and most urban form of the type, so an ordinary county-seat shop would be plainer, smaller and less deep; and that it gives no dimensions a map could use.

Used for: the merchant family living over or directly behind its own premises, and which end of the plot is the shop

dachedian-jilin-daily

王爽, "消失的大车店" (The vanished dachedian), 吉林日报, 25 April 2026 (http://jlrbszb.dajilin.com/pad/paper/c/202604/25/content_1049361.html)

What it is: A descriptive article in the Jilin Daily, a Chinese provincial newspaper, on the dachedian - the inn that took in passing carts and draft animals on the roads of the northeast - written partly from the author's memory of staying in one as a child, and describing the yard, the stable and its trough, the grooms' lean-to, the well and the yard wall.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the closest attested analogue to the caravan inn our town maps draw, and the only account read that describes the whole arrangement rather than just naming the institution; it is also what contradicts the drawn inn's second story, since it says the buildings in the yard were uniformly single-story. Its limits are that it is journalism and personal recollection rather than a survey; that it describes a twentieth-century survival in Manchuria rather than a Ming or Edo inn, and in the north rather than in the rice-growing south this setting also leans on; and that it counts nothing - no animals, no rooms, no dimensions - so every size on our sheet remains ours.

Used for: the wagon inn's siting on the main thoroughfare or in the belt outside a city; the back yard for the carts, the long stable with its feeding trough and tying rail, the grooms' lean-to and the yard well; and the single-story buildings that contradict the drawn inn's second story

lai-2003-daoism-today

Lai Chi-Tim, "Daoism in China Today, 1980-2002", The China Quarterly 174 (2003) 413-427, DOI 10.1017/S0009443903000275, read on a library mirror rather than in the publisher's own edition (https://library.fes.de/libalt/journals/swetsfulltext/17041744.pdf)

What it is: A peer-reviewed survey of Daoism in China in the two decades after 1980, built from the Chinese Daoist Association's own journals and statistics and from the author's fieldwork at temples in Beijing, Chengdu, Suzhou, Nanjing, Shanghai and Guangzhou and in a village on the Guangdong coast. It distinguishes the two orders - the monastic Quanzhen and the Zhengyi - and describes how each is ordained, where its clergy live, and how the state has regulated them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source for the thing that puts a Daoist priest's household on a map rather than a dormitory: that the majority of Zhengyi priests lived married at home rather than in a temple, which is what makes their housing invert the Buddhist pattern. The author states that of the premodern tradition directly and in the past tense, so the record is not projecting a modern survival backward on its own authority. The limits are of two kinds. What is his own is modern: the fieldwork, the association statistics and every count in the article belong to the years its title names, so no proportion for any earlier century can come from here, and the twentieth-century form he describes was shaped by confiscation, a ban on the at-home clergy and the burning of their manuscripts before the rebuilding of the 1980s. What is premodern is RELAYED: the sentence the record quotes carries his own footnote to Schipper's The Taoist Body, and the state-pressure sentence beside it a footnote to Goossaert on the Chinese clergy - neither read by this project, so the historical claim reaches the record at one remove and those two are where a session should go to put it on its own feet. It is mainland China throughout, with Taiwan only in passing and nothing at all on Japan. And it is read on a third-party library mirror of a subscription aggregator rather than at the publisher, which is a link of exactly the kind that vanishes: the DOI is recorded above against that day.

Used for: the married Zhengyi priest living at home rather than in a monastery, and the state's standing objection to it

lagerwey-1988-taoist-lineages

John Lagerwey, 「The Taoist lineages of Northern Taiwan」 (translated from the French by this project; original: 「Les lignées taoïstes du Nord de Taiwan」), Cahiers d'Extreme-Asie 4 (1988) 127-143, DOI 10.3406/asie.1988.915 (https://www.persee.fr/docAsPDF/asie_0766-1177_1988_num_4_1_915.pdf)

What it is: A study of the Daoist priestly families of northern Taiwan, reconstructed from the lists of lineage masters in their own liturgical manuals and from their family registers, with dated genealogical tables running from the eighth to the twenty-third generation. The author worked with his own master in Taipei and its district in 1986 and 1987 and then followed the lineages back to their mainland origin on the Guangdong and Fujian border country - the Liu to Jao-p'ing in Chaozhou prefecture, the Lin over the provincial line to Chao-an in Fujian, which he treats as one region because the two sub-prefectures adjoin.

Why it applies, and its limits: Where a general statement says a Daoist office is hereditary, this DEMONSTRATES it - names, dates and generations over about two hundred years - which is why the record hangs the hereditary half of its clergy rule here rather than on a summary. Its limits are that it is one regional tradition, probably Hakka in origin - the author hedges the word himself, since one of his lineages speaks the Chaozhou dialect and is not Hakka at all - in Taiwan and on the Fujian and Guangdong coast, so it is not evidence for Daoist practice across China; that a handful of lineages can show the office DID descend in families and can never give a rate; that transmission in its own tables runs to an adopted son, a son-in-law or a disciple as readily as to a son, so a strict father-to-son rule overstates it; and that it records at least two lines that simply stopped. Two things that cut the other way and belong here for balance: the Qing evidence is documentary rather than remembered - written family registers and liturgical manuscripts copied in 1908, 1928 and 1932, with masters dated from the middle of the eighteenth century - so for the hereditary claim this is period documentation and not a modern informant's account of the past; and the author is candid that the registers he reconstructs from contain manifest errors and gaps, which touches who descended from whom rather than whether the offices descended at all.

Used for: the hereditary transmission of a Daoist priest's office within a family, and the width of that transmission - son, adopted son, son-in-law or disciple

okabe-hatago-jawiki

大旅籠柏屋 (the Ohatago Kashibaya, the preserved lodging house of Okabe-juku), Japanese Wikipedia (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A4%A7%E6%97%85%E7%B1%A0%E6%9F%8F%E5%B1%8B)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on a lodging house of the Tokaido post station at Okabe, in Fujieda, Shizuoka - a rebuilding thought from an 1835 cost record to date from about 1836, registered as a national tangible cultural property in 1998 and open today as a museum. It gives the building's construction and its rooms floor by floor: two stories of wood under a tile roof, guest rooms above, and the main parlor, the kitchen and the proprietor family's own living space below.

Why it applies, and its limits: It settles that a highway inn of two stories is a real Japanese building and not an invention of this project's drawing. Its limits are the reason it does not settle the drawing. Nothing read describes a cart yard, a long stable, a feeding trough or a grooms' lean-to at a lodging house of this kind - this article describes the building and its rooms and says nothing of a yard at all - so it is no evidence for the fittings the wagon inn our maps draw is built around, and an analogue for a different institution. It is one building, and an exceptional one selected by its own survival: 大旅籠 names it the great hatago of its town, and its proprietors ran a pawnshop beside the inn and served as post-station officers, so it is the leading house of the street rather than the ordinary one on it. Its date, about 1836, is the very end of the period this setting draws on, and the station system it belongs to is that institution in its mature nineteenth-century form. It is a tertiary encyclopedia article rather than a survey, and the registration record it summarizes was not read. Nothing read says inns of its kind were usually two stories. And its ground-floor room list mixes the building's historical rooms with its present museum fabric - an exhibition room stands in the same list as the parlor and the kitchen, and the upper floor the citation rests on holds mannequins of two literary travelers at dinner.

Used for: that a two-story highway inn is attested in Japan, with its upper floor as guest rooms - recorded beside the single-story wagon inn the map follows, as the open question of which institution is the right analogue, and never as a warrant for the drawn form

neixiang-xianya-zhwiki

内乡县衙 (the Neixiang County yamen), Chinese Wikipedia (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%86%85%E4%B9%A1%E5%8E%BF%E8%A1%99)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the county yamen at Neixiang in Henan, the only complete Qing-dynasty county government office still standing, describing its layout and the regulation and ritual conception that layout follows.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the fallback orientation of our magistrate's manor as a rule rather than a preference - the seat sits to the north and faces south, by the regulation for a local government office and by ritual propriety - and the terms behind it mean proper rather than lucky, so the orientation is the formal one and not an auspicious one. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia article; that it describes one surviving building of one dynasty; and that it is Chinese office regulation standing in for a setting drawn from pre-Meiji Japan as well as from imperial China.

Used for: south as the formal orientation of a government compound's gate, by regulation and by ritual propriety, and the paired rules that go with it

kanazawa-jokamachi-study

金沢市 (City of Kanazawa), 城下町金沢学術研究1 第1分冊 日本の城下町と金沢城下町 - 発展過程と空間類型 (https://www4.city.kanazawa.lg.jp/material/files/group/22/kanazawajouka1-1-s.pdf)

What it is: A city-commissioned academic report, the first volume of Kanazawa's castle-town research series, comparing Japanese castle towns and typologizing their space, and tracing how Kanazawa's quarters were arranged around the castle as the city was rebuilt.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states where a government's offices stand - inside the castle, with the ruling house's own mansion, at the apex of a hierarchy the whole samurai quarter is arranged around - which is our rule that offices cluster on the grandest compound rather than floating mid-block. Its limits are that it describes one very large castle town of one of the greatest domains, so a county seat's handful of offices is a much smaller thing; that it is Japanese; and that it works in quarters and hierarchies rather than dimensions, so it sizes nothing on our sheet.

Used for: government offices standing with the ruling house's compound at the center of the plan

imagawa-2010-jokamachi-kaido

今川朱美 and 小田雄司, "城下町の形成と街道網の関係 - 広島を事例として -" (The relation between the formation of a castle town and the highway network, with Hiroshima as the case), 広島工業大学紀要研究編 44 (2010) 41-45 (https://libwww.cc.it-hiroshima.ac.jp/library/pdf/library_research44_10.pdf)

What it is: A university bulletin paper that types castle towns by how their streets meet the highway network, distinguishing the town whose main street runs to the castle's great gate from the town where the two cross, with Hiroshima as its worked case.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the second half of our siting rule in a scholar's words: the principal street is the one that runs from the main gate, the front entrances of townhouse and samurai plots range along it, and rank falls off with distance outward. Its limits are that it is a short bulletin paper about Japanese castle towns of one period with a single case; that it is about street types rather than buildings, so it gives no frontage width and no plot size; and that it says nothing about Chinese practice, where our offices rule also claims to apply.

Used for: offices and residences fronting the avenue that runs from the main gate, with rank falling off outward from it

yannopoulos-2015-water-lifting

Stavros Yannopoulos and others, "Evolution of Water Lifting Devices (Pumps) over the Centuries Worldwide", Water 7(9) (2015) 5031-5060 (https://res.mdpi.com/d_attachment/water/water-07-05031/article_deploy/water-07-05031.pdf)

What it is: A peer-reviewed review article in the open-access journal Water surveying the devices used to lift water from antiquity to the present across the world, with sections on the Chinese shadoof (jiegao) and the Chinese windlass (lulu) and on what became of each.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is what makes a north-China field well a piece of machinery on our maps rather than a hole in the ground, and it dates the windlass's rise to the Ming and Qing with the three changes that made it: animal power in place of human, several containers at once, and deeper wells. Its limits are that it is a review compiled from other people's work rather than fieldwork or excavation; that it gives no well depth in meters, so any figure in meters is ours and is labeled a guess; that it does not say where the operator stood, so our record does not either; and that it is a modern engineering survey using archaeological finds as illustrations of a long practice.

Used for: the jiegao as the Chinese shadoof (upright post, hinged beam, counterweight) and the lulu as a windlass on a wooden stand with wheel, axle, crank and ropes; the Ming and Qing rise of the lulu and its three innovations

endo-2013-kabu-ido

Takahiro Endo, "The Kabu-ido System: Innovations in an Indigenous Groundwater Management Institution", Digital Library of the Commons, Indiana University (2013) (https://dlc.dlib.indiana.edu/dlc/bitstream/handle/10535/8876/ENDO_0894.pdf)

What it is: A commons-studies paper on the kabu-ido, the institution by which the villages inside the Takasu ring levee on the Nobi plain limited how many wells could be sunk, with a dated table of the surveys, agreements and authorized well counts from 1854 onward.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the evidence that the number of wells in a farming community was a governed quantity fixed by the residents themselves - a permit bought with a fee, a survey of the wells standing, a cap negotiated between the upper and the lower villages, and patrolmen the villages provided for each other - with the local government expressly declining to interfere inside the levee. (The permit fee is this paper's; the sibling entry on the same institution records that the 1812 agreement carries no such charge and that the only money runs the other way, so the two accounts differ and the record should not lean on the fee.) It also corrects the reason: the quarrel was not scarcity but its opposite, the drainage the upper villages' artesian wells poured onto the lower villages' paddy. Its limits begin with the era: the institution the paper documents was established around the 1850s and ran to about 1905, so most of its recorded life is Meiji rather than Edo, and it reaches the setting's period only at the very end. Beyond that: it is one institution on one ring levee; that the cap is a total across the whole levee allotted among villages rather than a rule per village in the abstract; that it is Japanese; and that it is a working paper in a repository rather than a journal article, though a companion study of the same institution by the same scholar is registered here separately.

Used for: the kabu-ido cap and how it was administered; the 1854 survey and agreement and the 388 authorized wells of 1861; drainage rather than scarcity as the conflict it settled

abele-2018-kawata

Michael Thomas Abele, Peasants, skinners, and dead cattle: the transformation of rural society in western Japan, 1600-1890, PhD dissertation, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (2018) (https://www.ideals.illinois.edu/items/107042)
