What it is: An archive-based doctoral dissertation on the kawata communities of Kawachi and Izumi - the people who handled dead cattle and the leather trade - and on their place in Tokugawa village society, worked through village cases including Saraike and Oji.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers what the collar around our burakumin quarter is really about: the outcast settlement was a separate residential cluster inside the same village's territory, clearly separated from the peasants' plots, standing on poor ground, and at no fixed distance out - in Saraike the peasants lived nearer to two other villages than to the kawata of their own. Its limits are that it is an unpublished dissertation about two provinces of western Japan; that its village figure is schematic and its own caption says the proportions are wrong; that its span runs to 1890, so a case from its later chapters is Meiji rather than Tokugawa; and that it gives no distance in any unit, so the 60 ft on our maps stays a calibration against the drawn sheets and not a finding. One use goes further than the work does: kawaramono, people of the riverbank, is a NAME, and a name is not evidence that a given settlement stood across a watercourse from its village.

Used for: the outcast cluster inside the village territory with a clear separation and no fixed distance; the poor ground it stood on; kawaramono, "people of the riverbank", as the older name behind the reading that it stood across a stream

plos-transition-zone-drought

"Drought characteristics and their impact on vegetation net primary productivity in the climate-sensitive transition zone", PLOS ONE (2026), doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0343746 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12935246/)

What it is: An open-access remote-sensing study of drought and vegetation productivity in the climate-sensitive transition zone of northern China, whose description of its study area defines the region and states its rainfall.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use one sentence of it: northern China's 400 to 800 mm of annual rain, concentrated in summer showers, which is the rainfall that leaves a dry field there chronically drought-exposed and makes a well worth sinking in the middle of one. Its limits are that this is a modern instrumental climatology of recent decades rather than a historical one; that its region is defined by isotherms and isohyets and takes in both the north-China plain and the loess provinces, so it fits our sentence's own conflation of the two better than it fits either strictly; and that everything else in the paper - the drought indices, the satellite productivity data, the trends - is about the present day and is used for nothing here. The sentence we do take is the paper's own uncited description of where it worked, not a result it measured.

Used for: 400-800 mm of annual rain concentrated in the summer, for a named northern-China region

jsslkx-002-2021

T/JSSLKX 002-2021, 小型農田水利工程規劃設計導則 ("Guideline for the planning and design of small farmland water-conservancy works"), Jiangsu Provincial Water Conservancy Survey and Design Association, draft for comment, 2021 (http://jsszy.org.cn/UserFiles/file/20221103/20221103155002_6437.pdf)

What it is: A provincial design guideline for the small canals and ditches of a farmland irrigation scheme, issued for comment by the Jiangsu Provincial Water Conservancy Survey and Design Association in 2021, and referred by its own clause to the national standard GB 50288. It sets out where each grade of canal is laid, how the field canals relate to the plots and the roads, and the minimum dimensions a built channel must meet.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states as design law the canal doctrine our comb layout rests on, which no readable page carried before: every grade of canal sited on the higher ground within its own command area, mains and branches along the contour lines or the watershed divides, the laterals below them crossing the contours, two or three grades of fixed canal in the field with successive grades at right angles on flat ground, and the watering direction following the field surface's own fall for irrigated dry land as much as for paddy. It also gives the alignment maxim behind our swept bends - let the large bends take the lie of the land and straighten the small ones, which the guideline shows to be design law in Jiangsu today and cannot date any further back than that - and the two figures we use as floors, a 0.3 m minimum canal bottom width stated for the reason we give it, so the thing can be operated and maintained after it is built, and a 1.0 m minimum bank crest on a lateral or farm canal. Its limits are large, and every number taken from it carries them. It is a modern standard, published in 2021, for concrete-lined and machine-worked consolidated farmland, so it is evidence for the geometry and for the reasons its own clauses state, never a measurement of a premodern earthwork; its 200 m block length and its 1/1000 to 1/2000 grades are machinery-era figures we do not carry across; its 1.0 m is the width of the bank CREST, the earth walked on beside the channel, and reads as a channel width only to a careless eye; it fixes no side-slope coefficient and no canal width by grade at all, which is why the widths our record derives from it stay derivations; that nothing read establishes a 0.3 m floor for a HAND-dug field ditch, so that figure may inflate a drawn one rather than bracket it; and it is a draft for comment rather than a ratified national standard. Its own clause 9.1.6 puts its canal designs under GB 50288, the national irrigation and drainage standard this project has not been able to read on any page, which is what makes this guideline the nearest openly readable carrier of those numbers and also the reason an attribution taken through it is second-hand.

Used for: the placement law at every canal grade and at the field tier; mains and branches on the contours or the divides with the laterals crossing them; the orthogonal field grid and the watering direction that follows the fall, for irrigated dry land as well as paddy; the 0.3 m minimum canal bottom width and the reason given for it; the 1.0 m minimum bank crest of a lateral or farm canal, and GB 50288 as what stands behind it; the alignment maxim 大弯就势，小弯取直

conghua-2026-design

2026 年度广州市从化区高标准农田改造提升建设项目初步设计报告（评审稿） (Preliminary design report for the 2026 high-standard farmland improvement and upgrading construction project, Conghua District, Guangzhou; client the Conghua District Bureau of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, designer 中联合创设计有限公司), June 2026 (http://nyncj.gz.gov.cn/attachment/8/8037/8037125/10854794.pdf)

What it is: The review-draft preliminary design report for a district farmland improvement scheme in Guangzhou, published by the district's own agriculture bureau. Among its works schedules and design clauses it gives the built cross-section of each grade of canal in the scheme, in metres, tier by tier.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one openly readable document this project has found that gives canal widths by grade as BUILT rather than as a minimum: the lateral (斗渠) at 1.0 and 1.2 m and the farm canal (农渠) at 0.4 and 0.6 m, which puts a measured figure under the roughly 1 m distribution lateral in our width ladder and brackets our 0.3 m field ditch from above. Its limits begin with the quantity itself: the width of a lined rectangular section's floor is not the width of a hand-dug earthen ditch carrying the same water, which lies back on its side slopes and runs wider and shallower, so the RATIO between two lined widths is not straightforwardly the ratio between two dug ones. It is also a modern works schedule, dated 2026, for rectangular mortared brick and stone sections laid to a 1/2000 grade, so what it can fix is the LADDER'S PROPORTIONS - roughly three to one between successive grades - and never the material, the construction or the true width of a hand-dug premodern channel; it is one district's design report rather than a national standard, so its sections are what one designer specified for one scheme on one terrain; and it does not build the finest grade at all, the 毛渠, which is the tier our 0.3 m field ditch sits on. It cites GB 50288-2018 by number for its own scour and siltation velocities, so like the Jiangsu guideline it is a readable application of a standard we cannot read.

Used for: the built widths of the Chinese canal grades - lateral 1.0 and 1.2 m, farm canal 0.4 and 0.6 m - behind the distribution lateral in the water-width ladder

shanghai-tudi-zhengli

DG/TJ08-2079-2010 (J11790-2010), 土地开发整理工程建设技术标准 ("Standard for land consolidation engineering"), a Shanghai municipal engineering construction standard, printed 2011 and served by the city's housing and urban-rural development commission (https://zjw.sh.gov.cn/shsd/userfiles/255%E5%9C%9F%E5%9C%B0%E5%BC%80%E5%8F%91%E6%95%B4%E7%90%86%E5%B7%A5%E7%A8%8B%E5%BB%BA%E8%AE%BE%E6%8A%80%E6%9C%AF%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86.pdf)

What it is: A municipal technical standard for land development and consolidation works, published by the Shanghai city government's housing and urban-rural development commission. Its irrigation section names the grades of an open-channel canal system and says how each is laid out and sized.

Why it applies, and its limits: It names the five fixed grades of the Chinese irrigation ladder in order - main, branch and lateral as the canal system proper, farm and field as the in-field distribution - and puts the maoqu at the bottom of it, laid out to the size of the individual basin and, usefully for a map of a hamlet, dug by the farmers themselves. That is what tells us where the drawn net honestly stops and what lies below the last channel we can draw. Its limits: a municipal standard of 2010 for consolidated, machine-worked land, so the ladder it names is the one a present-day designer works to rather than a premodern one, and it gives no dimensions we use; and its PDF's embedded font inserts spaces between characters and a filler glyph at some clause starts, so a machine reading it and a person reading it see different strings.

Used for: the five fixed canal grades named in order, and the maoqu as the lowest of them - sized to the individual basin and dug by the farmer

ignou-silt-control

Indira Gandhi National Open University, "Unit 10: Silt Control", Irrigation Engineering course unit, eGyanKosh (https://www.egyankosh.ac.in/bitstream/123456789/32984/1/Unit-10.pdf)

What it is: A unit of the Irrigation Engineering course of India's national open university, on silt control at a canal headworks: how sediment travels in the lower layers of a flow, how a regulator is oriented against the parent flow and what that orientation does to the sediment the canal takes in, where an intake belongs on a bend, and the raised sill and skimmer wall at a mouth.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the offtake angle our drawn junctions follow, and states it as a reason rather than a convention: a canal taken off at 90 degrees to the main flow is the most objectionable orientation of the regulator there is, and a diversion angle of 30 to 45 degrees against the river's flow is what is normally recommended, because that produces a suitable curvature of the flow lines through the regulator. Its limits: it is a modern teaching text for engineered headworks with mechanical gates rather than an account of how a premodern village tapped a stream, so what transfers is the hydraulic reason and not the works; its angles are for a canal leaving a RIVER, and the same unit prescribes 60 to 80 degrees for a distributary leaving a parent canal, so a drawn junction has to say which of the two it is; it carries no lower bound below 30 degrees, so none is attributed to it; that the raised sill with a skimmer wall it also describes is a twentieth-century silt-excluder assembly at a gated barrage, with no premodern earthen counterpart, so it explains why silt enters a mouth low and clean water high and is not a feature this record draws; and both its access and its text are imperfect - a certificate warning in front of it, and an OCR layer that damages the very degree signs the finding turns on.

Used for: the offtake taken off at an acute angle pointing downstream - 90 degrees named the most objectionable orientation, 30 to 45 degrees the normal recommendation for a canal leaving a river, 60 to 80 for a distributary leaving a canal

canal-enwiki

English Wikipedia, "Canal" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canal)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on canals - how they are cut, why they have to be level, and the works that carry them between reaches at different heights.

Why it applies, and its limits: We use it for one physical fact that decides how a navigation cut is drawn and labeled on our maps: a canal needs to be level, small irregularities in the ground being taken up by cuttings and embankments, and where a canal meets a river or the sea at a different level the device that connects the two is a gated chamber, the pound lock - whose double-gated form the article dates to tenth-century China, which puts it in period for this setting rather than making it an anachronism. Its limits are those of any tertiary work: it is a general encyclopedia article, not a study of premodern East Asian navigation, and its center of gravity is the British canal age. Two things it is asked for go beyond plain physics and should be treated as unchecked: the tenth-century date is a historical claim resting on the article alone, and "a canal must be level" is true of a NAVIGATION cut and false of an irrigation canal, which runs at a designed fall - nothing here transfers to the comb net.

Used for: a canal being cut level and held at the level of the water it joins; the pound lock as the gated chamber that connects a canal to a river or the sea, and its tenth-century Chinese date

rwsshp-hand-dug-well

RWSSHP Resource Manual 3a, Hand Dug Well Construction Manual, Ethiopia Rural Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene Programme, 2007 (https://www.fhdesigns.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2023/01/Manual-3a-HDW-Construction.pdf)

What it is: A field manual for building a hand-dug, hand-lined, bucket-drawn village well, written for the Ethiopian government's rural water supply and sanitation program. It works through siting, digging, lining and finishing, and tabulates a traditional well against an improved one row by row.

Why it applies, and its limits: It writes down the siting rule that no premodern source bothers to write down, because a contractor has to be told it: such a well is not located in swampy or flood-prone ground, and the whole detailing of its head - a raised headwall, the top three metres of the shaft sealed, an apron, a drain, a diversion ditch to turn surface water away - exists to keep surface water out of the shaft. A well standing in a reed bed fails both at once, which is our rule reached from the other end. Its limits: the rule it writes down is a modern SANITARY norm, adopted here as a standard the map follows rather than as a finding about where premodern wells stood - this record's own harie-kabata entry describes a village whose water rises inside the houses. It is a modern rural water-supply document from Ethiopia, not an East Asian historical source, so what carries is the physical relation between a shaft, a water table and the ground around it rather than any detail of construction; its improved well is a concrete-ringed one; and the reason it gives is sanitary, keeping pathogens out of the water, where our record's reason is practical - that the rim and the windlass need somewhere dry to stand is implied by the raised headwall and the apron rather than stated anywhere, and our record says so.

Used for: a hand-dug well not sited in swampy or flood-prone ground; the raised headwall, sealed upper shaft, apron, drain and diversion ditch that keep surface water out of it

wateraid-hand-dug-wells

WaterAid, Hand-dug wells, technical brief, January 2013 (https://www.wateraid.org/us/sites/g/files/jkxoof291/files/technical-brief-hand-dug-wells.pdf)

What it is: A short technical brief from the international water and sanitation charity WaterAid on how a hand-dug well is sited, sunk, lined and finished.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the same rule the Ethiopian manual gives, in a document of the same modern water-and-sanitation sector: an apron or concrete slab and a drain to prevent water ponding at the well, and the top three metres of the lining grouted to make a sanitary seal. The two agreeing is weaker evidence than it looks: the Ethiopian manual says in its own introduction that the series draws on the programmes of Ghana, Malawi and Tanzania, so these are one lineage written to one sanitary standard rather than two independent observations, and what they agree on is present-day doctrine rather than a property of the artifact across centuries. Its limits are the same: a modern NGO document rather than a historical source, written for concrete-ringed construction, and its stated purpose is sanitary protection rather than the practical standing our record wants - it never says the lifting gear needs dry ground, and our record marks that step as its own.

Used for: the apron and drain that stop water ponding at a hand-dug well, and the sanitary seal over its upper shaft

cao-2019-abandoned-paddy

Cao, Zhu and Okuro, "Vegetation dynamics of abandoned paddy fields and surrounding wetlands in the lower Tumen River Basin, Northeast China", PeerJ (2019), open access under CC-BY (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6459177/)

What it is: An open-access ecology paper following a chronosequence of abandoned paddy fields in northeast China - under five years, five to fifteen, and over fifteen - and comparing what grows on them against a natural wetland reference nearby.

Why it applies, and its limits: It measures directly what our marsh rule assumes. On a temperate lowland plain, agricultural development converted most of the marshland into paddy fields; and a paddy let go returns by natural secondary succession to a wetland herb community, through annual weeds first and then to tussock-forming sedge, so that abandoned paddies are named as good ground for restoring wetland species. That is both halves of the sentence our record needed - paddy made out of marsh, and marsh made back out of paddy. Its limits, which the footnote states: this is a modern ecology paper about the plant process, not a historical source about the period, so it establishes what the ground does over a decade or two when it is let go and nothing whatever about how often a premodern farmer let one go or what the result looked like to him. The conversion it reports runs the same way: the marshland of that basin was turned into paddy by twentieth-century settlement and state reclamation, so the paper attests that paddy is MADE out of marsh as a physical fact and not that premodern paddy was won from it. And and it is one river basin in the far northeast, colder than the country our maps depict, so the species list is local even where the process is general.

Used for: marshland converted to paddy on a temperate East Asian lowland plain; abandoned paddy reverting to a wetland plant community by natural succession

king-forty-centuries

F. H. King, Farmers of Forty Centuries; Or, Permanent Agriculture in China, Korea and Japan (1911), Project Gutenberg ebook 5350 (https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/5350/pg5350-images.html)

What it is: The American soil scientist F. H. King's account of what he saw farming in China, Korea and Japan on a journey made in 1909, published in 1911 - field sizes, holdings, manuring, and the movement of night soil out of the cities, described at first hand and long out of copyright.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states plainly for Japan the two things our tract-size entry needed and could not get from Buck, whose own survey is in a lending-restricted scan on no page a reader can open: that the lands worked by one family are seldom contiguous, may be widely scattered and are very often rented - with the consolidation laws in force since 1900 named as what was passed to undo it, which is the strongest form the statement can take - and that the average worked by one family is nearer 2.5 acres, which sits beside our roughly 1 cho figure as an independent reading. Its limits: it is a traveler's eyewitness account rather than a survey, so its averages are ones he was told or read rather than ones he measured; it describes 1909, at the very end of the order our maps depict and after Meiji land reform had begun, so a figure from it is the last state of that world and not its typical one; and the book's admiration for what it describes is well known and shapes what it chose to record.

Used for: a Japanese family's lands seldom contiguous, often widely scattered and often rented, and the consolidation laws in force from 1900; the average worked by one family nearer 2.5 acres; and, at the city tier, the night soil carried out of a city to its gardens by the cartload and the liquid manure diluted before it is fed to the plants

skinner-2002-etudes-rurales

G. William Skinner, "Marketing and social structure in rural China", Etudes rurales 161-162 (2002), open access on OpenEdition Journals (https://journals.openedition.org/etudesrurales/7952)

What it is: The open-access publication, in a French rural-studies journal, of the analysis G. William Skinner first set out in the Journal of Asian Studies in 1964: the standard marketing community, a market town with the ring of villages that trade at it, and the spacing that pattern produces across a countryside.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source of the figure our town entries rest on, in the author's own words on a page a reader can open: in the modal case a marketing area is just over 50 square kilometers, market towns are less than eight kilometers apart, the longest walk in to the town is about 4.5 km, and the typical community is some 1,500 households in eighteen or so villages. That is what makes a market town the center of a farmed hinterland a person walks out into, and at the corrected area the argument our maps make holds better rather than worse, since fifty square kilometers is a morning's walk across. Its limits: it describes late imperial and Republican-era China, so it is the closer of the two reference cultures and not the other; the figures are a MODAL case from a model in which the area varies with population density, so they are the shape of a settlement pattern rather than a measurement of any one county, and the table they come from should be read before any other cell of it is quoted; and the analysis is a mid-twentieth-century social-science model, influential and much argued with, rather than a primary record.

Used for: the standard marketing community - about eighteen villages over just over fifty square kilometers, market towns under eight kilometers apart, the longest walk in about 4.5 km. This supersedes the ~300-500 km2 the record carried under skinner-marketing

jsidre-senmaida

"The Shiroyone Senmaida, the terraced paddies that represent the Noto satoyama and satoumi agricultural heritage site" (title translated from the Japanese by this project; original: 「世界農業遺産「能登の里山里海」を代表する棚田「白米の千枚田」」), 水土の知 (Journal of the Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering) 90(1) (https://www.jsidre.or.jp/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2022/02/90-1-18.pdf)

What it is: A two-page cover-photograph column by Hotta Taku of Ishikawa Prefecture's agricultural infrastructure division, in the journal of the Japanese Society of Irrigation, Drainage and Rural Engineering, on the Shiroyone Senmaida - the terraced paddies on the Noto peninsula that represent the Noto satoyama and satoumi agricultural heritage site.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the Senmaida figures our smallest-paddy finding rests on - about 18 square metres per basin, and 1,004 terraced paddies spread over about 4 hectares in all - and it states the reason for them, that no large machine can enter the terrace so the rice is still grown by hand with hoe and sickle. Its limits are the terrace's and the column's. Shiroyone is an extreme case, its basins made tiny by a steep slope worked entirely by hand, so it gives a floor and never a typical size. The figures carry no survey behind them - they are the official numbers the preservation council also publishes, restated in a journal, so the container is not better provenance than the source. And the terrace it describes is not an ancient one: the column dates the present layout to the first half of the Meiji period, the ground having been abandoned after a landslide in 1684 and an earthquake in 1729.

Used for: the Shiroyone Senmaida figures - about 18 m2 per paddy, 1,004 paddies over about 4 ha - from an engineering journal rather than a tourism page

satoyama-levee-grassland

"Earthworm species and density in semi-natural grasslands on rice paddy levees in Japanese satoyama", open access through PubMed Central (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7538448/)

What it is: Kishimoto-Yamada and Minamiya, in the Biodiversity Data Journal (2020): a peer-reviewed open-access study of the earthworms living in the semi-natural grasslands that grow on rice-paddy levees, sampled in five areas of Sado Island, Niigata, which describes along the way how those levee grasslands are kept.

Why it applies, and its limits: Its whole frame is the thing our bund entry needed a source for and had none: a paddy levee carries a GRASSLAND, one that farmers maintain by periodic mowing or herbicide, and in the paddies it studied by mowing two to five times a year with no herbicide at all - which is the measure of how hard the grass grows and therefore of how completely a bund greens over in the season our maps depict. Its limits: it is a modern ecological survey of present-day Japanese paddies, so the mowing regime is today's - though not all of it is post-consolidation ground, since two of its five areas had never been through farmland consolidation, which makes the sward it describes a closer analogue than a blanket disclaimer would allow; its subject is the soil fauna rather than the vegetation, so the grass is described only as the habitat; and it says nothing at all about how a green bund READS against a green field, which is the visual step our record takes in its own voice and labels as its own.

Used for: the paddy levee as a semi-natural grassland, mown two to five times a year to keep it down

obata-1977-taue

小畑晃男, "Studies on the Traditional Transplanting Methods of Rice in Wakayama Prefecture" (the journal's own English title; original: 「和歌山県における慣行田植法の地域性とその成立要因に関する研究」), 農作業研究 (Farm Work Research) 29: 24-29 (1977) (https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/jsfwr1966/1977/29/1977_29_24/_pdf/-char/en)

What it is: A study of customary rice-transplanting practice across Wakayama prefecture, reporting part of a nationwide survey of such practice carried out in 1975-76. It divides the prefecture into zones and sets out, for each, when transplanting happened, how long it took, and who did the work together.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the Japanese record's own instrument for the question our uniform paddy green rests on, and it answers it in two parts that do not sit in the same place. In the mountain zones, communal transplanting was organized at the hamlet unit of twenty to thirty households and in some places the entire work schedule for the year's transplanting was settled in advance by consultation - but there valley water could be drawn at any hour and the transplanting period ran past twenty days. In the plains, the window is seven to ten days, short enough for a district's basins to stand at one growth stage, and the paper attributes that concentration to the preceding crop's calendar while noting that communal work there is comparatively little. It also cuts against the mechanism our record had assumed, describing yui as helping one another by making use of the DIFFERENCE in transplanting dates. Its limits: one prefecture, and a mountainous one whose plains are small, so the plains zone here is a modest example of its kind; the survey was made in 1975-76 and records practice remembered as customary rather than practice observed in a premodern century; and the scan's text layer is unreliable, so its passages are quoted from the page image.

Used for: a village transplanting on one agreed schedule settled in advance, at the hamlet unit of 20 to 30 households; the seven to ten day window where the preceding crop makes it tight, and the twenty-day-plus window where water is free; yui as working because transplanting dates differ

fao-drainage-systems

FAO, "Drainage systems", chapter 3 of Drainage of irrigated lands (Irrigation Water Management training manual) (https://www.fao.org/4/ai587e/ai587e01.pdf)

What it is: The chapter of an FAO training manual that lays out the kinds of drainage system a field can be given - bedding, parallel grid, herringbone - and how the drains in each relate to one another and to the watercourse they empty into.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the drainage geometry our cross-slope collector is drawn to, and states it as ordinary practice rather than as a special case: the field drains run in the direction of the greatest land slope, the collector is constructed at the LOWER end of the field and takes them at right angles, it is laid along the lesser slope - across the fall - and the main drain it feeds is often a canalized stream running through the lowest parts of the agricultural area. Its limits: it is a modern extension manual for machine-cut drainage rather than a premodern source, though the layout it states follows from where water runs downhill and holds for a hand-dug ditch exactly as for a cut one, and nothing in the passages we take depends on machinery; and it never states the angle at which the collector meets the stream, nor uses the phrase valley stream at all, so that junction angle remains this record's own inference and is labeled as one.

Used for: the field drains running down the fall into a collector at the low end of the field, meeting it at right angles; the collector laid along the lesser slope; the main drain as a canalized stream in the lowest ground

fao-aina-ridging

P. O. Aina (Department of Soil Science, Obafemi Awolowo University), "Rainfall runoff management techniques for erosion control and soil moisture conservation", FAO (https://www.fao.org/4/t1696e/t1696e02.htm)

What it is: An FAO chapter surveying the techniques a small farmer has for holding rain where it falls and keeping soil from washing off - ridge and mound tillage, tied ridges, terraces, contour bunds, contour hedges, straw barriers and grass buffer strips - and saying which suits what ground.

Why it applies, and its limits: It settles which ground contour ridging belongs to, and it settles it against the reasoning this record had been carrying: ridge-and-furrow aligned parallel to the contour has the dual purpose of erosion control and surface drainage, and its advantages are GREATER the less steep the terrain and the more permeable the soil, while for a smallholder with only hand implements or animal traction it is named the satisfactory method. The measures the same chapter assigns to steep cultivated land are a different family - terraces, contour bunds, contour hedges, straw barriers and grass buffer strips. So contour alignment is a supportable option on the gentle ground our maps draw, and varying the furrow direction between plots is a drawing choice for legibility rather than a correction of a misapplied rule. Its limits: it is a modern conservation-agronomy text, written largely from African smallholder practice, and it addresses conservation PERFORMANCE - what works - rather than what Chinese or Japanese farmers actually did, so it tells us contour ridging is supportable on gentle ground and never that it was universal there.

Used for: contour-aligned ridge and furrow as an erosion-control and surface-drainage measure whose advantage is greater on less steep ground, and the satisfactory method for a hand-and-animal smallholder; terraces, bunds, hedges and grass strips as what steep cultivated land takes instead

contemporary-chinese-culture-daoism

Encyclopedia of Contemporary Chinese Culture (Routledge), "Daoism", republished on en-academic (https://contemporary_chinese_culture.en-academic.com/174/Daoism)

What it is: The "Daoism" entry of the Routledge Encyclopedia of Contemporary Chinese Culture, republished on the en-academic reference mirror, on how Daoist clergy of the Zhengyi and Quanzhen traditions live, train and serve.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the residence half of this project's householder clergy in the source's own words: a Zhengyi priest does not usually live in a temple though he is normally affiliated with one, and such priests are members of families of hereditary priests serving local communities. That is what puts temple families in ordinary houses around a precinct on these maps rather than in cells inside it. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia entry read on a mirror rather than in the publisher's own edition, and that, like the Patheos article beside it, it describes China and Taiwan today rather than any premodern century - which bites harder here than a date usually does, because the contemporary Zhengyi clergy's non-residence was shaped by the twentieth century, temples confiscated and the tradition rebuilt from the 1980s around household ritual specialists. The historical form of the claim would want a historian of the Chinese clergy, which this record has not reached.

Used for: the Zhengyi priest who does not live in the temple he serves, and the hereditary priestly family

meiji-jingu-access

Meiji Jingu, official access page (https://www.meijijingu.or.jp/access/)

What it is: The access page of Meiji Jingu's own site, giving the shrine's entrances, the approaches that lead in from them and how long the walk from each takes.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives a walking measure of a ranked-torii approach: the shrine buildings stand at roughly the center of the precinct, and it takes about ten minutes on foot from each entrance to the main hall. That is the span the first, second and third torii cover, and it is why a ranked pair of gates is off the edge of every settlement sheet this project draws. Its limits are that it is a visitor page giving a walking time rather than a distance, so any figure in meters beside it is this project's own arithmetic, and that Meiji Jingu was founded in 1920, so its precinct is a modern great-shrine layout rather than a premodern one, and an exceptionally large one at that - a forest planted for a national memorial - so ten minutes is a ceiling rather than a typical span. For a premodern approach measured in meters the record has Nagao Shrine, registered beside it.

Used for: the ~10-minute walk from each entrance to the main hall, which the three ranked torii span

nara-nagao-jinja

Nara Prefecture, cultural resources database, 長尾神社 (Nagao Shrine, Katsuragi) (https://www.pref.nara.lg.jp/ikasu-nara/bunkashigen/main00275.html)

What it is: The Nara prefectural government's cultural-resources page for Nagao Shrine in Katsuragi, an Engishiki-listed shrine, describing its approach and the horseback archery once performed along it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It measures the gap between two ranked gates and the way between them: from the first torii to the second at the precinct entrance is about 300 meters, and the approach is a little over 7 meters (4 ken) wide, on an approach whose horseback archery the page dates to the Kamakura period. Its limits are that it is a prefectural heritage page citing no survey; that one shrine is one instance rather than a distribution; and that what the page dates to the Kamakura period is the PRACTICE and the place name - the 300 m and the 7 m describe the approach as it now stands, and nothing on the page says either is unchanged.

Used for: about 300 m between Nagao Shrine's first and second torii, on an approach a little over 7 m (4 ken) wide. This supersedes the 200 m the record carried for the same pair

lin-2001-miaohui

林榮澤, "The temple fair and Chinese folk society: the Qing cases of north, northeast and northwest China" (title translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「廟會」與中國的民間社會 - 以清代的華北、東北、西北為例), 史耘 7 (July 2001), open PDF on the National Taiwan Normal University history department's site (https://www.his.ntnu.edu.tw/publish03/downloadfile.php?periodicalsPage=2&issue_id=39&paper_id=249)

What it is: A study of the Qing temple fair in north, northeast and northwest China, published in the history department's own journal at National Taiwan Normal University rather than in a major refereed venue, quoting county gazetteers and earlier accounts of the fairs at length.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the evidence for what stood on a temple's own ground: the fair was the countryside's one great trading and pleasure ground, with physicians, diviners, astrologers and physiognomists putting up sheds beside the storytellers and conjurors, and the traders who followed the fairs rented the temple's buildings and plots of ground between one fair and the next. That is the forecourt market and the diviners our town and city gates carry. Its limits are that its region is north China rather than the Jiangnan-and-Japan blend this setting draws on; that the fairs it quotes are at village temples as often as at great urban ones, so a permanent shopfront at a famous gate is not what it shows; that the renting sentence is footnoted to a Republican-era social survey while the fairs themselves are Qing; and that its scan's OCR is unreliable, so its quotations are read from the page image.

Used for: the periodic market held on a temple's own ground and the temple renting the stall space; diviners and the other fortune-telling trades at a temple fair

kejia-taiwan-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 客家裔臺灣人 (Hakka Taiwanese), the section on deities (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%AE%A2%E5%AE%B6%E8%A3%94%E8%87%BA%E7%81%A3%E4%BA%BA)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on Hakka Taiwanese, whose section on deities covers the tutelary Minzhu Gongwang and the temples that enshrine him.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states where a village's tutelary hall stands: usually built at the village's water mouth, the shuikou, with a named surviving instance built in 1760 on the bank of a stream in what is now Sanzhi, New Taipei. That is the geometry our village shrine follows, dated and on a watercourse rather than asserted in the abstract. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia, and that its "usually built at the water mouth" is the encyclopedia asserting a custom rather than a survey of where such halls stand, so the record holds one dated instance and a generalization; that the deity so sited is a Hakka tutelary of Tingzhou and Zhangzhou origin rather than the earth god this record's own prose names; and that its instances are Taiwanese Hakka settlements, one regional tradition rather than a general Chinese rule.

Used for: the village tutelary's hall built at the shuikou, with a named 1760 instance on a stream bank

weilongwu-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 围龙屋 (weilongwu, the Hakka hall-and-wing house), the section on the drying floor, fengshui pond, well and grove (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9B%B4%E9%BE%99%E5%B1%8B)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the weilongwu, the Hakka walled house built around an ancestral hall, with a section on the open ground, pond, well and grove that stand in front of it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the open ground before a hall as a named and proportioned feature whose first stated use is drying grain and other crops, with the gatherings of the new year, the festivals, weddings and funerals second, and its width carefully matched to the height of the main hall; and it gives the half-moon pond before it holding water against drought, raising fish, watering the fields, tempering the air and standing ready against fire. It also states that the arrangement is the rule for the hall-fronted forms rather than one instance. Its limits are that it is a tertiary article whose dating and normative statements carry no individual references; that it describes one regional house type with its ancestral hall on the axis, not a free-standing village shrine; that the width matched to the hall's height is the TYPE's prescriptive norm rather than a measured range, so it is a proportion to draw to and not a figure to check against; and that it gives no market and no opera on that ground.

Used for: grain drying and festival use on the ground before a hall; the fengshui pond's stated purposes; the drying floor's width matched to the hall's height

sumida-miyakodori-33-2

墨田区 (Sumida City, Tokyo), 『みやこどり』 no. 33-2, the ward's buried-cultural-property bulletin, on the graves of Honjo (https://www.city.sumida.lg.jp/kosodate_kyouiku/tiiki_kyouiku_shien/bunkazai_hogo/maizoubunkazai/index.files/miyakodori-33-2.pdf)

What it is: A numbered issue of the buried-cultural-property bulletin published by Sumida ward in Tokyo, reporting the excavated graves of the Honjo district and beginning with the 1985 dig at the Fugenji site, a branch temple of Sensoji that moved away after the Great Tokyo Earthquake.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the only measured grave DENSITY this record has: a trench of just 40 m2 held the traces of ten graves, one box coffin and nine barrel coffins, and the bulletin draws the conclusion itself, that a great many graves were made within one narrow burial ground. That is about 4 m2 a grave, which is the check on how tightly a burial ground packs - but a cumulative one: the ten graves were laid into that ground over the temple's whole period of use, in a district the same bulletin describes as layered, coffins stacked several deep, over two hundred years. So the figure is a FLOOR on the ground a graveyard needs and not its packing at any one moment. Its limits are that 40 m2 is the excavation trench and not the graveyard, so the density is local rather than whole-ground; that the graves are coffined body burials rather than the cremated urn plots these maps draw, so the figure corroborates the Chinese full-body side rather than the Japanese urn band; and that a ward bulletin reports one site rather than a distribution.

Used for: ten graves in a 40 m2 trench at an Edo commoner temple graveyard - about 4 m2, some 43 sq ft, a grave

danka-terauke-encyclopedia

Duncan Ryūken Williams, "Parish (Danka, Terauke) System in Japan", Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), on encyclopedia.com (https://www.encyclopedia.com/religion/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/parish-danka-terauke-system-japan)

What it is: The Encyclopedia of Buddhism's article on the Tokugawa parish system, signed by a historian of Tokugawa Buddhism and republished on encyclopedia.com: how every household came to be registered with a Buddhist temple, what the temple certified, and what it gave in return.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the parish logic our burial grounds rest on, in three parts: temple membership was not an individual affair but the household's, the household's main benefit was the funerary and continuing memorial services the temple provided for all its members, and the affiliation was certified by the local temple and the village officials. That is why a graveyard on these maps is the hall's own yard rather than a plot held apart from it. Its limits are that it describes a state-mandated anti-Christian registration specific to Tokugawa Japan while this setting reaches the same arrangement by another route, so the mechanism differs even where the outcome matches; and that it is a reference article rather than a study - though a signed one by a specialist in this exact subject, carrying its own bibliography, so it is not the anonymous summary a tertiary label usually means.

Used for: the household as the registered unit of temple affiliation, and the funerals and memorial rites the temple renders it

tokyo-kasoba-history

The Institute for Tokyo Municipal Research (公益財団法人東京市町村自治調査会), 『多摩・島しょ地域における火葬場の需給及び運営に関する調査研究報告書』 ("A study of the supply, demand and operation of crematoria in the Tama and island region"), March 2015, served openly as a PDF (https://www.tama-100.or.jp/cmsfiles/contents/0000000/470/all.pdf)

What it is: A planning study of where the Tama municipalities should build crematoria next, whose second chapter traces the law governing a cremation ground from the 1870s onward and whose case studies record the site areas of individual facilities.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries the two things about a crematory that no premodern Japanese source states plainly, and both come with the same discount: they belong to a licensed modern facility rather than an open pyre. First a stated set-back rule: the model standard issued with the burial and graveyard regulations of 1884 put a cremation ground at least 120 ken, about 216 m, from dwellings and from places where people congregate, on ground that is not upwind, walled, with a chimney and a device against the foul smoke. Second the extents: recorded sites run from 10 tsubo 5 go (34.65 m2) at a village ground to 600 tsubo (1,980 m2) at a large urban one, which is the band our drawn cores sit in - though those are Taisho and Showa plants with buildings, furnaces and access inside the figure, a different KIND of place rather than a larger or smaller version of ours, and the 1884 rule is a sanitary regulation written for a walled ground with a chimney and a smoke device. It also records the premodern instance of the same hazard, the removal in Kanbun 7 (1667) of some twenty-odd temple cremation grounds in Asakusa and Shitaya after their smoke reached the shogun on his way to visit a grave. Its limits are that the rule is Meiji 17 and measures from dwellings and crowded ground rather than from a highway, and that the measured sites are Meiji through Showa municipal facilities offered as a scale anchor for a premodern setting rather than as premodern evidence; the 1667 removal is the one premodern datum among them.

Used for: the 1884 set-back of 120 ken from dwellings and from crowded ground; recorded cremation-ground site areas from 10.5 to 600 tsubo; the 1667 concentration of the temple cremation grounds; the open-air pyre as a stone-built bed with no superstructure

kyototuu-mimizuka

京都通百科事典, 耳塚 (the Mimizuka, Kyoto) (https://www.kyototuu.jp/Sightseeing/HistorySpotMimizuka.html)

What it is: The entry on the Mimizuka, the ear mound raised in Kyoto over the trophies of the Korean campaigns, in Kyoto-tsu Hyakka Jiten, a regional encyclopedia site about the city.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the mound's base beside its height - about 49 m (30 ken) across, 7.2 m (4 ken) high, under a five-ring stone pagoda about 9 m tall - and that base is the anchor for how wide a monumental bone mound is drawn, which nothing else read supplies. Its limits are that it is a regional encyclopedia site rather than a primary record or a scholarly work and names no source for its figures; that the mound is a monumental war memorial rather than an ordinary funerary feature, so it bounds the top of the range and not the middle of it; that the figures are of the mound as it now stands, after later repair and its stone fence; and that the national historic-site designation file, which would carry surveyed dimensions, could not be opened.

Used for: the ear mound's 30 ken (about 49 m) width across, its 4 ken height and its 5 ken stone pagoda

feng-yizhong-jiangnan

冯贤亮, "Graves and charity graveyards: popular life and environmental protection in Ming-Qing Jiangnan" (title translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「坟茔义冢：明清江南的民众生活与环境保护」), 华东师范大学历史系, open PDF (https://www.sinoss.net/uploadfile/2010/1130/6012.pdf)

What it is: A scholarly paper by a historian at East China Normal University on graves and charity graveyards in Jiangnan under the Ming and Qing, quoting county gazetteers on individual endowments and tabulating the charity grounds of Zhenze county one by one.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the measured Chinese burial ground this record had been reasoning about without one: a Kangxi 9 endowment of 4 mu of field took 573 coffins, about 4.7 m2 and some 50 sq ft for a full-body grave - ground bought after Lake Tai burst its banks and the floating dead ran into the tens of thousands, so that figure is a mass burial's packing and a hard floor under the charity band, and individual charity graveyards are recorded from 3 fen to 10 mu apiece with county totals beside them. That turns the four-to-six-times multiple for Chinese full-body burial from arithmetic into a measurement. Its limits are that these are charity grounds for the unclaimed and the drowned, packed more tightly than a family grave sited by fengshui would be; that they are Jiangnan, where the paper itself says land pressure was acute; and that the mu is taken at the standard 666.7 m2, which the gazetteers do not state.

Used for: 4 mu holding 573 coffins, about 50 sq ft a full-body grave; charity graveyards ranging from 3 fen to 10 mu

dosojin-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 道祖神 (dosojin, the deity of the way) (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%81%93%E7%A5%96%E7%A5%9E)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the dosojin, the stone deity of roads and boundaries: where it is enshrined, in what form, and what it is there to keep out.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states the rule our wayside shrines are placed by, and states it as an organizing idea rather than a list: the deity is enshrined at spatial and social boundaries - a village's entrance and exit, a mountain pass, a crossroads, the foot of a bridge - standing by the roadside as a stone monument or image to ward off epidemics and evil spirits coming from outside. That is the landing, the crossing and the gate our city shrines mark. Its limits are that it is a tertiary encyclopedia which carries a sourcing-deficiency notice over the very sections the placement sentence sits in; that it is a Japanese folk-religion form rather than a general one; and that it does not put such a shrine at a wellhead, which this record had also claimed. It is a different work from the walking-tour company's English page on the same deity, which the record also cites.

Used for: the wayside deity enshrined at a village's entrance and exit, a pass, a crossroads and the foot of a bridge

kotobank-monzenmachi

Kotobank, 門前町 - several signed Japanese reference works printed side by side (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%96%80%E5%89%8D%E7%94%BA-142614)

What it is: The Kotobank aggregation page for the monzen-machi, the town that grows in front of a great temple or shrine, printing the entries of several signed Japanese reference works one after another.

Why it applies, and its limits: Three independent reference works agree on the form our gate quarters take: a settlement built in a street-village shape along both sides of the pilgrimage road, where merchants and craftsmen raised shops for the worshippers, with inns and shops and craftsmen's shops gathering, and lodging and commerce as the principal livelihood - the frontage following the approach, which is the map-relevant part. The Britannica entry adds the eating-and-drinking establishments as what was added to the festival market once it became permanent. Its limits are that these are tertiary dictionary entries with no sourcing of their own, that they describe Japan, and that none of them puts a sweet-seller at the gate, which is why that trade is cited to the highway teahouses instead.

Used for: the gate town's shops and inns along both sides of the approach, in a street-village form; the eating houses at the gate

kotobank-miyage

Kotobank, 土産 - 改訂新版 世界大百科事典, the entry signed 岩本通弥 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%9C%9F%E7%94%A3-583333)

What it is: The Kotobank page for miyage, the souvenir brought back from a journey, carrying the signed entry from the revised Heibonsha world encyclopedia on how the custom grew, what was sold, and who sold it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates a souvenir trade at a temple gate to the early modern period and names its mechanism: at Kumano and elsewhere the shugenja became half-monk and half-layman and came to sell souvenir goods, and later, as demand expanded, specialist souvenir shops came into being and formed a gate town - the goods being talismans and amulets above all, with lucky dolls, toys, picture books and sacred medicines beside them - the custom spreading from the middle of the early modern period as the highways were made up and commoner pilgrimage spread through the pilgrimage guides and oshi. That is the souvenir row our gate quarters draw, on a dated statement rather than on inference. Its limits are that it is a signed encyclopedia entry rather than a primary source; that it dates the flourishing to mid-Edo, so an earlier gate carries fewer such shops; and that it speaks of Japan, while this setting's temple economy also draws on China.

Used for: specialist souvenir shops at a premodern temple gate, forming the gate town, and the goods they sold

miyagegashi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 土産菓子 (souvenir confectionery) (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9C%9F%E7%94%A3%E8%8F%93%E5%AD%90)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on souvenir confectionery: how the sweets sold to travelers became the named products of the places that sold them.

Why it applies, and its limits: It puts the sweet trade where the record can support it. Once the Edo period came in and traffic on the highways increased, the sweets sold at the teahouses along the way developed in their own directions out of what travelers said of them, and travelers spreading word of those sweets was the greatest occasion for confectionery developing in the provinces. Its limits are that it is a tertiary article; that it places the teahouse on the HIGHWAY rather than at a temple gate, so it supports sweets on the pilgrim road and not a sweet-seller at the gate; and that it is a general statement about the period with no one place or date attached.

Used for: the sweets sold at the highway teahouses, and the traveler's word of mouth that made them regional specialties

xiangyouqian-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 香油錢 (incense-and-lamp-oil money) (https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/%E9%A6%99%E6%B2%B9%E9%8C%A2)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on xiangyouqian, the money given at a temple, explaining the name and the practice that lies behind it.

Why it applies, and its limits: It fixes the direction of a flow this record had backwards: in old times believers donated incense sticks, candles, lamp oil and gold paper to temples and monasteries for use in the offerings, and later gradually gave money in their place, which is why the money itself is named for the two goods. So incense and lamp oil reach a Chinese temple as a DONATION rather than leaving it as stock - the same relation the Japanese omamori already gave us, and the reason no third-party religious-goods shop is drawn at a temple's own gate. Its limits are that it is a tertiary article about a term - a stub of a few hundred characters carrying no references at all, the weakest work this page cites; that the conclusion drawn from it, no third-party shop at the gate, rests on the page's SILENCE rather than on anything it says; that it gives no temple's accounts and no annual figure, so the size of that income is still unsourced; and that it describes the practice generally rather than in a dated period.

Used for: incense, candles, lamp oil and paper donated to a Chinese temple, and money given in their place

shinagawa-kaizoji-muentou

品川区 (Shinagawa City, Tokyo), designated cultural property 海蔵寺無縁塔群 (the group of muen stupas at Kaizoji) (https://www.city.shinagawa.tokyo.jp/PC/sangyo/sangyo-bunkazai/sangyo-bunkazai-shitebunkazai/shina/20240108180212.html)

What it is: A ward's listing for a designated cultural property: the group of stupas for the unconnected dead at Kaizoji in Shinagawa, the temple that took the dead of the Shinagawa holding jail, the victims of the Tenpo famine and those drowned by a tsunami.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries every element of the pauper ossuary our city maps draw, on dated Edo evidence: more than seven hundred prisoners dead of the holding jail between 1691 and 1765, their bones gathered up and reinterred in 1708 under a raised burial mound with a single Kannon image set on top, and stupas for the unconnected dead raised beside it in 1865 and 1873, the later one enshrining 1,268 of them. Its limits are that it is a municipal heritage listing for one temple rather than a survey; that the temple stands in the Shinagawa post town and not outside a wall beside a crematory, so it supports the FORM of the ossuary and not its position; and that it gives no dimension for the mound.

Used for: the pauper ossuary as a mound of gathered bones with one image on top and muen stupas beside it, dated 1708 onward

greatmingmilitary-fortification-gate

Great Ming Military, "Chinese fortification: an overview of parts and terminology - Part 2: Gate and moat" (https://greatmingmilitary.blogspot.com/2019/06/chinese-fortification-p2.html)

What it is: The second part of a specialist blog series on Chinese fortification, on the gate and the moat: the gate tunnel, the barbican and its neck, the wengcheng, and what each of them was for tactically, illustrated from Ming military manuals.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the only readable text found that draws the comparison our gate rule rests on - the European barbican's narrow neck preventing a sortie against the wengcheng as a protected staging ground roomy enough to pass a body of troops either way. It is self-published and not peer-reviewed, so it sits below the scholarly work this record prefers; it is careful and consistent with the manuals it illustrates, but a claim resting on it alone is one specialist's synthesis rather than an attested statement, and it describes China, not Japan.

Used for: the sortie made from the wengcheng rather than through a sally port, and what a barbican's neck prevents

suzhou-panmen-gov

Suzhou Municipal People's Government, Municipal Bureau of Culture, Radio, Television and Tourism, 水陆盘门 (The Water-and-Land Panmen), 2021-10-29 (https://www.suzhou.gov.cn/szwgjyhsj/yhsjjbgk/202110/3ad7341d62c24548bd075701ca6bbeda.shtml)

What it is: A city government page for Panmen, the only Chinese city gate that preserves a land gate and a water gate side by side, describing both and giving measured dimensions: the barbican court between the land gate's two layers, and the water gate's two gate layers, their spacing and its depth.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives real numbers, from the body responsible for the monument, for the two features our city gates draw and had none for - a barbican court and a canal gate - and it settles the barbican's PLAN, which is roughly square rather than urn-shaped. Its limits are that it describes one exceptional surviving gate of a great Jiangnan city rather than a norm, that its figures are of the monument as it stands after restoration, and that it is a public-information page rather than an excavation report.

Used for: the wengcheng's measured court and its roughly square plan; the water gate as a doubled, deep gate rather than a postern

karamete-kotobank

Kotobank, 搦手 - 精選版 日本国語大辞典 and デジタル大辞泉 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%90%A6%E6%89%8B)

What it is: The Kotobank page for karamete, carrying two published Japanese dictionaries: the Shogakukan national-language dictionary, which defines it as a castle's rear gate and the express antonym of the ote or main front and dates its earliest attestation to 1235, and the Digital Daijisen entry for the rear gate itself.

Why it applies, and its limits: A dictionary is the right authority for what a term means, and the meaning is all we take: the rear gate is DEFINED against the main approach, which is what our postern comparison needs for its first term. Its limits are that it defines a word and not a building, so it gives no size, no construction and no use; that it is Japanese, while the wall it is set beside on our maps is Chinese in form; and that it says nothing about the umon, the shuimen or the European sally port, so the comparison drawing the three together remains this project's own.

Used for: the karamete-mon as a castle's rear gate, defined against the ote as its main front

touken-world-umon

刀剣ワールド 城, castle-terms glossary, 埋門 (umon) (https://www.homemate-research-castle.com/useful/glossary/castle/2122201/)

What it is: A castle-terminology glossary entry for the umon, the gate cut through the lower part of a castle's stone wall or moat face: concealed so that an enemy does not read it as an entrance, built plainly and so that it can be filled in easily, kept impassable except when wanted, and intended among other things as the route by which the lord of the castle escapes. It names surviving examples at Takamatsu and Nagoya.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the closest thing the East Asian record offers to a sally port's FUNCTION - a small concealed opening kept shut and opened when needed - which is the term our postern comparison leans on hardest. Its limits are that it is a curated commercial glossary with no citations of its own, tertiary and written for enthusiasts; that it describes Japanese castles rather than a Chinese city wall; and that the better sources for it, a cultural-property survey or the city that holds the famous surviving example, were not reached.

Used for: the umon as a small concealed postern, built to be filled in and used as an escape route

xian-fortifications-enwiki

en.wikipedia Fortifications of Xi'an (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortifications_of_Xi%27an)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Ming walls of Xi'an, covering the circuit, the four corner watch towers and the ditch outside the wall, whose width and depth it gives in meters and feet.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the one measured moat width this record could read for a Chinese provincial-capital enceinte, which is what the drawn figure is checked against. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary whose own citation for the figure was not followed; that Xi'an is among the largest walled circuits ever built, so its ditch is a ceiling and not an average; and that the measurement is of the ditch as it stands today after conservation.

Used for: the measured width and depth of a Chinese provincial-capital moat, against which the drawn 66 ft is judged

zhonghua-gate-enwiki

en.wikipedia Zhonghua Gate, Nanjing (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhonghua_Gate,_Nanjing)

What it is: The English Wikipedia article on the Zhonghua Gate at Nanjing, the largest surviving Chinese city gate, which gives the length, clear width and height of each of the four gate tunnels in line and the distance between them.

Why it applies, and its limits: Four measured clear widths at one Ming gate are exactly what a rule about the opening a road passes through needs, and they are the only such set this record could read. Its limits are that it is tertiary; that this is the grandest gate of a Ming capital rather than a provincial seat's, so it stands at the top of the band and not in the middle of it; and that the figures describe the monument as restored.

Used for: the clear widths of the four tunnels of a great Ming gate, which correct the record's Nanjing figure

jah-song-military-cities

刘炜, 黄茜, 徐腾, "A study of the building of mid-Northern-Song military cities based on the Wujing zongyao" (title translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「基于《武经总要》的北宋中期军事城池营建研究」), 『建筑史学刊』 (Journal of Architectural History) 2026(2): 122-132 (https://www.jgcm.ac.cn/jah/cn/article/pdf/preview/10.12329/20969368.2026.02011.pdf)

What it is: A peer-reviewed architectural-history study of how mid-Northern-Song military cities were built, worked from the Wujing zongyao, the state military compendium of 1044: the wall's form, the spacing of the projecting mamian, the towers set on them, and the arc-shaped corner tower the compendium calls a dituan.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is scholarship reading the period's own manual, and it answers the question our tower rule turns on with the reason attached - the corner tower was curved deliberately, to increase the attacker's difficulty and reduce the surface exposed. Its limits are that it describes Song practice as a compendium prescribed it, three to five centuries before the Ming and Edo anchor these maps take, and that a manual's prescription is not proof that every city built to it; the paper itself notes the form is absent from Han and Tang texts, so it is dated as well as prescriptive.

Used for: the Song corner tower as deliberately arc-shaped and why; the mamian spaced along the curtain

sinoss-cao-city-defense

曹文明, "The defense works of the ancient Chinese city: the form of the rampart and its development" (title translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「中国古代的城防设施：城垣的形制与演变」), 中国社会科学报, on the Ministry of Education's social-science portal (https://www.sinoss.net/c/2010-05-04/526722.shtml)

What it is: A short article by a specialist on the defense works of the ancient Chinese city - the rampart's form and how it developed, the projecting mamian platforms built against the outer face, and the wengcheng thrown around a gate - published in the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences newspaper and carried on the Ministry of Education's social-science portal.

Why it applies, and its limits: It states in one sentence what the wall's projections are FOR - striking a besieger at the wall's foot from two sides - which is the reasoning behind every tower rule these city maps follow. Its limits are that it is a newspaper article rather than a research paper, with no apparatus and no figures, so it is good for the settled point it states and not for any number; and that it speaks of the Chinese city across its whole history rather than of one period.

Used for: the mamian as a platform built against the outer face so that a besieger is struck from two sides

qq-xian-southwest-corner

"Why is the southwest corner of the Xi'an city wall round?", a popular-history piece on the Tencent news portal, 2026 (https://news.qq.com/rain/a/20260206A06Z5M00)

What it is: A popular-history article on why the southwest corner of Xi'an's wall is round, reporting the explanation it says archaeology and history most accept - that the Ming rebuild of 1370 followed the old line of the Tang imperial city and reused a round base platform standing at that corner - and citing the Ming shilu for the date.

Why it applies, and its limits: The record says the century of that inherited corner is disputed, and this is the readable page carrying the side of the dispute the encyclopedia article does not: a Tang origin against a Yuan one. Its limits are severe and are why it is used only for that: it is journalism rather than scholarship, it reports what it says the field accepts without citing a study, and it concerns one corner of one wall.

Used for: the Tang dating of the round southwest corner at Xi'an, against the Yuan dating the encyclopedia gives

qimin-yaoshu-zhongkui

賈思勰 齊民要術 (Jia Sixie, Qimin Yaoshu, c. 540), 卷第三, 種葵第十七 (the chapter on planting mallow), Chinese Wikisource (https://zh.wikisource.org/wiki/%E9%BD%8A%E6%B0%91%E8%A6%81%E8%A1%93/%E5%8D%B7%E7%AC%AC%E4%B8%89)

What it is: Book 3 of the sixth-century Chinese agricultural treatise, in the chapter on planting mallow, which sets out how a garden bed is made and how large it is, with the author's own interlinear notes giving his reasons, and then describes the winter-crop method for a commercial market garden of thirty mu backing onto the wall of a town with a market, with ten wells sunk along its length.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is a primary text that states a dimension AND the reason for it - the bed is kept small because water cannot otherwise be spread evenly over it by hand, and because nobody should have to step into it - which is the rarest and most useful shape of evidence a drawing rule can rest on, and it sizes the very thing this record was asking about, a garden serving a walled town. Its limits are that it is Northern Wei north China, far earlier than the Ming and Edo anchor; that it prescribes good practice rather than reporting what was usual; that the text is read from a crowd-transcribed wiki copy rather than a critical edition, so a disputed character would have to be settled against a scholarly one; and that its measures are in bu and mu, which this record has not converted from a metrology source - and a Northern Wei bu is not a Ming bu, so converting with a later metrology would be positively wrong rather than merely unsupported. Every figure in feet derived from it is our own arithmetic.

Used for: the hand-worked garden bed at two paces by one and the reason for that size; the thirty-mu market garden backing onto a city wall and the layout of its ten wells

madian-mosque-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 马甸清真寺 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%A9%AC%E7%94%B8%E6%B8%85%E7%9C%9F%E5%AF%BA)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Madian mosque in Beijing, whose history section describes the place rather than only the building: the trunk road running north out of Deshengmen, the tribute horse trains that sold their culled animals there, the merchants in horses, cattle, sheep and camels who lodged there, the market that formed of itself, and the later move of the horse market into the guanxiang outside the gate, where at its height there were 48 horse inns.

Why it applies, and its limits: The gate suburb is a shape our city maps draw at every main gate, and this is the only readable page found that describes one as a place with trades and a count rather than defining the word. Its limits are that it is tertiary; that this is the busiest gate of a capital and one trade's premises, so the count is a ceiling for a provincial seat rather than a measurement of one; and that the figure carries no date beyond "at its height".

Used for: what stood in one described gate suburb - a livestock market and the inns that went with it - and the 48 horse inns at its height

zhangjiakou-fort-zhwiki

zh.wikipedia 张家口堡 (https://zh.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%BC%A0%E5%AE%B6%E5%8F%A3%E5%A0%A1)

What it is: The Chinese Wikipedia article on the Zhangjiakou fort, which records that its guanxiang was established in 1480 when the fort was enlarged, because the population inside had grown past what the walled ground could hold, and names the crossroads and streets that formed within the suburb.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the one readable case of a gate suburb that formed for the OPPOSITE reason to the general pattern this record quotes - the walled ground filled first and the overflow went outside - which is worth a reader knowing beside the pattern. Its limits are that it is tertiary, that one case is not a refutation of a general pattern, and that this is a frontier garrison on the Mongolian trade route rather than an ordinary county seat.

Used for: a gate suburb established as overflow in 1480, and streeted

nagayamon-kotobank

Kotobank, 長屋門 - 世界大百科事典, 日本大百科全書 (the entry signed 工藤圭章) and ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%95%B7%E5%B1%8B%E9%96%80)

What it is: The Kotobank page for the nagayamon, the gatehouse with a range of rooms to either side of the doorway, carrying three published encyclopedias: what the gate expressed, how its form was fixed by the house rank of the daimyo or bannerman who held it, which commoners were permitted one, and what the rooms flanking a commoner's version held.

Why it applies, and its limits: Our setting makes a merchant's walled and gated compound a granted right rather than a purchase, and this is the historical arrangement it is modeled on, stated by three independent works in the language of permission and tied to rank and to office. Its limits are that these are tertiary encyclopedia entries; that they describe Tokugawa Japan while the walls on our city maps take their form from the Chinese side of the setting's ancestry; and that they regulate the GATE and say nothing about a compound wall.

Used for: the gate whose form followed its holder's house rank, permitted outside the warrior class to village officials and town elders; the stables and sheds in a commoner gate range

myoji-taito-kotobank

Kotobank, 苗字帯刀 - 日本大百科全書 (the entry signed 北原章男), 改訂新版 世界大百科事典 (signed 水林彪), 百科事典マイペディア and 山川 日本史小辞典 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%8B%97%E5%AD%97%E5%B8%AF%E5%88%80)

What it is: The Kotobank page for myoji-taito, the privilege of a surname and the wearing of swords, carrying four published reference works: who among commoners was granted it and in what forms, that a domain could grant it only within its own territory, that licensing it was a means by which the early modern state reached into the localities, and that from the middle of the period the domains issued it for money.

Why it applies, and its limits: It carries both halves this record needs from one page - the privilege as a lord's grant tied to office and to merit, which is the setting's own arrangement almost word for word, and the later practice that contradicts the setting's rule that money cannot buy it, which is what lets the deviation be stated precisely rather than assumed. Its limits are that these are tertiary summaries; that they describe Tokugawa Japan only; and that none of them says a wall or a gate could be obtained this way, so the departure is recorded for the surname privilege and read across to the compound by us.

Used for: the surname granted to purveyor merchants and town elders, in perpetuity or for one generation, and limited to the domain; the grant as an instrument of rule; the domains issuing it for monetary contributions in the later period

townhouse-jawiki

ja.wikipedia タウンハウス (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E3%82%BF%E3%82%A6%E3%83%B3%E3%83%8F%E3%82%A6%E3%82%B9)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the town house, whose historical section describes the Edo back-lane tenement: ridge-split along the lane, nine shaku by two ken, a four-and-a-half-mat room with a mat and a half of earth floor for the stove and sink, rented by the great majority of the common inhabitants, with the shared well and privy at the lane's end.

Why it applies, and its limits: It names the back-to-back pair our rows are packed in - mune-wari, one roof over two ranks sharing a rear wall - as the standard form rather than as a deduction, and gives the unit its size. Its limits are that it is tertiary; that its subject is Edo, so the dimensions are the standard nine-shaku-two-ken formula rather than a measured survey; and that it describes the rented tenement and not the merchant house in front of it.

Used for: the ridge-split back-lane pair and its unit size, and the shared well and privy at the end of the lane

machiya-shoka-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 町屋 (商家) (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%94%BA%E5%B1%8B_(%E5%95%86%E5%AE%B6))

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the machiya as a merchant house: the shop at the street front, the plot behind it, and the back-lane tenement entered through a wooden gate set between two front shops, with the number of tenement rows following the width of the shop's frontage.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the depth rule from the other end - what a plot's frontage buys is one row along the lane or two facing rows, never a third rank behind them - which is the historical reason our rows stack at most two deep, and it puts the single entrance where the map puts it. Its limits are that it is tertiary; that it describes the Japanese town house of Kyoto and Edo rather than the Chinese courtyard housing the setting also draws on; and that the frontage figures are typical rather than surveyed.

Used for: the one wooden gate between two front shops as the way into the tenements, and one row or two by the frontage

roji-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 路地 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%B7%AF%E5%9C%B0)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the roji, the narrow passage caught between one building and the next: its width between one back-lane tenement and another, that almost nobody but those connected with the adjoining buildings used it, and the widening at the back of the merchant house or the middle of the lane where a shared well or water supply stood.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the measured width our drawn lane is judged against, and the widening at the shared well that the map draws, both for exactly the kind of lane the map is packing. Its limits are that it is tertiary, that the width is a range for Edo back-lane tenements rather than a survey figure, and that the article covers the modern sense of the word alongside the historical one.

Used for: the roji at three to six shaku between tenement buildings, who used it, and the widening at the shared well

song-society-enwiki

en.wikipedia Society of the Song dynasty (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_the_Song_dynasty)

What it is: The English Wikipedia survey of Song society, which records that the curfew was abolished in 1063 and the marketplaces of Kaifeng were then open every hour, against the strict dusk curfew over the two official markets of Tang Chang'an, and that Kaifeng's houses stood along the streets rather than inside walled and gated wards.

Why it applies, and its limits: It dates the institution our record says had lapsed before the period these cities are modeled on, which is what disposes of the dusk-curfew explanation for lodging outside a gate. Its limits are that it is tertiary and that its own footnotes into the Song urban-history literature would be the better citation; and that a single date for a change that came unevenly across a large empire is a simplification.

Used for: the ward curfew as a Tang institution abolished in 1063, well before the period these cities are modeled on

chinanews-ancient-firefighting

China News Service, "Firefighting in the past: the Tang put fires out with the squirt, and the Qing had many popular firefighting organizations" (title translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「古代消防：唐代用溅筒灭火 清代民间消防组织多」), 2015-08-19 (https://www.chinanews.com.cn/m/cul/2015/08-19/7477344.shtml)

What it is: A news-agency cultural feature on firefighting in the Chinese past, which quotes the Ming Wanshu zaji for the ward-and-post organization of the county town of Wanping - a headman responsible for fire and theft, each post with a head and three to five firemen, the night watch with clappers and bells, and the patrol post where the gear was kept - and records the 1743 order of the governor of Hunan that every prefecture and county organize registered volunteer fire companies.

Why it applies, and its limits: It answers whether a place below the capital kept an organized fire watch, which our fire-tower rule turned on, and it does so with a named primary source for the Ming case and a dated edict for the Qing one.
