Its limits are that it is journalism rather than scholarship, that the Ming detail reaches us through the article's paraphrase of the Wanshu zaji rather than from the text itself, and that it establishes a WATCH and not a standing lookout tower.

Used for: the night watch and the patrol post of a Ming county town, and the registered volunteer fire companies ordered in 1743

hinomi-yagura-kotobank

Kotobank, 火の見櫓 - 世界大百科事典 and 日本大百科全書, with the 火の番 passage on the same page (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E7%81%AB%E3%81%AE%E8%A6%8B%E6%AB%93-120594)

What it is: The Kotobank page for the fire-watch tower, carrying two published encyclopedias which agree independently that in Kyoho-era Edo one tower served about every ten machi, with a ladder and a bell on the watch hut in the machi between, and a third passage on the shogunal standing fire watch, its brigade mansions at several places in the castle town, and the watch house set in every machi.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the tower-to-neighborhood ratio our dispersal rule rests on, from two works that state it separately, and it separates what was per-machi (the watch house) from what was not (the tower). Its limits are that these are tertiary summaries; that the ratio is Edo's, the largest wooden city there was, in one era, so a provincial seat two orders of magnitude smaller is being reasoned to rather than described; and that the Japanese arrangement is only half of the setting's ancestry.

Used for: one fire tower to about ten machi with a ladder and bell between, the shogunal brigade mansions, and the watch house in every machi

jishinban-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 自身番 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E8%87%AA%E8%BA%AB%E7%95%AA)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the jishinban, the Edo-period neighborhood watch house: its patrol and reporting duties, the ladder on the roof - which the article itself calls a small-scale fire tower - and the bell beside it, and the arrest and firefighting tools kept inside, down to the standard, the hook, the hand pump, the buckets and the ladders.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the source that puts the bell, the ladder and the gear at the TOWN's watch post, which is where our unwalled-seat fire posture places them and which no page had previously supported. Its limits are that it is tertiary and specific to Edo-period Japanese towns, and that it attaches all of it to the neighborhood watch house and nothing at all to an intendant's office, which is the half of our posture that stays unsupported.

Used for: the roof ladder and bell on the watch house, and the firefighting gear kept inside it

hyoshigi-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 拍子木 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%8B%8D%E5%AD%90%E6%9C%A8)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the hyoshigi, the pair of wooden clappers, including the section on night rounds in which a watch walks calling out to mind your locks and your fire while striking them together.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the night patrol with clappers that our fire posture describes, and the call that goes with it. Its limits are stated where it is used: the bodies the article names for that round are twentieth-century civil-defense and fire corps, so the page carries the practice without dating it to the Edo period, and the Edo dating remains uncited.

Used for: the night round walked with clappers and its fire-watch call

tensuioke-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 天水桶 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%A4%A9%E6%B0%B4%E6%A1%B6)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the tensuioke, the traditional firefighting cistern: a vessel for storing rainwater, used in the Edo period mainly as firefighting water in urban areas.

Why it applies, and its limits: It attests the stored water our fire posture lists, dated to the period and to the town. Its limits are that it is a short tertiary article, Japanese and Edo-specific, giving no count of how many a street kept and no size, so nothing on the map is drawn from it.

Used for: rainwater stored against fire in an Edo town

dozo-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 土蔵 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9C%9F%E8%94%B5)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the dozo, the thick-walled plastered storehouse: the kinds it is divided into by what it holds, the rice store among them, and a section on fire resistance giving wall thicknesses of about 300 mm and more, outer doors faced in earth and plaster, and the record of interiors that survived the great fires.

Why it applies, and its limits: It turns "fireproof kura" from an adjective into something a map can draw and a reader can check, and it names the rice store as one of the kinds such a building was built for, which is the thing our unwalled seat protects first. Its limits are that it is tertiary and Japanese, and that its fire-survival claim is stated generally rather than from a study, so it supports the form and not a survival rate.

Used for: the plastered storehouse as the fire-resistant form, its wall thickness and earth-faced doors, and the rice store among the kinds it held

gogura-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 義倉 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%BE%A9%E5%80%89)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the charitable granary, which carries within it the description of the gogura: an Edo-period store placed one to a village or to several, a temporary holding place for tax rice and other produce on its way out, and kept under strict guard.

Why it applies, and its limits: It identifies the building our fire posture says was protected before anything else, and confirms that the tax rice had a store of its own rather than sitting in a general warehouse. Its limits are that it is tertiary; that it describes the village store rather than one inside an intendant's compound, which is the attachment this record still cannot support; and that it gives no dimension.

Used for: the tax-rice store placed one to a village or to several, and kept under guard

jinya-kotobank

Kotobank, 陣屋 - 世界大百科事典 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E9%99%A3%E5%B1%8B-82659)

What it is: The Kotobank page for the jin'ya, carrying the Heibonsha world encyclopedia on the several kinds of seat the word covers, on the intendant's official residence also being called the daikan-jin'ya, on what stood inside such a compound - the residence, the office for public business, the staff houses, the rice and levy stores, the judgment yard and the gaol - and on the jin'ya-machi that grew around one.

Why it applies, and its limits: It makes the identification our unwalled tax seat rests on a published one rather than this record's own guess, and it names the rice store inside the compound, which is the thing the fire posture says was fireproofed. Its limits are that it is a tertiary summary and that it describes Tokugawa Japan only, so the Chinese county seat our maps also draw on is not covered by it.

Used for: the daikansho as the daikan-jin'ya, what its grounds held, and the jin'ya-machi that grew around one

tokaido-qa-mlit

Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism, Kanto Regional Development Bureau, Yokohama National Highway Office, Tokaido Q&A 17, "What is the relay of men and horses?" (title translated from the Japanese by this project; original: 「人馬の「継ぎ送り」とはどういうことですか？」) (https://www.ktr.mlit.go.jp/yokohama/tokaido/02_tokaido/04_qa/index2/a0217.htm)

What it is: A question-and-answer page in the national highway office's public guide to the Tokaido, on the obligation each post station carried to keep porters and horses permanently on hand: 36 horses at first, and from 1638 a hundred post horses and a hundred porters.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the documented order of magnitude for the draft animals a settlement on a trunk road had to hold standing, which is what our gate caravan cluster is sized against, from the ministry that maintains the road. Its limits are that it is a government public-information page rather than a study; that it states an OBLIGATION on a station and not the animals of any one arriving train; and that it is the Japanese post system rather than a Chinese wagon route, which is the other half of the setting's ancestry.

Used for: the standing requirement of a Tokaido post station, 36 horses rising to a hundred horses and a hundred porters from 1638

sukego-kotobank

Kotobank, 助郷 - 日本大百科全書 (the entry signed 丸山雍成) and ブリタニカ国際大百科事典 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E5%8A%A9%E9%83%B7)

What it is: The Kotobank page for the sukego, the villages near a highway post station that supplied men and horses when the station's own were not enough, carrying two published works on the 1694 settlement that fixed the duty at two men and two horses per hundred koku of assessed yield, on the catchment beginning at two or three ri and widening past ten, and on its commutation into money.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the evidence that a trunk-road settlement swamped by arriving traffic did not answer with a bigger yard but by widening the ring it drew animals from, which is what withdraws this record's town-against-city contrast. Its limits are that these are tertiary summaries of published reference works; that they describe a corvee obligation rather than commercial stabling; and that the system is Tokugawa Japanese.

Used for: the neighboring villages supplying men and horses at two per hundred koku, and the catchment widened from two or three ri past ten

tokyo-archives-hirokoji

東京都公文書館 (Tokyo Metropolitan Archives), the publisher's page for 都史紀要42 The hirokoji of Edo: their use and their management (title translated from the Japanese by this project; original: 『江戸の広小路－その利用と管理』) (https://www.soumu.metro.tokyo.lg.jp/01soumu-archives/06kanko_butsu/0604t_kiyo/0604t_kiyo42)

What it is: The Tokyo Metropolitan Archives' own page for its published study of the Edo hirokoji, summarizing what those widened streets were - fire-clearance open ground on which no permanent building could stand - and what filled them: removable stall shops trading goods, markets, street performance and reed-screened entertainment booths, until many became pleasure quarters.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is the archive's own account of the firebreak this record describes and of the reason a cleared strip did not stay clear, which is the whole of what our entry on why no firebreak is drawn depends on. Its limits are that it is a publisher's summary of a book rather than the book; that it is Edo, the largest and most fire-prone city of the period, so the scale is a ceiling; and that it names no dimension for a strip.

Used for: the hirokoji as fire-clearance ground closed to permanent building, and the stalls, markets and booths that filled it

subai-ancient-city-sites

宿白 (Su Bai), "A preliminary investigation of ancient city sites within modern cities" (title translated from the Chinese by this project; original: 「現代城市中古代城址的初步考查」), published by the Peking University Institute of Humanities and Social Sciences and reproduced with attribution by the Institute of Archaeology and Cultural Heritage, Lanzhou University, 2024-04-22 (https://whyc.lzu.edu.cn/index.php/portal/article/index.html?cid=22&id=259)

What it is: Su Bai's own method for reading a Chinese city's older plan out of its modern street grid, illustrated across north China: the square city with one gate to a side and a great cross-street with a lesser cross in each quarter, the yamen and the market laid out in the middle of it, what a Ming prince's city had to demolish to stand on that ground, and the fixed corners that ritual buildings came to take. Su Bai (1922-2018) founded historical-period archaeology at Peking University.

Why it applies, and its limits: It is scholarship by the field's founder on exactly the question our government quarter answers, where a planned seat's compound stands, and it settles it with named cities rather than by assertion. Its limits are that it is a survey method illustrated from examples rather than a measured census; that the cities are mostly northern and mostly larger than a provincial seat; and that it supports the compound at the crossing without supporting the bureaus lining the avenues around it, which our record now says in so many words.

Used for: the square city's great cross and the yamen and market in the middle of it; the fixed southeast corner two Shanxi Confucian temples took

akiba-jinja-jawiki

ja.wikipedia 秋葉神社 (https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%A7%8B%E8%91%89%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE)

What it is: The Japanese Wikipedia article on the Akiba shrines, the fire-quelling cult whose small shrines are among the most widely distributed in Japan, noting that such a shrine is often built of stone because stone does not burn easily, that they are usually small, and that several of them may stand within a single town block.

Why it applies, and its limits: It gives the density our temple-quarter rule needs - several small shrines to one town block - and the reason a block would raise one, which is a placement fact a map can use. Its limits are that it is tertiary and describes one cult; that its statement about material runs against the vermilion wooden shed the map draws, which the record now labels a drawing convention on that evidence; and that it says nothing about a temple quarter, so the placement between temples remains unsupported.

Used for: the small neighborhood shrine, several to a town block, and the fire cult that explains why a block raised one

shichiya-kotobank

Kotobank, 質屋 - 世界大百科事典 and 日本大百科全書 (https://kotobank.jp/word/%E8%B3%AA%E5%B1%8B-73884)

What it is: The Kotobank page for the pawnbroker, carrying two published encyclopedias on the Edo-period trade as short-term lending on movable property, with counts: 2,700 pawnshops in eighteenth-century Edo, 2,731 in the Edo pawnbrokers' guild in 1723, 628 in Kyoto in 1699, and about 2,400 in Osaka at the end of the shogunate.

Why it applies, and its limits: It supplies the count a capital's amenity ratio is built from, given twice by two independent works, which is what turns a per-head figure from an assertion into arithmetic a reader can follow. Its limits are that these are tertiary summaries; that a guild roll counts members rather than premises; and that the page gives no population, so the one-per-so-many ratio this record quotes is our own division against a figure taken from elsewhere.

Used for: the Edo pawnshop count, at 2,700 in the eighteenth century and 2,731 in the 1723 guild, with Kyoto and Osaka beside it

Attested instances (anchors, not works)

Named real-world cases the rules are calibrated against. They are evidence, but they are measurements rather than publications, so they are listed separately and cited inline by name.

Anchor What it anchors
Suzugamori 74 x 16.2 m (~243 x 53 ft), serving Edo for 220 years - the execution-ground size anchor
Pingyao Market Tower attested at 133.4 m2 plan (~38 ft square); ~60 m mamian tower spacing - the wealthy-county-seat anchor
Xi'an mamian bastions ~20 m wide projecting ~12 m; ~120 m tower spacing (the peaceful tier)
Himeji moats averaging ~20 m (max 34.5 m) - the provincial-city moat tier
Osaka outer moat ~70-90 m - the grand-city moat tier, deliberately ABOVE our range
Fushimi Inari Senbon Torii: ~800 gates over ~400 m - the donation-row regime
Kasuga Taisha / Meiji Jingu / Nagao ranked ichi/ni/san-no-torii 200 m-1.3 km apart - the other regime
Northampton largest excavated urban tannery at 36-37 pits - far past anything in this pool
Longsheng largest terrace 0.62 mu (~0.10 acre); 15,862 terraces in one village
Edo Kokucho time bell billed ~400-410 blocks 'within earshot' - the bell-audibility anchor
Shunde county ~4.6% dike-pond in 1581 while containing townships already over 50% - the scatter was normal

Setting canon

l7r.md and budgets.md (the GM's own notes) are cited inline by filename rather than keyed here - they are canon rather than research, and an entry resting on them carries the setting-canon evidence class.
